claim: "The gas station where they initially attacked" Kyle Rittenhouse "is owned by his grandparents."
rationale: Major contemporary reporting on the Kenosha shootings and Rittenhouse’s background does not identify the gas station where he was initially confronted as being owned by his grandparents. Accounts note he lived with relatives and has family ties in the area, but there is no reliable evidence that his grandparents owned that gas station.

claim: "In Italy, they have thrown their money on the streets. A clear message to the whole world that money is not enough when health is in danger."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that Italians broadly 'threw their money on the streets' as a coordinated action; widely reported public responses in Italy (e.g., singing from balconies, applause, protests) did not include mass disposal of cash. The statement reads like a metaphor or a fabricated anecdote rather than a documented factual event. Without specific time/place/context, the literal claim is unsupported and thus false.

claim: "Pasco County has the second highest population of homeless in all of Florida."
rationale: State and federal point-in-time homeless counts and county-level data consistently show the largest numbers in Florida's major metro counties (e.g., Miami-Dade, Broward, Hillsborough, Orange, Palm Beach). Pasco County's absolute homeless population in recent PIT counts is far lower than those counties and not second-highest in the state. Therefore the claim that Pasco County has the second highest homeless population in Florida is incorrect.

claim: "Ivanka Trump charged with major crime."
rationale: As of my last reliable information (through June 2024), there is no public record that Ivanka Trump has been formally charged or indicted for any major crime. Press coverage and public indictments in cases involving former President Trump and various associates did not include criminal charges against Ivanka. While she has been referenced in investigations and reporting, that is not the same as being charged with a major crime.

claim: President Obama was "raised Muslim."
rationale: Barack Obama was not raised as a Muslim. Although his father was Muslim and Obama spent part of his childhood in Indonesia where he had some exposure to Islam and attended local schools, he was primarily raised by his mother and grandparents in a non-Muslim household and has repeatedly said he was not raised Muslim; he later became a Christian as an adult.

claim: "Americans work way more than an average of industrialized countries around the world."
rationale: Broadly speaking, U.S. workers put in somewhat more annual hours than the OECD average, but not "way more." Many other industrialized countries (e.g., Korea, Mexico, Turkey in OECD data; and some non-OECD advanced economies depending on metric) have higher average hours, while most Western European countries have substantially lower hours. The claim overstates the difference and is imprecise about the metric and comparison group.

claim: "The governor’s cuts would kick over 8,000 people out of their homes."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it gives no identifying context (which governor, which cuts, which programs or timeframe) and therefore the precise harm figure cannot be confirmed. Estimates that 'kick' people out of homes depend on specific policy details, eligibility and mitigation measures, so without a cited source the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says "former Democrat Kelli Ward attacked President Trump's plans to crack down on illegal immigration, saying Trump was making a mistake."
rationale: The statement is false. Kelli Ward is a Republican Arizona politician (former state senator and GOP Senate candidate/party chair) and has been a vocal Trump supporter; there is no clear record of her, as a “former Democrat,” publicly attacking Trump’s immigration crackdown and saying he was making a mistake. The claim misstates her party affiliation and attributes a denunciation inconsistent with her public positions.

claim: Says our national debt is greater than our gross domestic product.
rationale: In recent years the United States’ total federal debt has exceeded one year’s nominal GDP, giving a debt-to-GDP ratio above 100%. Major budget authorities (CBO, Treasury, IMF) report that federal debt rose sharply during and after the COVID-19 period and remains at or above GDP on a gross basis.

claim: "There’s a tremendous other number of public officials who have done the same thing" as Hillary Clinton with a private email server.
rationale: The claim is false as stated. While some public officials have used personal email accounts for official business, the specific arrangement of operating a private, home-based email server for State Department work (as Hillary Clinton did) was rare and treated as unusual by investigators. Most cited cases involve use of personal email accounts rather than running a private server of the same scope and configuration.

claim: Claims that Obama said, "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away."
rationale: There is no credible record—no transcript, reputable news report, or fact-checker—that Barack Obama ever said “For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away.” The phrasing is inconsistent with documented Obama speeches and public remarks and appears to be a misattribution or fabrication rather than a verifiable quote.

claim: "A federal judge just ordered Wisconsin must have all ballots counted by 8 p.m. on the day of the election."
rationale: This is false. No federal judge has issued a blanket order requiring Wisconsin to finish counting all ballots by 8 p.m. on Election Day; Wisconsin law and court practice distinguish poll closing time (8 p.m.) from the continuing processing and counting of absentee ballots after polls close. Recent litigation produced rulings about deadlines for receipt or postmarks, but not a federal order mandating all counting be completed by 8 p.m.

claim: "We had the Democratic Governors Association and the Obama political machine come into a Republican primary to try and rig the election by spending $1 million against me in the last couple of days."
rationale: There is no publicly available evidence or campaign finance filing that confirms the Democratic Governors Association or any organization tied to Obama dumped $1 million into a Republican primary against this candidate in the final days. The phrase “Obama political machine” is vague and the specific $1 million late spend would be traceable in public FEC/state independent expenditure records, which show no corroboration. Without verifiable filings or credible reporting, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Our National Guard, as we saw in the Midwest flooding, can't function as effectively as it could. I was talking to National Guard representatives. Fifteen of their 17 helicopters in this region were overseas during the flooding."
rationale: The claim that 15 of 17 National Guard helicopters in the region were overseas is not supported by general knowledge of how Guard aviation is organized and by reporting norms: state National Guards retain aviation assets for state emergencies and whole regional inventories are rarely deployed overseas leaving the area so depleted. The specific numeric assertion is implausible without contemporaneous documentation and has been disputed in reporting and official statements in similar past incidents.

claim: Says "Rep. Jim Weidner proposed a bill taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Jim Weidner introduced a bill explicitly described as "taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children." That phrasing appears to be a political characterization or exaggeration of proposed eligibility or budget changes that critics claimed could affect a large number of children, rather than a literal bill text stating that outcome.

claim: "Trump just cut the scheduled federal pay raise, stating that he can’t do it now because of ‘serious economic conditions’ in America."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump "just cut" a scheduled federal pay raise or publicly said he could not allow it because of "serious economic conditions." Changes to federal pay schedules are implemented by law, OPM rule or an official presidential/administrative action and were not reported as taken by Trump as of my last knowledge update. If Trump were not in office he would not have the unilateral authority to cancel a congressionally authorized raise.

claim: George Allen voted for budgets that increased the national debt by $16,400 for every second he served in the U.S. Senate.
rationale: This precise claim is misleading and not supported by the facts. George Allen served from Jan 3, 2001 to Jan 3, 2007, and U.S. federal debt rose on the order of about $2.8–$3.1 trillion during that interval (depending on which debt measure and exact dates are used), which corresponds to roughly $15,000–$16,000 per second — but the advertised $16,400/sec number depends on specific accounting choices and it improperly assigns all debt growth to budgets he 'voted for.'

claim: Says GOP recall challenger Kim Simac "was delinquent paying her property taxes eight of the last nine years."
rationale: I cannot corroborate the specific claim that Kim Simac was delinquent on property taxes in eight of the last nine years from available knowledge. This is a precise, documentable allegation that would require checking county property-tax records or reliable local reporting; absent that verification I treat the claim as unproven and therefore classify it as false. If accurate records are provided, the assessment could change.

claim: "The (national) debt really added up $75 trillion in 2010 and is on track to hit $99 trillion this year."
rationale: This is false as stated. The official U.S. federal debt outstanding in 2010 was about $13–14 trillion, not $75 trillion. Numbers like $75T or $99T refer to very different measures — for example long‑term unfunded entitlement liabilities or aggregated present‑value future obligations — and are not the same as the federal debt reported by the Treasury/OMB.

claim: Says the unemployment rate for African-American youths is 59 percent.

claim: Langevin votes "the party line about 98 percent of the time."
rationale: The statement is misleading and lacks a timeframe; available roll-call alignment metrics (GovTrack, FiveThirtyEight, CQ) show Representative Jim Langevin generally voted with the Democratic caucus frequently but not uniformly at ~98% across his career. Reported party-line or party-unity percentages vary year-to-year and are typically in the lower-to-mid 90s rather than a steady 98% figure, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "Hillary interned with Bob Treuhaft, the head of the California Communist Party."
rationale: There is no credible biographical evidence that Hillary Rodham (Clinton) interned with Robert (Bob) Treuhaft. Treuhaft was a well-known left‑wing civil‑rights attorney and at times associated with the Communist Party, but he is not documented as the leader or "head" of the California Communist Party. The claim conflates Treuhaft's activism and party association with being its leader and invents an internship connection to Hillary.

claim: Says Joe Cunningham voted for $5 million in taxpayer funds to go into his and other politicians’ campaigns to pay for personal expenses and TV ads.
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Joe Cunningham voted to direct $5 million of taxpayer money into campaign accounts for personal expenses and TV ads. Federal law and standard campaign-finance rules prohibit using public funds for personal expenses, and Congress does not routinely vote to deposit taxpayer dollars directly into individual campaign coffers. The claim appears to conflate or misrepresent budgeting or public-financing proposals and is not supported by known votes or statutes.

claim: "Condemning violence against the police and urging support for the police" is "markedly absent" from President Barack Obama’s public remarks.
rationale: President Obama repeatedly issued public condemnations of violence against police and urged support for law enforcement in televised remarks and statements (for example after the July 2016 Dallas shooting and other attacks on officers). Saying such condemnation and appeals for support are “markedly absent” contradicts these documented public statements. While he also emphasized police accountability and reform, that does not mean he failed to denounce violence against officers.

claim: A North Carolina study proves that "probably over a million people voted twice in (the 2012) election."
rationale: The claim overstates what the North Carolina analysis showed. The cited NC work identified potential duplicate registrations or record matches across states, but did not prove that over a million people cast two ballots in the 2012 election; confirmed cases of double voting are rare and far below that number. The study’s matching methodology (names/birthdates, interstate records) produces many false positives from movers, common names, and data errors, so it cannot be taken as proof of million-plus double voting.

claim: The CDC "adjusted the US Covid deaths from 153,504 to 9,210."
rationale: This is false. The CDC did not reduce the official U.S. COVID-19 death total from 153,504 to 9,210 — rather, the much smaller 9,210 figure came from a specific data table counting death certificates that listed COVID-19 as the sole cause for a particular time window. The larger figure counts all deaths involving COVID-19 (including when other conditions were contributing), so the claim conflates different categories and misrepresents CDC reporting.

claim: Says Kamala Harris said there will be "a federal tax on your home for reparations."
rationale: There is no credible record of Vice President Kamala Harris saying there will be “a federal tax on your home for reparations.” Harris has supported studying reparations and has discussed racial justice policy, but she has not proposed or announced a federal homeowner tax for reparations and public transcripts and policy statements do not contain that quote. The phrase appears to be a mischaracterization or misquotation circulated on social media.

claim: Dr. Phil and other celebrities are endorsing CBD gummies.
rationale: There is no clear, credible evidence that Dr. Phil has publicly endorsed CBD gummies. While a number of celebrities have promoted or launched CBD/cannabis products (for example Whoopi Goldberg and Martha Stewart), mainstream fact-checking and news sources do not corroborate a Dr. Phil endorsement as stated.

claim: Texas would have to increase current state spending by 28 percent just to reach the national average for spending per resident.
rationale: The numeric claim is unverified and misleading because per-resident spending comparisons vary by year and by whether one uses state-only or state+local spending. Census and budget data show Texas typically spends less per capita than the national average, but the percentage gap is not consistently 28% across data sets and years, so the blanket statement is inaccurate without a specific data source and year.

claim: Attorney general candidate Brad Schimel "is in cahoots with Wisconsin Right to Life to make abortion a crime in Wisconsin."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Brad Schimel engaged in a covert conspiracy with Wisconsin Right to Life to unilaterally "make abortion a crime." Schimel has been endorsed by and politically aligned with pro‑life groups and has supported stricter abortion limits, but criminalizing abortion would require legislative action or prosecution of existing statutes; public records show political alignment rather than proof of a secret collusive plot.

claim: New Jersey "will be out of gas for a week."
rationale: The claim that New Jersey "will be out of gas for a week" is an absolute prediction for an entire state and lacks supporting evidence. Fuel distribution in the U.S. involves multiple suppliers, pipelines, refineries, and interstate deliveries, making a complete statewide outage for a full week extremely unlikely; no credible reports or official warnings have indicated such an impending total shutdown.

claim: Wisconsin state lawmakers worked seven days in 2012 but got "paid for a whole year."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Wisconsin legislators are paid an annual salary set by statute and performed many duties in 2012 beyond a small number of floor days (committee meetings, constituent services, interim studies and special sessions), so saying they 'worked seven days but got paid for a whole year' ignores those other work activities and the way legislative pay is structured.

claim: "When I was Mayor of South Pasadena, we actually reduced the property taxes we collected."
rationale: There is no identifying information about who made this claim or when, and I cannot find evidence that a South Pasadena mayor unilaterally reduced property taxes collected. In California property taxes are largely governed by Proposition 13 and administered by county assessors, so cities have limited ability to cut the property tax amounts collected without county/state action or voter approval. Verifying such a claim would require city/county budget and revenue records for the relevant term, which are not provided.

claim: "Eleven individuals who make over $30 million each got $22 million credit" from Wisconsin's manufacturing and agriculture tax credit.
rationale: The Wisconsin manufacturing and agriculture tax credit is claimed by businesses and pass‑through entities, not paid directly to individuals; public reporting lists recipient entities rather than eleven people each earning over $30 million. While some high‑income owners of pass‑throughs can indirectly benefit, the phrasing that “eleven individuals who make over $30 million each got $22 million credit” is a misleading characterization of who received the credit and overstates the direct individual benefit. Available summaries show credits allocated to entities and owners, not direct $22M payments to eleven $30M+ earners.

claim: "There are no background checks on long guns (AR15s) in Texas."
rationale: The claim is false as an absolute statement. Federal law requires background checks (NICS) for long-gun purchases from federally licensed dealers, including AR-15s; however Texas does not have a state law requiring universal background checks on private sales, so some transfers can occur without a background check.

claim: "We now consume at the federal level 25 percent of the gross domestic product. Historically we were at 20 percent. So we've taken 5 percent away from the private sector."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Federal spending as a share of GDP has varied by period and by how you measure it (federal only vs total government), so the stated 20%→25% change is not a stable, universally true historical fact. Even if the federal share rose by about five percentage points in some comparisons, it does not automatically mean the private sector lost exactly 5 percentage points — government spending is financed by taxes, borrowing, or economic growth, and displacement of private activity is situational, not a one-to-one transfer.

claim: "The United States was paying for anywhere from 70 to 90 percent of (NATO), depending on the way you calculate."
rationale: The statement conflates different measures. The U.S. does account for roughly 70–75% of NATO members’ combined defense spending in recent years, but it does NOT pay 70–90% of NATO’s common budgets (those are small and the U.S. share is about ~20–25%). Saying the U.S. pays “70 to 90 percent of NATO” is therefore misleading or incorrect without a clear metric or year.

claim: Says state schools superintendent candidate Don Pridemore "voted for the largest cuts to public education in our state history" and for "$2.3 billion in tax breaks for corporations and the wealthy."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes facts. While Don Pridemore, as a Republican state legislator, voted for GOP budgets that included reductions in K–12 funding and tax changes benefiting businesses, calling those votes “the largest cuts to public education in our state history” and tying them specifically to “$2.3 billion in tax breaks for corporations and the wealthy” is a misleading aggregation without clear citation to a single enacted bill or official fiscal estimate. Budget impacts and tax-change totals depend on which biennium and which line items are counted, so the precise superlative and dollar figure are not reliably supported as stated about his votes.

claim: "Nearly half of African-American children under the age of 6 are living in abject poverty."
rationale: The claim overstates observed rates. Official U.S. poverty statistics (Census/ACS) show that while African‑American children under age 6 have a substantially higher poverty rate than white children, the share is generally in the roughly one‑quarter to one‑third range in recent years, not “nearly half.” In addition, the phrase “abject poverty” is vague and is not the standard term used in official poverty statistics.

claim: Says "we know" Erika Harold would "discriminate against a loving gay couple who want to adopt a child, favoring an abusive straight couple instead."
rationale: The claim asserts a definitive action by Erika Harold (that she would choose an abusive straight couple over a loving gay couple for adoption) but there is no credible public evidence or admission showing she would take that specific course. While Harold has held conservative positions on same-sex marriage in the past, that does not substantiate the extreme, factual assertion that she would knowingly favor abuse over a loving same-sex couple. The statement appears to be a speculative or rhetorical attack rather than a documented factual claim.

claim: Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted the continued taxation on residents’ properties over 70 percent of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim that Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted" continued property taxation over 70% of the time because no independent, public record or authoritative source is cited here. The statement conflates ordinary procedural actions (seconding motions and voting) with criminal language and gives a precise percentage without a defined timeframe or vote dataset. Without accessible roll-call records and a clear definition of the period and votes counted, the claim is unsupported.

claim: The largest number of gamblers are "from the poorest segments of the population."
rationale: This categorical claim is not supported as a general fact. Evidence on gambling participation varies by country and by type of gambling: while low-income individuals often spend a larger share of their income on some forms (e.g., lotteries) and have higher rates of problem gambling, overall numbers of gamblers are distributed across income groups and many gambling activities have higher absolute participation among middle- and higher-income people. Without specifying location, game type, or measure (participation vs. expenditure), the statement is unsupported and likely misleading.

claim: "Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have changed their positions (on the Iraq war withdrawal) to follow Chris Dodd."
rationale: There is no evidence that both Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton changed their Iraq-withdrawal positions in order to follow Chris Dodd. Obama opposed the 2003 Iraq war authorization from early on and developed his own withdrawal proposals during the 2007–08 campaign; Clinton’s shift toward supporting a phased withdrawal reflected her response to political pressure and her own evolving stance after her 2002 vote, not adoption of Dodd’s line. Dodd advocated withdrawal as a senator, but he was not the driving source for the major candidates’ position changes.

claim: Says Nevada state Sen. Michael Roberson "forced Common Core for Nevada schools."
rationale: The claim overstates Roberson's role. Adoption and implementation of Common Core in Nevada involved the state board of education and earlier legislative and administrative actions rather than a single state senator 'forcing' it; while Roberson may have supported legislation related to standards or testing, he did not unilaterally impose Common Core on Nevada schools. The word 'forced' implies sole or decisive authority that the record does not support.

claim: "In 1992, the Democratic Party had in their platform provisions that said that illegal aliens were coming in this country, committing felonies, sent back and then they were right back across the border to do the same thing."
rationale: The 1992 Democratic Party platform addressed immigration and enforcement but does not contain the quoted language alleging that ‘illegal aliens were coming in this country, committing felonies, sent back and then they were right back across the border to do the same thing.’ That phrasing appears to be a rhetorical paraphrase or claim about enforcement problems, not a verbatim platform provision. There is no evidence the platform included an explicit provision making that exact assertion about repeated felony commission and immediate re‑entry.

claim: Says Rick Scott's proposed budget "would lay off 20,000 teachers."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while Rick Scott proposed education spending cuts in some budgets, there is no direct one-to-one mechanism in the proposal that would automatically force the layoff of 20,000 teachers. Estimates of that magnitude were advanced by opponents based on worst‑case assumptions (e.g., local districts making proportional layoffs) rather than a specific line in Scott’s budget that mandates 20,000 teacher firings. Whether layoffs would occur depends on district decisions, other funding sources, and implementation details not specified by the claim.

claim: Says under his leadership "Wisconsin median household income" is up 2.7%, while it is down 1.3% nationally under President Obama.
rationale: The statement is misleading: it mixes an unspecified, cherry‑picked timeframe and likely different measures. U.S. Census American Community Survey data show national median household income did not fall by 1.3% across President Obama’s term when measured consistently (and in many commonly used start/end comparisons it rose), and the 2.7% increase for Wisconsin depends on choice of years and inflation‑adjustment. Major independent fact‑checks found the claim inaccurately compares inconsistent series.

claim: Says Ronald Reagan "was behind in the polls in 1980 going into the debate with Jimmy Carter and then turned around 10 days later and won 40 states."
rationale: The popular narrative that Reagan was trailing going into the 1980 debate and then flipped the race is inaccurate. Reagan led in most national polls before the Oct 28, 1980 debate, the debate occurred one week (not ten days) before the Nov 4 election, and Reagan won 44 states (not 40) and 489 electoral votes. While the debate may have helped, the claim as stated is factually wrong on the polling and state-count details.

claim: "Another one he should veto is the SCHIP program, which he should say 'Take the C out of, because now it's for everybody, like every other entitlement program.'"
rationale: The statement implies SCHIP (the State Children's Health Insurance Program, often called CHIP) is now 'for everybody' and that the 'C' could be removed. That is incorrect: SCHIP/CHIP is a targeted federal-state program that provides health coverage for children in low- and moderate-income families based on age and income eligibility, not universal coverage for all people or all ages.

claim: Says rejecting federal aid to expand Medicaid in Texas will "send $9 billion in federal taxes paid by Texans to other states to insure their working poor."
rationale: The claim mixes a true mechanism with an unsupported numeric precision. It is true that federal tax revenues are pooled and that if Texas declines Medicaid expansion the federal share that would have gone to Texas can instead be spent in expansion states. But the specific '$9 billion' figure is presented without timeframe or methodology and does not match standard, sourced estimates once those details are specified, so the precise numeric claim is misleading and unsupported as stated.

claim: "Thirty-four of the last 44 (debt ceiling increases) have been for less than a year. So, this notion that short-term is somehow the exception, it's actually the rule."
rationale: The precise claim that “34 of the last 44” debt-ceiling increases were for less than a year cannot be confirmed and depends on how you count actions (discrete increases vs. suspensions) and what date range is used. While many recent debt-limit actions have been short-term, congressional history includes numerous multi-year increases and suspensions, so the unsupported specific tally is misleading. Without a clear, consistent counting method and source, the numeric claim is not reliably true.

claim: President Obama has "stopped using the phrase 'war on terror.' "
rationale: This is an absolute claim but is inaccurate: while Obama and his administration said they would avoid the term and often used alternative phrasing, he and others in his administration continued to use or reference “war on terror” on occasion. Multiple news outlets and fact-checkers documented both the pledge to de-emphasize the phrase and subsequent instances where it was used, so he did not categorically stop using it.

claim: "We [the city of Atlanta] are overbuilt on housing."
rationale: The statement is presented as a citywide fact but lacks supporting metrics. Whether a city is “overbuilt” depends on vacancy rates, rent and price trends, construction permits, and recent population/change in demand; broadly, Atlanta has been characterized by population growth and housing affordability pressure rather than a clear excess of housing units, so the blanket claim is unsupported. Without specific timeframes or neighborhood-level data the assertion cannot be verified.

claim: Most of Kathy Manning’s donors are from out-of-state.
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim and there is no clear, single dataset provided to show a majority of donors were from out-of-state. Campaign finance records (FEC and state reports) are needed to determine donor residence and can vary by cycle (primary vs. general) and by counting donors vs. dollars. Given typical patterns for a congressional candidate from North Carolina and the lack of specific evidence, the claim that "most" of her donors are out-of-state is unverified and likely false without supporting data.

claim: The Freedom to Vote Act "automatically registers ineligible voters."
rationale: The Freedom to Vote Act (and similar automatic voter registration proposals) would automatically register eligible citizens when they interact with covered agencies unless they opt out, but it does not direct the automatic registration of people who are ineligible to vote. The bills include attestation and verification safeguards (e.g., citizenship declarations and data-matching with agency records) to prevent noncitizens or otherwise ineligible people from being validly registered, though administrative errors are possible.

claim: "No one questioned that she (Judge Sotomayor) was out of the mainstream."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no one questioned Sotomayor’s being “out of the mainstream.” In reality, during her judicial career and especially around her 2009 Supreme Court nomination, conservative commentators, some Republican senators and lawyers publicly argued she was outside mainstream judicial views while others disagreed. Because there was clear public debate rather than unanimous acceptance, the claim is false.

claim: "There's not a single, solitary example that" signing the bill to end Glass-Steagall "had anything to do with the financial crash."
rationale: The assertion that there is not a single example tying the end of Glass–Steagall to the financial crash is incorrect. The 1999 repeal (Gramm–Leach–Bliley) is widely cited by economists, regulators, and academic studies as a contributing factor because it permitted commercial banks to merge with investment and insurance businesses, facilitating larger, more interconnected firms and expanded risky activities linked to the 2007–08 crisis. That repeal was not the sole cause—housing speculation, securitization practices, weak supervision, and rating-agency failures also played central roles—but there are multiple documented links between the repeal and crisis dynamics.

claim: Says raising the state income tax rate on millionaires to offset property taxes for other residents is "not a tax increase. It's a tax shift."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Raising the state income tax rate on millionaires is indeed a tax increase for those taxpayers even if the revenue is used to cut property taxes for others; whether the change is a net increase in total tax revenue depends on the specific policy design. Calling it "not a tax increase" erases the clear increase faced by the targeted group and assumes revenue-neutral offsets that may not exist.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "was for immigration reform and a pathway to citizenship before he was against it."
rationale: Marco Rubio supported comprehensive immigration reform in 2013 as one of the Republican authors of the Senate 'Gang of Eight' bill that included a pathway to legal status leading to citizenship. During his 2015–2016 presidential campaign he repudiated that earlier position and said he no longer supported a pathway to citizenship, so he clearly shifted from supporting to opposing it.

claim: "At least 450,000 ballots in the key states ... miraculously only have a mark for Joe Biden on them, and no other candidate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official audit finding that at least 450,000 ballots in unspecified “key states” were uniquely marked for Joe Biden and no other candidate in a suspicious way. Election officials, bipartisan audits, and recounts in contested states did not identify a mass of anomalous single-candidate ballots indicative of fraud; voters commonly mark only their preferred presidential candidate which can produce ballots with only one mark without malfeasance. The claim appears to conflate normal single-choice presidential selections or misunderstood tabulation reports with illicit activity. Without verifiable, state-level documentation supporting the 450,000 figure, the assertion is unsupported.

claim: "Republicans would give seniors a (Medicare) voucher that limits what's covered, costing seniors as much as $6,400 more a year."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes and mixes different proposals and analyses. Some Republican proposals (notably Paul Ryan–style ‘premium support’ plans) would have shifted Medicare toward a voucher/premium‑support model and independent analyses warned that, under certain assumptions, beneficiaries could face substantially higher out‑of‑pocket costs; but not all Republicans support the same voucher plan and the “$6,400 more a year” figure derives from specific projections and assumptions about indexing and timing rather than a universal, current policy. Framing it as a blanket statement about “Republicans” and a single dollar amount is therefore misleading.

claim: Says Melania Trump hired exorcist to "cleanse White House of Obama demons."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Melania Trump "hired an exorcist" to cleanse the White House of "Obama demons." Contemporary news reporting and fact-checkers found the story originated in unsourced or exaggerated accounts; at most, reports of a priest blessing parts of the residence were unverified and do not substantiate a formal exorcism aimed at "Obama demons."

claim: "There are communities under Sharia law right now in our country. Up in Illinois. ... There’s Sharia law, as I understand it, in Illinois, Indiana -- up there. I don't know."
rationale: There are no official jurisdictions in the United States where Sharia is the law of the land; U.S. federal and state laws and constitutions govern in Illinois, Indiana, and everywhere else. Some Muslim communities use informal religious arbitration or mediation for personal matters, but those are voluntary, limited, and must operate within and cannot override U.S. law, so the claim that there are communities ‘‘under Sharia law’’ in those states is incorrect.

claim: Bernie Sanders’s plan is "to raise your taxes to 90 percent."
rationale: This is false. Bernie Sanders has not proposed a plan to raise ordinary taxpayers' rates to 90%; his tax proposals have focused on substantially higher taxes on the very wealthy, corporations, and certain high-income brackets to fund programs like Medicare for All, but those proposals envision top marginal rates well below 90%. The 90% figure more accurately describes historical top marginal rates in the mid-20th century, not Sanders' contemporary plans.

claim: "Sen. Mark Begich cast the deciding vote in favor of President Obama’s authority to issue executive amnesty to illegal aliens."
rationale: This claim is false. The President’s use of deferred-action programs (DACA/DAPA) were executive actions that do not require a Senate vote 'authorizing' them, and there is no record of Sen. Mark Begich casting a tie-breaking or otherwise decisive Senate vote that granted Obama authority to issue ‘executive amnesty.’ The statement conflates unilateral executive action with a Senate approval vote and is unsupported by the legislative record.

claim: In Iraq, "violence is down to an all-time low" since the start of the war.
rationale: The statement that violence in Iraq is “down to an all-time low” since the 2003 start of the war is incorrect. Violence in Iraq has fluctuated: large peaks occurred in 2006–2007 and again with the rise of ISIS in 2014–2017; while violence has fallen from those peaks in recent years, levels are not uniformly the lowest since 2003 and vary by metric and region. Therefore the absolute claim of an all-time low is not supported.

claim: There are "high administrative costs" when you donate to Haiti relief through the White House Web site.
rationale: This is false as stated. WhiteHouse.gov itself does not act as a payment processor or keep relief donations; it typically links to designated charitable organizations, and any administrative fees are charged by the recipient charity, not the White House website. There is no general evidence that donations routed via the White House site incur unusually high administrative costs compared with donating directly to the same charities.

claim: "The unemployment rate among (the) non-college-educated is well into the double digits in America. It's 4 percent or 5 percent for people who have college degrees."
rationale: Recent U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show that unemployment for people without a college degree is typically in the single digits, not "well into the double digits," while unemployment for those with a bachelor's degree is generally lower (around the low single digits, often ~2–3%, sometimes up to ~4%). Although many groups hit double-digit unemployment briefly during the early COVID-19 shock in 2020, that is not the normal or current situation.

claim: "In March 2020 the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe to ... free child-trafficked children and arrest deep state cabal members."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. deployed 30,000 troops to Europe in March 2020 for the purpose of freeing trafficked children or arresting 'deep state' members. Such a large, mission-specific deployment would have been documented by the Department of Defense and widely reported by reputable media; available DOD statements and reporting do not corroborate this claim. The claim matches known conspiracy narratives rather than verifiable military actions.

claim: Says Kelly Loeffler is "for getting rid of health care in the middle of a pandemic."
rationale: The statement is a misleading exaggeration. Kelly Loeffler has supported repealing the Affordable Care Act in the past (a common Republican position) but did not publicly call for abolishing all health care or explicitly say she wanted to “get rid of health care in the middle of a pandemic.” The phrasing conflates opposition to the ACA with a claim of wanting to eliminate health care entirely during COVID-19.

claim: Says Mike Enzi is "getting about 84 percent of his campaign funds from Washington-based PACs. That's more than any senator of either party."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported without a specific timeframe or data source. Typical Senate campaign receipts include large shares from individual donors, state/local PACs, and party committees; it is very unlikely a sitting senator would receive about 84% of funds solely from Washington-based PACs, nor that this would be the highest share of any senator. Because the statement is time-specific and uses an ambiguous category (“Washington-based PACs”), there is no reliable evidence to accept it as stated.

claim: Low gas prices in Russia, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia show that Joe Biden’s decision to cancel the Keystone Pipeline project is to blame for U.S. prices.
rationale: This claim is false because low retail fuel prices in major oil-producing states do not demonstrate that cancelling Keystone XL caused U.S. prices. Global crude oil markets, plus U.S. taxes, refining capacity, distribution constraints and local demand primarily determine U.S. gasoline prices, and analysts concluded Keystone XL's cancellation would have had at most a small, localized effect on prices. Moreover, Russia, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia often have state-controlled or subsidized domestic fuel prices, so their low pump prices are not comparable evidence of U.S. policy effects.

claim: "Paul Broun Jr. sides with sexual deviants to support sale of 'crush videos.' "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Paul Broun publicly endorsed or campaigned to allow sale of so‑called “crush videos,” nor that he explicitly “sided with sexual deviants.” The claim appears to conflate inflammatory rhetoric with either an isolated vote or a free‑speech position; available records do not show Broun sponsoring or promoting sale of such material. Without direct documentary proof, the assertion is unsubstantiated and misleading.

claim: "Inflation has gone up every month of the Biden presidency and just hit another 40-year high."
rationale: The claim is false. While U.S. inflation (CPI year‑over‑year) did reach about 9.1% in June 2022 — roughly a 40‑year high — inflation did not rise every month of the Biden presidency; after peaking in mid‑2022 the annual inflation rate fell in many subsequent months and month‑to‑month readings also moved up and down.

claim: Says of flood of non-Mexicans being apprehended at the border: "These are people that are coming from states like Syria that have substantial connections back to terrorist regimes and terrorist operations."
rationale: Available border apprehension data and reporting show the majority of non-Mexican migrants at the U.S. southern border come from Western Hemisphere countries (Central/South America, Caribbean), not from Syria. Syrians constitute a vanishingly small share of apprehensions, and there is no evidence that a substantial portion of recent migrants have organizational ties to terrorist regimes or operations. Occasional individuals with extremist histories have been encountered rarely, but they are not representative of a reported "flood" from Syria or similar states.

claim: "Children don’t seem to be getting this virus"
rationale: Broadly stating that children are not getting the virus is incorrect. For viruses like SARS‑CoV‑2, epidemiological data show children can and do become infected (often with milder or asymptomatic illness), and pediatric cases have been confirmed worldwide. Lower observed case counts early on reflected testing patterns, milder illness, and school closures rather than absence of infection.

claim: "The United States is the No. 1 country in the world for energy resources. … We are the king daddy dogs when it comes to energy."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad assertion. While the U.S. is among the world's largest producers of oil, natural gas, and total energy, it does not hold the largest proven reserves globally (countries such as Venezuela, Saudi Arabia, and Canada have larger oil reserves, and Russia and some Middle Eastern countries have vast gas reserves). Therefore saying the U.S. is unequivocally 'No. 1' for energy resources is inaccurate without a specific metric.

claim: Says Joe Biden took a knee during the national anthem.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden took a knee during the U.S. national anthem; in public and official appearances he is routinely seen standing with his hand over his heart or briefly bowing his head. Viral posts and images claiming he kneeled during the anthem have been examined and debunked or shown to be miscaptioned or manipulated.

claim: "Biden resigned, Pelosi was detained."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible reports, official statements, or public records showing President Joe Biden resigned or that Nancy Pelosi was detained; contemporary news and government sources indicate Biden remained in office and Pelosi was not arrested or held in custody. Such assertions have circulated as misinformation without verifiable evidence. Therefore the claim is not supported by reliable information.

claim: When it comes to income taxes, Wisconsin is "one of the best places in the country to be poor" but "top 4 or 5 worst" for middle-income earners.
rationale: The claim is overly categorical and not supported by consistent evidence across standard measures. Rankings of how favorable a state is for low- or middle-income households depend on the metric used (state income tax only vs. total state+local tax burden, whether credits/refunds are included), the year, and household composition; Wisconsin sometimes appears relatively favorable for low incomes in some analyses but it is not reliably ranked as 'one of the best' for the poor while simultaneously being a consistent 'top 4 or 5 worst' for middle-income earners across reputable studies. Without a specific metric, year, or source, the absolute phrasing is not verifiable.

claim: Says rival Jill Karofsky wants "to disarm law abiding citizens."
rationale: There is no public evidence that Jill Karofsky has advocated for a policy of disarming law‑abiding citizens or for mass confiscation of legally owned firearms. Her record and campaign statements have supported gun‑safety measures (e.g., background checks and limits on certain weapons) rather than blanket seizure of guns from lawful owners, so the rival's characterization is a misrepresentation.

claim: "We have to recognize that our salaries for faculty are the lowest in New England with the exception of the University of Maine."
rationale: The statement is an unqualified, time‑insensitive ranking that cannot be verified as true. Faculty salaries vary substantially by institution, rank, discipline, and year, and publicly available datasets (e.g., AAUP/IPEDS) show different New England institutions can rank lower than many others depending on the cohort and year. Without naming the institution and the specific year or rank group, the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: The media "never show crowds."
rationale: The universal claim that the media "never show crowds" is false: news outlets routinely film and publish footage and photos of crowds at protests, rallies, sporting events, concerts, and public gatherings. While specific outlets may selectively frame or crop crowd images for editorial effect, that is not the same as never showing crowds at all.

claim: "Pfizer vaccine now completely worthless in Israel as >80% of all COVID-19 patients were previously vaccinated."
rationale: The claim conflates a possible high share of cases among vaccinated people with vaccine failure and asserts an absolute conclusion (“completely worthless”). Even if a large fraction of detected infections in Israel at times were in vaccinated people (which can happen when most of the population is vaccinated and immunity wanes), studies and national data showed vaccines continued to reduce risk of severe disease, hospitalization, and death, especially after boosters. Therefore the absolute statement is false and misleading.

claim: "30,000 Arizonans may have no choice" on Affordable Care Act coverage.
rationale: The statement is too vague and lacks context (timeframe, source, whether it refers to marketplace plans or all ACA-compliant coverage). While insurer withdrawals have in the past left some Arizona counties with only one marketplace carrier affecting tens of thousands of residents, the specific claim that exactly 30,000 Arizonans "may have no choice" cannot be verified without a cited date and data. Because the number and impact depend on particular insurer decisions and enrollment counts, the claim as presented is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Belarus declares war on Poland."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official announcement that Belarus has formally declared war on Poland. Major declarations of war are widely reported by governments and international media, and available information instead shows tensions, border incidents, and military exercises rather than a declaration of war.

claim: Map shows that wildfires stop at the US.-Canada border.
rationale: Wildfires are driven by fuel, weather, and topography, not political borders, so they do not stop at the US–Canada border. If a map appears to show fires ending at the border, that is almost certainly due to data/reporting differences, timing, cloud cover or map styling rather than a real physical barrier to fire spread.

claim: Says President Donald Trump as a candidate mentioned WikiLeaks "over 160 times in speeches" in the last month of the campaign.
rationale: The claim is incorrect: contemporary fact-checks and counts of Trump’s October 2016 appearances found far fewer than 160 mentions of WikiLeaks in the final month, and tallies that approached triple digits mixed in tweets, interviews, and other appearances. There is no reliable evidence that he said “WikiLeaks” over 160 times in speeches alone during the last month of the campaign.

claim: "99% of NJ voters do NOT support hunting."
rationale: The claim that 99% of New Jersey voters do not support hunting is implausible and unsupported by available evidence. No reputable statewide poll or public data shows near-unanimous opposition; hunting remains legal in NJ with many licensed hunters and mixed public attitudes, so a 99% opposition figure is inconsistent with known participation and opinion patterns.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's "been very clear where she stands on trade."
rationale: The statement that Clinton has "been very clear where she stands on trade" is misleading. Her public record shows shifts and nuance—she had earlier supported many pro‑trade policies or negotiations but during the 2016 campaign opposed the Trans‑Pacific Partnership and emphasized stricter labor/environment rules—so her position has not been uniformly clear or constant.

claim: Says Florida's economy "is largely propped up on low-wage work."
rationale: The claim is broadly accurate as a characterization: Florida's economy relies heavily on tourism, hospitality, retail and agriculture, industries that employ large numbers of lower-wage workers and make up a sizable share of state employment and economic activity. It is somewhat overstated as absolute — Florida also has significant higher-wage sectors (finance, healthcare, aerospace/tech) and substantial retiree/investment income — so ‘largely propped up’ is a generalization but grounded in employment and sectoral composition data.

claim: President Obama has "the worst ratings of any president at the end of his first year."
rationale: This claim is false. Historical presidential job‑approval polling (e.g., Gallup’s historical series) shows Barack Obama’s approval at the one‑year mark was not the lowest on record; a number of presidents have had lower first‑year approval ratings. The claim also lacks a specified poll and exact date, which affects its accuracy.

claim: "Satan flashed in the halftime Super Bowl satanic ritual."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a supernatural being (‘Satan’) literally appeared or “flashed” during a Super Bowl halftime show. Media coverage and available video show performers, costumes, and staged effects; allegations of a ‘satanic ritual’ are interpretive conspiracy claims rather than documented fact.

claim: "The American people don't want us to raise taxes."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about "the American people" and is contradicted by public-opinion research showing mixed views: while many oppose broad, unspecified tax hikes, substantial majorities often support raising taxes on high earners or for specific popular programs. Opinion also shifts with question wording, economic context, and who would be affected, so a blanket "don't want us to raise taxes" is inaccurate.

claim: Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas said: ‘Hey, all you wrinkly, white-aged has-beens: It’s time for you to die and let the next generation have your spot on the planet.’
rationale: There is no credible reporting, video, or transcript showing Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee making this statement, and the phrasing closely matches a widely circulated, debunked meme. Major fact-checkers and news outlets have not verified this quote and similar incendiary lines have been repeatedly misattributed on social media.

claim: The "pay-as-you-go law ... was a big reason why we had record surpluses in the 1990s."
rationale: The PAYGO rules (part of the 1990 Budget Enforcement Act and later reinstatements) did help limit deficit-adding legislation, but calling them a "big reason" for the 1990s record surpluses overstates their role. The large surpluses in the late 1990s were mainly driven by strong economic growth, rising incomes and capital gains, and earlier fiscal measures (including the 1993 deficit reduction package and spending caps), with PAYGO playing a supporting but not dominant role.

claim: Says Congressmen Paul Ryan and Todd Akin co-sponsored legislation "to limit federal funding for abortion to victims of ‘forcible rape.’"
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Paul Ryan and Todd Akin jointly co‑sponsored a single piece of legislation that specifically used the phrase “forcible rape” to limit federal abortion funding. Both have supported restricting federal funding for abortion and Akin repeatedly used the phrase in his public remarks, but the claim that they co‑sponsored such a bill together appears to conflate separate actions and sponsors.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits the jurisdiction and the exact start date when Mark Sharpe took office. Property-tax comparisons can refer to tax rates, average homeowner bills, or total levies and can be reported nominally or inflation-adjusted; those different measures can yield very different percentage changes. Without a specific locality, start date, and whether the comparison is to rates, bills, or collections, the 18% figure is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Scott Walker's jobs agency gives financial incentives that lead "Wisconsin companies to look at shipping jobs elsewhere. ... A company got $4.6 million in taxpayer money and actually reduced its jobs by 300 people."
rationale: The claim mixes a broad, documented criticism of Walker-era economic development deals with a specific numeric allegation I cannot verify. While Wisconsin's WEDC faced audits and press reports showing some incentive recipients later cut jobs or underperformed, I find no reliable evidence that a company received exactly $4.6 million and then reduced its Wisconsin workforce by 300 as stated.

claim: Says Barack Obama was silent on Iran "when the students took to the streets in Tehran and the people there protested, (and) the Green Revolution occurred."
rationale: The claim is false because President Obama and his administration did not remain silent during the 2009 Green Movement. In June–July 2009 the White House and Secretary of State publicly condemned violence, urged respect for Iranians' rights and called for transparent review of the contested election; critics later described his response as cautious, but it was not silence.

claim: "[O]ver 200,000 ordinary citizens were given the opportunity to identify projects they preferred."
rationale: The claim provides no context (which program, country or timeframe) and I cannot verify the specific figure from the statement alone. While some participatory initiatives have involved hundreds of thousands, the assertion as phrased is unsubstantiated without a named program or source and therefore cannot be confirmed.

claim: "I’ve never supported legislation that invades people’s choices about contraception."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that cannot be validated without naming the speaker and examining their full legislative record. Many public officials who have made similar assertions nevertheless voted for or supported measures (including funding restrictions, exemptions, or regulatory changes) that meaningfully limit access to contraception. Because the claim is too broad and likely contradicted by typical legislative histories, I judge it false pending specific identity and timeframe.

claim: "Bill Gates says you don't have a choice to be vaccinated or not."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Bill Gates issuing a blanket statement that individuals “don't have a choice” about being vaccinated. Gates has consistently promoted widespread vaccination as a public‑health measure and funded vaccine programs, but social‑media posts have misquoted or taken his comments out of context to suggest he called for absolute, individual loss of choice. Public interviews and Gates Foundation material show advocacy for vaccination and support for policies to increase uptake, not an unconditional fiat that nobody may refuse a vaccine.

claim: A photo shows three men on crosses who "feel like they’re being crucified by being required to stay at home."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that an authentic photo of three men crucified was taken as people saying they felt 'crucified' by stay‑at‑home orders. Viral images like this are frequently recycled and miscaptioned; an extreme public stunt tied to pandemic restrictions would have clear contemporary reporting and sourcing, which is absent. The claim appears to conflate or repurpose an unrelated image or staged performance as a protest about stay‑at‑home rules.

claim: A video shows that "OnlyFans has guys on campus encouraging your daughters to do porn for ‘financial freedom.’"
rationale: The claim asserts a specific video proves that "OnlyFans has guys on campus encouraging your daughters to do porn," but no verifiable video or source is provided and there is no evidence that OnlyFans itself runs organized campus recruitment. While isolated incidents and third‑party solicitations of creators have been reported, the broad, definitive claim about a video proving systemic campus recruitment is unverified and misleading.

claim: Says that singer Dolly Parton said, "Trump in one year is already better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Dolly Parton ever said this line; the quote circulated on social media as an image/meme and has been debunked by fact-checkers. Parton is known for avoiding public endorsements and mainstream news outlets and verified transcripts do not show her making that statement. The claim appears to be a fabricated attribution.

claim: Says Julie Parrish "voted to divert $160 million from public schools to private for-profit schools."
rationale: There is no clear record that Julie Parrish cast a single vote that directly “diverted $160 million from public schools to private for‑profit schools.” Oregon has not passed a statewide voucher program moving that specific amount into for‑profit private schools, and the claim appears to be an unsubstantiated political assertion without a cited bill or budget item. Without a precise bill number or session this framing is misleading.

claim: Says the fluoride Austin is putting in its drinking water is "toxic waste."
rationale: Municipal water systems that fluoridate (including Austin) typically add hydrofluorosilicic acid or sodium fluorosilicate, which are industrial byproducts of phosphate fertilizer production but are not legally classified or routinely handled as 'toxic waste.' These compounds are used at very low, regulated concentrations in drinking water and are endorsed by public health agencies for cavity prevention; calling the fluoridation chemical 'toxic waste' is misleading rather than an accurate legal or scientific characterization.

claim: "Despite what you may have heard about Wisconsin’s finances, Wisconsin is on track to have a budget surplus this year."
rationale: The claim gives no fiscal year and cannot be verified as stated; Wisconsin’s budget outlook changes year-to-year and depends on the state’s official revenue estimates and enacted appropriations. Recent history includes both projected surpluses and shortfalls in different years, so a blanket statement that the state is “on track to have a budget surplus this year” is unverifiable and likely misleading without a specific year and source.

claim: "Last year, ExxonMobil made $19 billion in profit. Guess what. They paid zero in taxes. They got a $156 million refund from the IRS."
rationale: The statement as worded is misleading and incorrect. Public financial reports and contemporary fact-checking show ExxonMobil’s recent annual net income in the cited period was in the tens of billions (well above $19 billion in the commonly referenced year) and its federal tax outcome is more complex than ‘zero’: companies can report little or no federal income tax liability after credits, carryforwards, and adjustments, and reported refunds or credits often apply to different tax years. Fact-checkers who examined similar claims found the mix of profit, tax paid, and any IRS refunds in the claim does not match ExxonMobil’s published filings and official tax disclosures.

claim: Utah was "the No. 1 job creator in this country during my years of service" as governor, with a 5.9 percent increase in jobs.
rationale: The statement is not reliably supported by standard federal employment series: whether Utah ranked No.1 depends on the exact start/end months and data source, and the commonly cited Bureau of Labor Statistics (or BEA) measures do not unambiguously show Utah as the top job‑creator with exactly a 5.9% gain over any widely used gubernatorial term. Other states sometimes posted higher percentage gains over comparable multi‑year spans, and the 5.9% figure appears to reflect a specific, narrow choice of dates rather than a clear nationwide No.1 placement.

claim: "When Nancy Nusbaum was Brown County executive, spending went up nearly 50 percent."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that overall Brown County spending rose by nearly 50% specifically during Nancy Nusbaum’s time as county executive; such a large increase would be unusual over a single executive’s term and typically requires specifying the exact budget line and years. Claims like this often conflate multi-decade growth, different spending categories (operating vs. capital), or include inflation and pass-through funds. Without a precise timeframe and budget category the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: There is no credible record or mainstream news reporting that Ted Cruz uttered the quoted line; such an inflammatory, specific defense of Josh Duggar would have been widely covered and attributed if genuine. Cruz's documented public statements do not match this wording, suggesting the quote is a misattribution or fabrication. If the phrase appears online it likely originated from a parody, altered transcript, or a different speaker.

claim: Says his budget provides "the highest state funding level in history" for education.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it lacks the identity of “his,” the state and budget year, and the exact metric used. Claims of "highest state funding in history" are frequently misleading: totals can be higher in nominal terms but lower when adjusted for inflation or measured per pupil, and may include one‑time or federal funds. Without those specifics the claim cannot be confirmed and is therefore judged false.

claim: "Eighty percent of the net new jobs created in the state of Texas since 2009 went to the foreign-born."
rationale: State and federal labor and Census analyses do not support the claim that 80% of net new Texas jobs since 2009 went to the foreign-born. Independent fact-checks and employment/ACS data show immigrants accounted for a substantial but far smaller share of job gains; there is no credible evidence that they received four-fifths of all net new jobs in Texas over that period.

claim: The Keystone pipeline creates "35 permanent jobs" after construction, according to a government report.
rationale: This matches the U.S. government review: the U.S. State Department’s environmental impact statement for the Keystone XL project estimated about 35 permanent U.S. jobs created during operation. That report and subsequent media summaries contrasted the small number of long‑term jobs with a larger number of temporary construction positions.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. Biden's banking nominee (commonly referenced as Saule Omarova) proposed expanding Federal Reserve infrastructure and the option of public consumer accounts in academic work, but she did not call for eliminating all private bank accounts or outlawing private banking. Critics have framed her proposals as wanting to 'end private banks,' but her writings describe a public alternative and regulatory changes rather than a blanket ban.

claim: "$1.8 billion Of Soros’ money just intercepted – he could officially go to prison for years"
rationale: There are no credible reports or official actions showing $1.8 billion of George Soros's funds were "intercepted" nor any criminal charges that would plausibly send him to prison for years. A seizure of that magnitude involving a high-profile figure would be widely reported by major news outlets and involve formal DOJ or international legal records, which do not exist. The claim appears to be a sensational, unverified rumor without supporting evidence.

claim: "One of the most troubling aspects of the Rubio-Schumer Gang of Eight bill was that it gave President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees, including Syrian refugees, without mandating any background checks whatsoever."
rationale: The Gang of Eight (2013, S.744) was a comprehensive immigration reform bill that did not grant the president blanket authority to admit refugees without vetting. U.S. refugee admissions are governed by the Refugee Act and interagency vetting procedures (State/USCIS/DHS/FBI biometric and name checks and security clearances), and Syrian refugee admissions after 2015 underwent multiple security screenings; the bill did not eliminate those checks.

claim: "In two years, Gov. McAuliffe has vetoed more bills that the previous three governors issued in each of their four-year terms."
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that Gov. McAuliffe’s vetoes in any two-year span exceeded the full four‑year veto totals of each of the previous three Virginia governors. The claim is imprecise about which two years and which three governors it references, and available historical veto records do not support such an extraordinary broad comparison without additional context or specific counts. Given the ambiguity and lack of supporting data, the statement is not supported.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: This overstates the difference. Common analyses show taxpayers with roughly $1 million in income face effective federal tax rates in the low-to-mid 20s percent while taxpayers around $100,000 face rates in the low-to-mid teens, yielding a ratio nearer 1.5–2, not four. Therefore the claim that $1M earners pay about four times the effective rate of $100k earners is inaccurate.

claim: "There is a growing body of evidence that radiation in excess of what the government says are the minimum amounts you should be exposed to are actually good for you and reduce cases of cancer."
rationale: The claim overstates the evidence: while a minority of laboratory and ecological studies have proposed 'radiation hormesis' (possible beneficial effects at very low doses), the dominant scientific and regulatory view is that there is no reliable, reproducible evidence that exposure above recommended limits reduces cancer risk. Epidemiological data are inconsistent and limited, and high or cumulative ionizing radiation exposure is well-established to increase cancer risk. Therefore the statement that growing evidence shows excess radiation is actually good and reduces cancer is not supported.

claim: "General Motors is sending Mexican made model of Chevy Cruze to U.S. car dealers-tax free across border."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad simplification. While some Chevy Cruze models were manufactured in Mexico and, when they met NAFTA/USMCA rules of origin, could be imported without U.S. import duty, imports still clear customs and must meet origin rules and other fees; they are not universally or arbitrarily sent “tax free.” Additionally sales taxes apply at point of sale and trade rules changed over time, so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "In fact, there’s more state funding for education today than any other time."
rationale: The claim is overbroad and cannot be verified as stated — whether funding is "more than any other time" depends on the metric (nominal dollars, inflation‑adjusted dollars, or per‑pupil funding) and the timeframe or state. Nominal state education spending is higher than in the distant past because of inflation and population growth, but inflation‑adjusted and per‑pupil funding have not uniformly reached all‑time highs across states and years. State-by-state variations and recent one‑time federal relief also mean a blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "Lots of studies seem to indicate that minors find it very easy to get marijuana, easier than to get alcohol."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. National surveys and peer‑reviewed studies show adolescents often report marijuana is readily available, but many studies also find alcohol is at least as easy or easier for minors to obtain (commonly via social sources), and findings vary by time, place, and how 'ease of access' is measured. Therefore it is not accurate to say that 'lots of studies' uniformly indicate marijuana is easier for minors to get than alcohol.

claim: President Barack Obama is "ending Medicare as we know it."
rationale: The claim is a political slogan, not a factual description. President Obama did not terminate Medicare or eliminate core Medicare benefits; the Affordable Care Act included reforms and cost-saving measures (e.g., reduced payments to some providers and Medicare Advantage plans, closing the Part D 'donut hole', creation of cost-control mechanisms) but preserved the program and its guaranteed benefits. Those changes do not constitute 'ending Medicare as we know it.'

claim: "(Assembly Democrats) wanted to raise the gas tax by $2.4 billion. We said no to that....They’re down on the ground. They’re sweating. They’re twitching. It’s ugly, ‘cause I keep saying no."
rationale: The claim that “Assembly Democrats wanted to raise the gas tax by $2.4 billion” cannot be confirmed as stated because no specific jurisdiction, bill, or time frame is given and I cannot find a clear, verifiable record tying Assembly Democrats to a $2.4 billion gas-tax proposal. Major gas-tax proposals in recent years have used a variety of revenue estimates and time horizons, and without a bill number or state this precise figure appears unsubstantiated. The colorful description of lawmakers reacting is rhetorical and does not validate the numeric claim.

claim: Says after Hurricane Sandy, New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg "refused to allow the National Guard into the city to restore civil order because Guardsmen carry guns!"
rationale: This claim is false. The New York National Guard was mobilized to assist after Hurricane Sandy by state and federal authorities, and the mayor does not have unilateral authority to "refuse" National Guard deployments — governors activate and control state Guard forces. Contemporary reporting and fact-checks found no credible evidence that Bloomberg barred the Guard from the city on the basis that "Guardsmen carry guns."

claim: Chinese workers made "90,000 banners" for Trump’s 2020 re-election campaign and the president chose to hire "Chinese workers instead of American workers"
rationale: I could find no credible evidence that exactly 90,000 banners for Trump’s 2020 re‑election were made by Chinese workers, nor that the president personally decided to ‘hire Chinese workers instead of American workers.’ Campaign merchandise is commonly manufactured overseas by third‑party vendors, but the specific numeric claim and the implication of a direct hire by the president are unsubstantiated. Reporting at the time noted some U.S. campaign merchandise is produced abroad, but not the specific 90,000 figure or direct hiring choice stated here.

claim: The state and local tax deduction is a major benefit for moderate-income households because "50% of households that claim State & Local Tax deduction make under $100K."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While a substantial share of filers who itemize and claim the SALT deduction may have incomes under $100K, the vast majority of the dollar value of the SALT deduction accrues to higher‑income taxpayers (especially those above $100K). Therefore claiming it is a "major benefit for moderate‑income households" based on a single 50% filer statistic is inaccurate.

claim: Thanks to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, "Vietnam is drafting and presenting unprecedented labor reforms, changing their Constitution to recognize worker organizations in Vietnam for the first time."
rationale: This claim overstates and misstates events. While TPP negotiations and related pressure (and later CPTPP obligations and bilateral commitments) prompted Vietnam to promise and enact some labor-law changes, Vietnam historically already recognized a state-controlled union structure (the Vietnam General Confederation of Labour) and did not amend its constitution to recognize independent worker organizations 'for the first time.' Major constitutional recognition of independent unions has not occurred and reforms have been limited and contested.

claim: About "1 percent of all the gun sellers are responsible for more than half of the guns that are used in crimes."
rationale: Multiple analyses of ATF gun-trace data and follow-up reporting have found that a very small share of federally licensed dealers—on the order of about 1 percent—account for a majority (>50%) of firearms recovered and traced to crimes in specific years and jurisdictions. The statement reflects those empirical trace-based findings, though it simplifies the underlying data and causation.

claim: "I have no financial interests in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified because the speaker is unspecified and no supporting evidence or disclosures are provided. Without identity-specific financial records, public filings, or other documentation, I cannot confirm the absence of any direct or indirect financial ties to Saudi Arabia, so I mark the claim as false per instruction to prefer false when uncertain.

claim: Barack Obama wants to "restore" the estate tax that George W. Bush "repealed."
rationale: The claim is misleading. George W. Bush's 2001 tax law phased down the federal estate tax and resulted in a temporary repeal for 2010, not a permanent repeal, and Barack Obama did advocate reinstating or maintaining an estate tax after that temporary lapse. Saying Bush "repealed" it outright and implying Obama opposed that reinstatement misstates the facts.

claim: "Rick Scott's even saying he wants more offshore drilling."
rationale: Rick Scott, as Florida governor and later as a U.S. senator, has publicly advocated for expanding offshore oil and gas drilling and for opening more federal waters to exploration. Multiple statements and policy positions from his campaigns and tenure indicate he has said he wants more offshore drilling.

claim: Photo shows Kim Jong Un’s weight loss
rationale: A single photograph is insufficient to prove weight loss. Visual appearance can be altered by camera angle, lighting, clothing, posture or photo editing; proving a change in body mass requires multiple verified images across time, measurements, or an authoritative medical/official statement. Without provenance, dates, and comparative evidence, the claim is unsupported.

claim: GOP candidate for California governor Travis Allen "on the floor vote … refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens."
rationale: Legislative voting records and contemporary news reporting show Travis Allen voted with Republicans opposing expansion of driver’s licenses to undocumented immigrants (he opposed AB 60). Thus the claim that he “refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens” is inaccurate. Public record indicates he did not break with his party on that floor vote.

claim: "Replacing marriage licenses with domestic union contracts does not alter state or federal benefits."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as a blanket statement. Many state and especially federal benefits are tied to the legal status of "marriage" as defined in statutes and regulations, so replacing marriage licenses with a different instrument (e.g., "domestic union contracts") would likely change eligibility unless laws and regulations are expressly amended to treat the new contract as equivalent. Such changes would affect things like federal tax filing status, Social Security spousal benefits, immigration sponsorship, and other spouse-dependent programs.

claim: "The average cost of child care in this country is more than what it costs to send a child to college for one year."
