claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: This wording is misleading. Humanitarian agencies (notably the UN/OCHA) warned in 2017 that roughly 20 million people in four countries (Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northeast Nigeria) faced famine or were at risk of dying without urgent aid; the figure was about 20 million and the timeline was conditional (‘in the coming months’ if aid did not arrive), not an unqualified statement that more than 20 million would die within six months. Without a date or source the claim overstates certainty and slightly alters the commonly reported figure and conditional timeframe.

claim: Speaking of an HIV outbreak in Indiana during his time as governor, says "we immediately deployed health resources."
rationale: This claim is misleading. During the 2015 Scott County, Indiana HIV outbreak the state and governor were criticized for delaying harm-reduction measures (notably syringe-exchange programs) and only authorized broader measures after months and federal involvement, so it is inaccurate to say the state 'immediately deployed health resources' as a factual description of the early response. While some state actions and later deployments did occur, they were not immediate in the way the quote implies.

claim: "Within the three miles surrounding the University Circle area, infant mortality exceeds some Third World countries."
rationale: Multiple public-health reports and news investigations have documented that certain Cleveland neighborhoods within a few miles of University Circle have historically had infant mortality rates in the range of roughly 20–30 deaths per 1,000 live births. Those neighborhood-level rates exceed the infant mortality rates reported in some low- and middle-income countries, so the broad claim is supported, though it depends on year and which countries are used for comparison.

claim: In the plot to kidnap Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, "the perps were ANTIFA and BLM anarchists."
rationale: Investigations, arrests, federal and state indictments, and court filings showed the suspects belonged to a right‑wing militia (commonly called the Wolverine Watchmen) with anti‑government/militant views, not Antifa or BLM. There is no credible evidence linking Antifa or Black Lives Matter organizers to the planning or execution of the Whitmer kidnap plot; claims to the contrary were part of misinformation circulating after the arrests.

claim: Says Donald Trump "cashed in" on Sept. 11,  "collecting $150,000 in federal funds intended to help small businesses recover — even though days after the attack Trump said his properties were not affected."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and public records show Donald Trump’s businesses received about $150,000 from federal post‑9/11 small‑business disaster relief programs. Within days after the attacks he publicly said his properties were not materially affected, creating a contrast with the later receipt of those federal recovery funds.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s polling numbers show that he’s "the highest with Hispanics that any Republican has ever been."
rationale: Historical and exit-poll data show Republicans have received higher Hispanic support than Donald Trump’s typical polling. For example, George W. Bush received roughly 40–44% of the Hispanic vote in 2004, while Trump’s nationwide Hispanic support was much lower in 2016 and 2020 and, although improved in some 2024 polls and among particular Hispanic subgroups, has not been shown to be the highest any Republican has ever received overall.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: The claim is false because while multiple studies and analyses find voter fraud in Texas is extremely rare, it is not literally non-existent. State records, prosecutions, and media reports document isolated instances of illegal voting and voter-fraud prosecutions in Texas, and academic reviews (and organizations like the Brennan Center) characterize the rate as vanishingly small but not zero.

claim: "Every state that has put in a graduated income tax, the middle class always pays more."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that does not hold up. Whether the middle class pays more after a state adopts a graduated (progressive) income tax depends on the specific bracket thresholds, rates, deductions, exemptions, and credits set by that state; in many cases middle‑income taxpayers see no increase or even a decrease in liability. Because outcomes vary by policy design and taxpayer circumstances, it is incorrect to say the middle class "always" pays more in every such state.

claim: Ninety-five percent of the money used for union-operated worker training centers comes from employers.
rationale: There is no credible national evidence that 95% of funding for union-operated worker training centers comes from employers. Funding for these centers is mixed and can include union dues, federal and state grants, participant fees, and employer or jointly negotiated contributions; proportions vary widely by program and locale. While some apprenticeship or joint labor-management programs receive substantial employer-paid contributions, the blanket 95% figure overstates and lacks supporting data.

claim: Senate Democrats who left the state for weeks to delay a vote on union bargaining power exercised a "Wisconsin filibuster" provided by the state’s constitution.
rationale: False. The senators fled the state to deny a quorum under Wisconsin’s constitutional quorum requirement, which prevented the Senate from conducting business; that is not the same as a filibuster. A filibuster normally refers to extended debate or other floor tactics to block a vote, whereas this was a quorum-denial tactic (sometimes called colloquially a "Wisconsin filibuster").

claim: "24 of every 100 kids in school today speak Spanish."
rationale: The statement is unqualified and therefore misleading. National data (e.g., U.S. surveys) show Spanish is the largest non-English language among children but generally represents about one-fifth or slightly less of school-age children nationally, with wide variation by state and district; without a specified country, age range, or definition of "speak Spanish," the flat claim that 24 of every 100 kids in school speak Spanish is not supported.

claim: Says Donald Trump has written 10 checks to Hillary Clinton "and four of those checks were not to her Senate campaign. … It was to her presidential campaign."
rationale: Public campaign‑finance records and contemporary fact‑checks do not support the specific claim that Donald Trump personally wrote 10 checks to Hillary Clinton with four going to her presidential campaign. While Trump has made some donations to various Democrats in past decades, the precise tally of “10 checks” and “four” to her presidential bids is not borne out by FEC records or reputable reporting. The statement appears to conflate or invent specific numbers that are not documented.

claim: Says 12 restaurants and food companies are "supporting Trump’s re-election."
rationale: The claim as presented is unverified because it gives no names, timeframe, or evidence that precisely 12 restaurants/food companies are actively ‘supporting Trump’s re-election.’ Corporate political activity (endorsements, donations, hosting events) is publicly documented, and no widely reported, substantiated list naming exactly 12 such firms has been found. Without specific sources, the assertion appears unsupported and likely inaccurate.

claim: "About 95 percent of (Ohio’s) electricity comes from burning coal."
rationale: Recent and historical data show Ohio's electricity generation has been supplied by a mix of sources (coal, natural gas, nuclear, and renewables), with coal typically providing a plurality but far less than 95%. In the past two decades coal's share has commonly been in the range of roughly 30–70% and has declined as natural gas and renewables have grown, so a figure of about 95% is not supported.

claim: Says Charlie "Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money."
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks specifics (which 'Duke', what policy, and what timeframe), and there is no clear evidence that Charlie Crist directly enacted a law or regulatory change that made it easier for a company to 'take your money.' Utility rate decisions in Florida are made by regulators and the legislature rather than the governor alone, so the assertion as stated cannot be verified. Given the ambiguity and absence of concrete supporting facts, the claim is judged false.

claim: Says Rick Scott took $200,000 in campaign contributions from a company that "profited off pollution."
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that Rick Scott received exactly $200,000 from a single company described accurately as one that “profited off pollution.” Public campaign finance records do show Scott has taken contributions from energy and industrial firms over multiple cycles, but the claim’s specific dollar amount and the normative label “profited off pollution” are not corroborated by clear, sourced reporting. Because the statement mixes a precise figure with a subjective characterization without naming the company, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: State tax and budget analyses have long shown that a large majority of New York State personal income tax revenue comes from downstate: New York City together with Westchester, Nassau and Suffolk typically account for about 70% of PIT collections. The precise share varies by year, but 70% is a commonly reported and reasonable approximation of how concentrated income-tax receipts are in those counties.

claim: Alison Alter "has exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars to fund her campaign."
rationale: I find no verified evidence that Alison Alter unlawfully "exploited a loophole" to obtain over $64,000 in public funds. Candidates in some jurisdictions can legally receive public matching or grant funds under local programs; describing that as an "exploit" alleges misconduct that is not supported by available factual records. Without specific jurisdiction, dates, or documentation, the assertion appears to mischaracterize lawful campaign financing as improper.

claim: Perpetrators of school shootings "have been drugged in many cases … many of these young boys have been on Ritalin since they were in kindergarten."
rationale: This broad claim is not supported by available evidence. Multiple fact-checks and academic reviews find no consistent pattern that a majority of school shooters were medicated with Ritalin from kindergarten; while some perpetrators have had psychiatric histories or used medications at some point, those are anecdotal and do not establish the stated widespread pattern or causation. The statement overgeneralizes from a few cases and conflates correlation and causation.

claim: Says "over 40 percent of recent county bonds are for Precinct One, northeast Travis County," because he "is quick to identify projects that help make the East Side a desirable place to live."
rationale: The statement that “over 40 percent of recent county bonds are for Precinct One” is not supported by publicly documented county bond allocations. County bond packages are usually itemized across many precincts and countywide projects, and allocating more than 40% to a single precinct would be notable and documented; no clear evidence for that specific percentage or time period is available. The praise about identifying projects is subjective and does not validate the numeric claim.

claim: "Cancer and matters to do with kidney failure kill more people in Kenya today than malaria, tuberculosis and AIDS combined."
rationale: Country-level burden estimates from WHO/Global Burden of Disease indicate that malaria, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS together still account for more annual deaths in Kenya than cancers plus kidney disease. Non-communicable diseases including cancer and chronic kidney disease are rising, but available data do not support that they already exceed the combined mortality of malaria, TB and AIDS nationwide.

claim: "I can tell you with certainty (cap and trade) would have a devastating impact on our economy."
rationale: The claim asserts certainty that a cap‑and‑trade program would have a "devastating" effect on the economy; that strong, universal prediction is not supported by evidence. Empirical experience with cap‑and‑trade (e.g., regional and national systems) and multiple economic analyses show costs are generally modest and highly dependent on program design, with revenue recycling and transitional measures mitigating negative impacts. Therefore the categorical claim of certain devastation is false.

claim: "This week the House of Representatives voted to remove the word ‘lunatic’ from federal law."
rationale: There is no evidence the full U.S. House this week voted to remove the word “lunatic” from federal law. While lawmakers have periodically proposed bills or amendments to update archaic mental‑health language, removing a term from the U.S. Code requires a passed bill (House and Senate) and the president’s signature; that final action would have been widely reported. The claim likely confuses a proposed measure, committee action, or public discussion with an enacted House vote.

claim: Says North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis "called Obamacare ‘a great idea.’ "
rationale: There is no clear, credible record of Thom Tillis saying the specific phrase “called Obamacare ‘a great idea.’” During the 2014 Senate campaign he criticized the Affordable Care Act and opponents circulated edited claims; at most he was reported to have acknowledged some aspects of health reform as reasonable “in concept,” not to have called the law itself a “great idea.” Given the lack of a verifiable verbatim quote, the precise claim is false.

claim: After they bought GST Steel, "Mitt Romney and his partners loaded it with debt, closed the Kansas City plant and walked away with a healthy profit, leaving hundreds of employees out of work with their pensions in jeopardy."
rationale: Bain partners including Mitt Romney were part of the 1993 leveraged buyout of GST Steel; the company later closed its Kansas City plant, entered bankruptcy, and pension obligations were ultimately shifted to the federal PBGC. Contemporary reporting and later fact-checking found that the buyout saddled the company with debt, Bain-related owners realized profits, and hundreds of workers lost jobs and faced pension jeopardy.

claim: "Given the results of the primary, the vote of one New Hampshire superdelegate is equal to the votes of about 10,000 grassroots activists."
rationale: The statement is misleading. A New Hampshire ‘‘superdelegate’’ is an individual unpledged delegate whose single vote at the national convention counts the same as any other delegate’s vote; it is not literally equal to a fixed number of primary voters. Any conversion of primary votes into delegate-equivalents depends on the year’s turnout and the specific delegate allocation rules, so claiming a superdelegate equals about 10,000 grassroots activists is an oversimplification and not generally true.

claim: Members of Congress and their families and staff are exempt from repaying student loans.
rationale: There is no law or policy that broadly exempts members of Congress, their families, or staff from repaying student loans. Elected officials and their relatives are subject to the same federal student loan repayment rules as other borrowers, though individual members or staff can qualify for standard programs (e.g., Public Service Loan Forgiveness, income-driven repayment) or temporary relief measures. Any forgiveness or relief requires meeting normal eligibility criteria, not a blanket exemption for Congress-related persons.

claim: "Jeff Greene can buy anything" ...  he owns two mansions.
rationale: The phrase “can buy anything” is a hyperbolic absolute that cannot be verified and is false as a literal claim—no individual can legally or practically purchase every good or service. It is true that Jeff Greene is a very wealthy real-estate investor and has owned multiple high-value homes, but that does not make the absolute statement accurate. The claim mixes an unprovable blanket assertion with a plausible note about owning mansions.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood called Joe Biden an "incompetent, lying, flip-flopping, insincere, double-talking, radical socialist."
rationale: There is no credible public record—no news reporting, video, or verified transcript—showing Clint Eastwood saying that exact string about Joe Biden. While Eastwood has occasionally criticized politicians, the specific phrasing appears to be a misattribution or manufactured quote circulated on social media rather than a documented statement.

claim: "Justin Amash is rated Michigan’s No. 1 conservative" by National Right to Life.
rationale: The National Right to Life Committee issues pro‑life scorecards and grades members on abortion‑related votes rather than labeling someone generically as a state’s “No. 1 conservative.” There is no widely documented NRLC designation calling Justin Amash “Michigan’s No. 1 conservative”; at best NRLC might have given him a high pro‑life score in a particular year, but that is not the same as the quoted claim.

claim: Says John McAfee tweeted before his death that he stored computer files in the Florida condo building that later collapsed.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that John McAfee tweeted he stored computer files in the Florida condo that later collapsed. Contemporary reporting of McAfee’s final tweets did not include any verifiable post claiming files were stored in the Surfside/Champlain Towers building, and the collapse occurred a day after his death, making the specific claim uncorroborated and likely a rumor or misattribution. Without primary-source tweets or reputable news confirmation, the assertion is unsupported.

claim: "Every year since Gov. Walker and the Republicans have been in control of the Legislature we’ve created fewer jobs, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics."
rationale: BLS state employment data do not show a monotonic year‑by‑year decline in jobs for Wisconsin during the years Gov. Scott Walker and Republicans controlled the legislature. Annual nonfarm payroll gains after 2011 fluctuated and in several years (for example early‑to‑mid 2010s) job gains were larger than in preceding years, so the statement that "every year...we've created fewer jobs" is false.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: I cannot verify this exact wording as a documented, attributable public quote from a known politician. It resembles a general rhetorical attack sometimes heard in campaigns, but no reliable record confirms someone said these precise words, so the claim as presented is unproven and likely a misattribution or paraphrase. Without a source or speaker, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: Says Tim Tebow wrote, "The government might be preparing us for a cashless society, but it was predicted by the Bible."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or primary source showing Tim Tebow wrote or publicly authored the quoted line about a cashless society being predicted by the Bible. That phrasing has circulated on social media as a misattributed or anonymous religious/political comment rather than a documented Tebow statement. Given the absence of a verifiable tweet, article, or recorded quote from Tebow, the attribution appears incorrect.

claim: "One man sacrificed for his country. One man opposed a flawed strategy in Iraq. One man had the courage to call for change. One man didn't play politics with the truth. One man stands up to the special interests."
rationale: The statement is a set of vague, evaluative endorsements about an unspecified 'one man' and contains both subjective judgments and unstated factual claims. Without identifying the individual or providing independent evidence for sacrifice, specific opposition to Iraq policy, refusal to "play politics with the truth," or actions against special interests, the claims cannot be verified as true. Because the assertion is ambiguous and unsubstantiated, it is judged false as presented.

claim: A video shows "the COVID-19 vaccine when it hits your blood."
rationale: The claim is misleading: approved COVID-19 vaccines are given intramuscularly and their components are taken up by local cells or cleared by the body, not instantly causing visible structures 'hitting your blood' as shown in sensationalized videos. Numerous expert analyses and fact-checks have shown such footage is typically unrelated microscopic imagery, artifacts, or misinterpreted blood/clot footage rather than direct visualization of vaccine particles in circulation.

claim: Says the "only valid reason to oppose voter ID is that you plan to cheat," and "every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID."
rationale: The claim is false because it makes an absolute statement that all Democrats in Congress oppose voter ID, which is demonstrably untrue: some Democratic members (particularly moderates) have publicly supported certain voter ID measures or endorsed forms of identification requirements. The quoted line that the “only valid reason to oppose voter ID is that you plan to cheat” is an opinion many individuals have expressed, but it does not make the blanket factual claim about every Democrat accurate.

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: The claim bundles two specific statistics that I cannot verify against official Milwaukee or Wisconsin traffic and crime reports. Publicly available data and news summaries do show increases in vehicle thefts and traffic fatalities in many U.S. cities in 2021, but I find no clear authoritative source confirming exactly 65 deaths labeled specifically as 'due to reckless driving' in Milwaukee in 2021 nor a confirmed figure of more than 9,000 stolen cars that was exactly double 2020. Given the lack of corroborating official statistics and potential ambiguity in terms, the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Donald Trump "has the second-highest disapproval ratings of anyone running for president."
rationale: The statement is presented as a universal fact but disapproval rankings vary by poll, timing, and which candidates are included. At different times and in different reputable polls either Donald Trump or Joe Biden has had the highest disapproval, and third-party or primary candidates can alter rankings, so you cannot reliably say Trump has the second-highest disapproval of 'anyone running' without specifying a particular poll and date.

claim: John McCain and George Bush have "absolutely no plan for universal health care."
rationale: Both John McCain (notably in his 2008 campaign) and President George W. Bush publicly opposed implementing universal health care and instead promoted market-based reforms and incremental measures. Neither put forward a plan to establish universal, government-guaranteed health coverage (they proposed HSAs, tax/market reforms, Medicare Part D, etc.).

claim: "David McCormick paid for attacks on Donald Trump."
rationale: The claim is presented without context and there is no clear, widely reported evidence that a person named David McCormick personally funded coordinated 'attacks' on Donald Trump. While David McCormick (the GOP politician/businessman) has criticized Trump publicly and his campaign or allied groups may have run contrast ads, the broad assertion that he 'paid for attacks on Donald Trump' is unsupported as stated. Without specific details (which David McCormick, when, what payments), the claim cannot be verified.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Multiple epidemiological studies and public-health data show that the Omicron variant (and its early sublineages) caused, on average, less severe disease, lower hospitalization rates, and lower mortality per infection than the Delta variant; there is no credible evidence that Omicron is '5 times' more toxic or more deadly than Delta. While Omicron is more transmissible, its intrinsic virulence was generally observed to be lower in populations with comparable immunity levels, so the claim contradicts the broad scientific consensus.

claim: Exporters are using a federal loophole to "deceptively sell products made from cat and dog fur" to U.S. consumers.
rationale: There is no well-documented, ongoing scheme showing exporters are broadly exploiting a recognized federal 'loophole' to systematically sell products made from cat and dog fur to U.S. consumers. U.S. federal law (the Dog and Cat Fur Products Act and related import restrictions) generally prohibits commerce in dog and cat fur, and while isolated instances of mislabeling or illicit shipments have been reported, those are enforcement or fraud incidents rather than proof of an established legal loophole enabling deceptive mass imports. The claim as stated overgeneralizes and lacks specific documented evidence.

claim: "One thousand people a day are moving to Texas, which means there will be 15 million more people over the next 25 years."
rationale: The arithmetic is incorrect: 1,000 people per day is ~365,000 per year, which over 25 years equals about 9.125 million, not 15 million. The claim also implicitly assumes all movers permanently add to population and ignores out-migration, deaths, births, and changing rates over time, so the projection is unreliable.

claim: "Clinton campaign official arrested by FBI on child rape/trafficking charges"
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public DOJ/FBI record that any official of the Clinton campaign was arrested on child rape or trafficking charges. Major news organizations and law-enforcement public records would have widely covered such an arrest; instead, similar claims have been repeatedly debunked and traced to conspiracy theories. Without a named individual and verifiable sources, the assertion appears fabricated.

claim: "Together we added more jobs than any other area" while I was Dane County executive.
rationale: The claim as stated is unsubstantiated because it gives no timeframe or definition of “any other area.” Rank-order claims about jobs require specific data (years and comparator geographies). Without that, and given that larger metro areas typically add more jobs, the broad assertion cannot be verified and is therefore judged false.

claim: Each Georgia taxpayer would have to send $5,000 to the treasury to cover the state’s debt.
rationale: The claim gives a precise per-taxpayer number without sourcing and is inconsistent with common estimates. Georgia’s state-level debt and the count of taxpayers vary, but dividing typical reported state debts (tens of billions) by millions of taxpayers does not reliably produce exactly $5,000, and taxpayers are not required to make a one-time lump-sum payment to “cover” state debt. The figure therefore cannot be verified as stated.

claim: "First, he was in favor of my plan, now he's attacking it."
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it lacks any identifying details (who “he” is, what the “plan” is, and a timeline or evidence of the change). Without specific names, quotes, or documentary evidence showing initial support and later opposition, the claim cannot be confirmed. Given the absence of verifiable context, it should be treated as unsupported.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "voted to cut $700m from Medicare."
rationale: The claim is misleading and lacks necessary context; there is no clear, standalone Senate vote by Ron Johnson identifiable as directly 'cutting $700m from Medicare.' Votes affecting Medicare are usually about long-term savings, program changes, or funding for specific components, and claims that cite a precise $700 million cut typically conflate or misstate the underlying bill or amendment. Without a bill name and date, the assertion cannot be verified and appears inaccurate as stated.

claim: "Piles of bricks are being staged in cities around the country, indicating riots are planned."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that cities nationwide are staging piles of bricks to plan riots. Numerous fact-checks and reporting show many photographed brick piles are construction materials, removed curbing, landscaping supplies, or debris from repair work, and social media posts have misattributed intent. The claim extrapolates isolated images into a coordinated nationwide plot without substantiation.

claim: "Health care is the greatest contribution to spending increases in the state budget."
rationale: The claim is too general and lacks key context (which state and what time period), so it cannot be verified as stated. While health care—especially Medicaid and rising medical costs—frequently is a major driver of state budget growth, other categories such as K–12/higher education, pension obligations, or debt service are the largest contributors in many states and years. Therefore the blanket statement is unsupported without specific state-level budget data.

claim: "This Is Real: Biden Waves To An Empty Field."
rationale: The claim that “Biden waves to an empty field” asserts there were no people present, but there is no verifiable evidence provided to show the location was truly empty. Camera framing and selective clips commonly omit attendees or show them off-camera, so without a dated, full-source video or independent on-site verification the assertion is unproven and likely misleading.

claim: "Six people in Florida die as a result of (not expanding Medicaid) every day."
rationale: The statement presents a precise, causal daily death count as a fact, but that figure is not established empirically. Estimates that link non-expansion of Medicaid to excess deaths exist, but they are model-based, vary by methodology and timeframe, and do not support a single definitive rate of exactly six Florida deaths per day. Because attribution depends on assumptions and different analyses produce different numbers, the claim as a definite fact is unsupported.

claim: The Obama administration is using as its "legal justification for these airstrikes (on the Islamic State), an authorization for military force that the president himself has called for repeal of."
rationale: The Obama administration primarily relied on the 2001 AUMF (and inherent Article II/self‑defense authority) as the legal basis for strikes against ISIS, arguing ISIS was an associated force of al‑Qaeda. President Obama had publicly called for repeal of the 2002 Iraq AUMF, not the 2001 AUMF that the administration cited for ISIL operations.

claim: Says "Every time the Legislature 'suspended' the kicker, most recently the corporate kicker in 2007, Salem spent every penny and failed to stabilize the state's revenues."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. While Oregon has redirected or “suspended” kicker refunds (the corporate kicker was redirected in 2007), legislatures have not uniformly “spent every penny” nor have the results been identical each time; redirected funds have been used for a mix of one‑time budget fixes, reserve deposits, and debt payments, and the effect on long‑term revenue stability has varied. Saying every suspension resulted in spending all funds and failure to stabilize revenues is factually inaccurate.

claim: Housing prices dropped for the 30 months prior to Barack Obama taking office, "and they have stabilized, they've been about flat since the president came in."
rationale: While U.S. house prices had been declining since about mid‑2006 (roughly 30 months before Obama’s January 2009 inauguration), they did not simply ‘stabilize’ and remain flat after he took office. Major measures such as the S&P/Case‑Shiller indices continued to fall in many markets through 2009–2012 before bottoming and later recovering. Therefore the claim that prices were about flat since he took office is misleading and inaccurate in the aggregate.

claim: "Australia Closing Borders in a few hours for 6-months"
rationale: The claim of Australia "closing borders in a few hours for 6-months" is false as stated. There has been no credible federal announcement or legal order instituting an immediate nationwide six‑month border closure; such a major action would require formal government orders and would be widely reported. Past closures (e.g., during COVID) were publicly announced and implemented through legal instruments, not sudden unannounced measures.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was literally present when we pressed the reset button with Russia just a few months after Russia had invaded Georgia."
rationale: Hillary Clinton, as U.S. Secretary of State, was physically present when she presented a symbolic "reset" button to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at their March 2009 meeting. Russia's invasion of Georgia occurred in August 2008, so the symbolic reset event took place several months (about seven months) after that conflict. The statement accurately describes her literal presence and the relative timing.

claim: "Most of, if not all of, the [DeKalb school construction] projects always came in on or were under budget."
rationale: The claim is a broad, near-universal assertion that most or all DeKalb school construction projects always came in on or under budget. Public construction programs typically include some projects with cost overruns, and absent contemporaneous audited project-level accounting or comprehensive reporting demonstrating that nearly every project met or beat budget, the claim is unsupported. Given the strong wording (“most of, if not all” and “always”), the available general evidence and typical pattern of mixed outcomes make the statement implausible.

claim: The United States has a "record number of abortions year after year after year."
rationale: This statement is not supported by U.S. abortion statistics. National totals peaked in the early 1990s and then declined for decades; recent years show fluctuations and no sustained, consecutive year-after-year record increases. Different data sources (CDC vs. Guttmacher) report differing year-to-year counts, but neither shows continuous record-breaking increases year after year.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "wants to go to a single-payer plan" for health care
rationale: Hillary Clinton has publicly and repeatedly rejected adopting a single-payer (Medicare-for-All) system, especially during her 2016 campaign, and instead advocated building on the Affordable Care Act and pursuing incremental reforms. She did not campaign in favor of replacing private insurance with a single-payer plan, so the claim that she "wants to go to a single-payer plan" is inaccurate.

claim: "Taxpayers are paying a fortune for the use of Air Force One on the campaign trail" by President Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: The claim is misleading. While a sitting president (e.g., Barack Obama while in office) used the presidential aircraft for travel that included campaign events and those trips involve federal costs for transport and security, Hillary Clinton, as a private candidate, did not use Air Force One. The statement also vagely inflates costs by calling them “a fortune” without distinguishing official presidential travel (federally funded) from campaign-only travel (which campaigns must generally pay for).

claim: "Last year we had the eighth fastest-growing economy in the country in West Virginia."
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable because it omits which year and which measure of economic growth (real GDP, nominal GDP, personal income, employment, etc.) is meant. State growth rankings vary by metric and year, and without that context there is no reliable way to confirm West Virginia was exactly the eighth fastest-growing. Because of this missing information the claim cannot be affirmed as factual.

claim: "Supreme Court issues its first bench warrant ever."
rationale: There are no credible reports or historical records showing the U.S. Supreme Court recently issued a “first-ever” bench warrant. Bench warrants are ordinarily issued by trial courts and lower federal/state courts; the Supreme Court’s criminal/enforcement powers are limited and it rarely issues arrest-type orders, so the blanket claim is incorrect or misleading without additional context.

claim: "A grant for $5,000 [from the Governor’s Workforce Board] went to teach an employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter."
rationale: I could not find corroborating evidence that a Governor’s Workforce Board specifically awarded a $5,000 grant to train a single employee at a firm described as making “ornamental business card holders.” Such anecdotes are commonly exaggerated or mischaracterized; workforce board grants typically fund broader training programs and are documented publicly. Without a verifiable source tying that exact dollar amount, recipient description, and purpose to an official grant, the claim is not supported.

claim: The Iran deal says that "if any other country tries to undermine (Iran's) nuclear program, we have to help them defend themselves against Israel, Egypt, Saudis, our own allies."
rationale: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (the Iran deal) is a nuclear non-proliferation agreement that sets limits, monitoring, and sanctions-relief conditions for Iran's nuclear program; it contains no provision obligating parties to help Iran defend itself against attacks by Israel, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, or other countries. The quoted language does not appear in the JCPOA text and would be inconsistent with the deal’s focus and with the positions of the negotiating states.

claim: "Jamaica has not recorded any case of the coronavirus."
rationale: This claim is false. Jamaica reported its first confirmed COVID-19 case in March 2020 and thereafter publicly reported many additional confirmed cases and deaths through its Ministry of Health and international bodies. Therefore the statement that Jamaica has not recorded any case of the coronavirus is incorrect for the pandemic period.

claim: "The recidivism rate is nearly 29 percent and has been climbing steadily since detainees began being released from Guantanamo."
rationale: The claim mixes a particular snapshot statistic with an incorrect trend. U.S. government tracking has at times produced a combined “confirmed + suspected” re‑engagement number near the high‑20s percent for detainees released from Guantánamo, but the numbers depend on narrow definitions and have not shown a simple, steady upward climb since releases began. Different reports separate “confirmed” and “suspected” cases and the rates have fluctuated over time rather than rising monotonically.

claim: Says it was "a crime for Nixon to wiretap the Democrats at Watergate but OK for Obama to wiretap Republicans at Trump Tower."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama ordered wiretaps of Trump Tower; the allegation originated from a 2017 tweet and was investigated without supportive findings. By contrast, the Watergate break-ins and wiretaps were unlawful actions by Nixon operatives that led to prosecutions. Any surveillance in 2016–17 used legal processes (e.g., FISA warrants) targeting specific individuals rather than a presidentially ordered blanket wiretap of Trump Tower.

claim: "Hillary Clinton is in jail at Gitmo at the moment."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Hillary Clinton is detained at Guantánamo Bay. An arrest and detention of a former U.S. secretary of state would be major, widely reported news and would appear in official records; publicly available lists and reporting about Guantánamo detainees do not include her.

claim: "Iceland declares all religions are mental disorders."
rationale: Iceland has not declared religions to be mental disorders; its constitution and laws protect freedom of religion and provide for recognition of religious organizations. There is no official law or government statement classifying religion as a psychiatric condition, so the claim is a misrepresentation or hoax.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: This claim is false. PepsiCo never admitted that an employee contaminated its products with HIV/AIDS; past widely circulated rumors and hoaxes alleged such contamination but independent tests and company statements found no HIV in beverages. Additionally, HIV is not transmitted via sealed beverage contamination and cannot survive long outside the human body, making the claimed scenario implausible.

claim: Says "Biden wants a nationwide lockdown to combat a virus that has a 99%+ survival rate."
rationale: The claim is false. Biden’s public COVID-19 proposals emphasized a national strategy, increased testing, masks, vaccinations and targeted interventions rather than calling for an across-the-board nationwide lockdown, and characterizing the virus as having a uniform 99%+ survival rate is misleading because COVID-19 fatality risk varies by age, health status, and over time. Combining a misleading survival statistic with an inaccurate policy claim makes the overall statement incorrect.

claim: "For the first time in over a decade, business leaders around the world have declared that China is no longer the world’s No. 1 place to invest; America is."
rationale: This is an overgeneralized and unsupported claim. There has been no single, global declaration by business leaders that China is no longer the top place to invest and that America is instead; surveys and FDI data show mixed sentiment and continued substantial investment in China, even as US attractiveness has risen in some polls. Saying it is the “first time in over a decade” is likewise unsupported by consistent, worldwide evidence.

claim: Ron Johnson didn’t "show up" for a day of impeachment hearings.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported as stated: Ron Johnson is a U.S. Senator and not a member of House impeachment committees, so saying he “didn’t show up for a day of impeachment hearings” lacks a clear factual basis without a date or which body’s hearings. I am not aware of reliable reports that Senator Johnson was scheduled as a participant in a specific impeachment hearing and then failed to attend. Without more specifics the assertion cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: "Hundreds of illegal immigrants subject to detainers were released in the last week since the new sanctuary policy was adopted by the Travis County Sheriff's Office."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and official statements about the Travis County Sheriff’s new sanctuary-style detainer policy did not corroborate that “hundreds” of people were released in a single week. Coverage and sheriff’s office data around the policy change described a much smaller number of cases handled differently (measured in single- or low-double digits), so the claim appears to be a substantial exaggeration.

claim: TriMet is "spending 4.2 million in fed funds to save $168K per year."
rationale: The claim is presented without context and I have no verifiable evidence that TriMet used exactly $4.2 million in federal funds to achieve only $168,000 per year in savings. Federal grants are typically one‑time capital funds and reported projects include broader benefits beyond a simple annual operating savings number, so the assertion as stated appears misleading or incomplete. Without a specific project, timeframe, or source, the arithmetic payoff claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "In 1960, most black children were raised in two-parent, monogamous families." Today "we have only 20 percent of black children being raised in two-parent, monogamous families..."
rationale: The claim mixes a true historical point (a clear majority of Black children lived with two married parents in 1960) with a false contemporary figure. Contemporary U.S. Census/Pew analyses show the share of Black children living with two married parents has fallen substantially since 1960 but is roughly on the order of ~35–45%, not as low as 20%. Thus the broad direction is correct (a decline) but the specific modern figure is incorrect.

claim: "Since 2004, more than 2,000 suspected terrorists have legally purchased weapons in the United States."
rationale: This claim overstates and misinterprets available data. There is no authoritative evidence that more than 2,000 confirmed 'suspected terrorists' legally purchased firearms since 2004; numbers widely circulated come from loose matches to watchlists or background-check hits that include many false positives and cases later resolved, not confirmed purchases by known terrorists. Federal law also bars known terrorists from buying guns, and fact-checking organizations have found the claim unsupported.

claim: "Nearly 200,000 Florida voters may not be citizens."
rationale: The headline figure originated from a flawed cross‑match of Florida DMV records and voter rolls that produced many false positives (name mismatches, duplicates, people who later naturalized, and data-entry errors). Independent fact‑checks and state/local follow‑ups found only a tiny number of confirmed noncitizen registrants or voters, so the claim that "nearly 200,000" Florida voters may not be citizens is misleading. The underlying data and matching methodology, not evidence of widespread noncitizen voting, explain the large number.

claim: A Trump television ad shows Mexicans swarming over "our southern border."
rationale: While Trump campaign ads have used footage of migrants crossing the U.S. southern border and audio referencing 'our southern border,' those videos do not specifically identify the people shown as Mexican and the descriptor 'swarming' is subjective. Publicly known ads typically used footage of migrant caravans composed largely of Central American migrants and generic border-crossing clips, so the precise claim that the ad 'shows Mexicans swarming' is not supported.

claim: Says Democratic opponents Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies.
rationale: The statement treats both Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith as supporters of 'sanctuary policies,' but their records differ. Erica Smith, a progressive, has backed strong immigrant protections and limited cooperation with ICE, whereas Cal Cunningham has taken more moderate stances—supporting DACA and comprehensive reform but not endorsing sanctuary-city policies. Lumping them together as both supporting sanctuary policies is therefore misleading.

claim: Says Kentucky Attorney General Daniel Cameron "married his mentor Mitch McConnell's granddaughter."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public biographical information showing Kentucky AG Daniel Cameron married a granddaughter of Senator Mitch McConnell. Cameron has political ties to McConnell, which may explain the 'mentor' language, but the specific claim that he married McConnell's granddaughter is unsubstantiated. Public records and mainstream news coverage of both men’s families do not support this assertion.

claim: "In 2009, Jim Doyle and the Democrats rushed through a budget repair bill with billions in tax increases and held no public hearings."
rationale: This claim is false and appears to conflate events. The high-profile controversy over a rushed “budget repair” measure and limited public hearings occurred in 2011 under Governor Scott Walker, not in 2009 under Democrat Jim Doyle. In 2009 Doyle and the legislature processed the biennial budget through the normal committee and floor process; there is no substantiated record that Democrats in 2009 rushed a budget repair bill with no public hearings as described.

claim: "Our minority graduation rate went from levels below Milwaukee and Madison, to above 80%" when I was Beloit school superintendent.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim with the information provided. The statement names a precise change in 'minority graduation rate' relative to Milwaukee and Madison while citing an individual’s tenure as superintendent, but no time frame, cohort definition, or independently verifiable data are provided; public state and district graduation statistics would be required to confirm it. Because the claim is specific and uncorroborated here, I treat it as unverified (reported as FALSE).

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The claim states these acts can be felonies in Florida, which is accurate: odometer tampering is criminalized as a felony in Florida, and statutes protect marine traps such that disturbing or tampering with lobster traps can be charged as a felony. Purchasing marijuana can also be a felony depending on quantity/intent (trafficking or possession above statutory thresholds), though small personal amounts are typically misdemeanors. So the examples can be felonies, but applicability depends on facts and amounts.

claim: "It’s been proven over and over again Medicaid has the worst outcomes in the industrialized world as far as the quality of health care."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad assertion not supported by evidence. Research comparing Medicaid beneficiaries to privately insured patients shows mixed results—worse outcomes on some measures, similar outcomes on others—and international comparisons are not straightforward because Medicaid is a U.S. program covering a specific low-income population, not a national health system. There is no robust body of evidence proving Medicaid has the worst quality outcomes across the industrialized world on all or most measures.

claim: "This kind of snowstorm happens every 10 or 15 years."
rationale: The statement is a vague, unsubstantiated periodicity claim with no region, storm type, or data cited. Snowstorm frequency varies by location, season, and climate patterns, and most storms do not follow a strict 10–15 year cycle without supporting climatological analysis. Without specific historical records or definitions, the claim cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: "In 2014 ... in McDowell County, W.Va., one of the poorest counties in the nation, life expectancy for men was 64 years. In Fairfax County, Va., a wealthy county, just 350 miles away, life expectancy was nearly 82 years, an 18 year differential. The life expectancy gap for women in the two counties was 12 years."
rationale: Multiple reputable county-level life expectancy estimates for 2014 (reported by major outlets and based on national mortality data) show McDowell County, WV had male life expectancy around 64 years while Fairfax County, VA was about 81–82 years, a roughly 18-year gap; the female gap between those counties is commonly reported at about 12 years. These figures come from standardized county mortality analyses for 2014 and were widely cited in news coverage of geographic health disparities.

claim: The New York Times published an old stock photo of a young girl and claimed Israeli forces killed her during its recent war with Hamas.
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that The New York Times recently published an old stock photo of a young girl and explicitly claimed Israeli forces killed her as stated. Claims like this have circulated on social media in past conflicts, but reputable fact‑checkers and NYT corrections are typically cited when such a major miscaptioning occurs; no clear, verifiable instance matching this exact allegation was found. Without a specific date, photo, or article, the broad claim appears to be a mischaracterization or an unverified social‑media claim.

claim: "Medicare does just as good, if not better, at keeping people healthy" as Medicare Advantage.
rationale: This broad claim is not supported by consensus evidence. Comparative studies show mixed, outcome-specific results—Medicare Advantage often performs as well or better on many preventive care measures and some utilization outcomes, while findings for mortality and complex-care outcomes are mixed and confounded by selection bias. Because results vary by metric and population, it is incorrect to state categorically that traditional Medicare does ‘just as good, if not better.’

claim: Says Jacob Blake "declared he had a gun in the car and was going to go get it" and was "brandishing" a knife
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Jacob Blake himself declared he had a gun in the car and said he was going to retrieve it; officers' audio contains warnings about a possible weapon and at least one officer said he had a knife, but footage does not show Blake verbally announcing a plan to get a gun nor clearly brandishing a weapon. Investigations and video reviews recovered only a small folding knife associated with Blake and did not find a firearm in the car.

claim: "Iraq is costing each household about $100 a month."
rationale: The claim is presented without timeframe or which country’s households it refers to, so as a blanket statement it is misleading. Estimates of the Iraq war’s cost vary widely (trillions of dollars over many years) and per-household figures depend on time period and accounting rules; depending on assumptions you can get numbers below or above $100/month, so the unqualified claim is not reliably true. Without precise boundaries it cannot be affirmed.

claim: "If Sen. Hillary Clinton could enact all of her campaign proposals, taxpayers would be faced with financing more than $777.6-billion in new spending over one White House term."
rationale: This figure appears to be a partisan, aggregate tally of gross costs for selected proposals rather than a vetted, nonpartisan estimate of net taxpayer outlays over one term. Hillary Clinton's campaign included specified funding sources and offsets for several major items, and independent analyses did not support a single uncontested $777.6 billion net taxpayer burden over a four-year term.

claim: "I have a record on the environment of creating green energy ... taking trash and turning it into cash."
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks verifiable specifics (no named speaker, dates, programs, or documented accomplishments). Without independent evidence of concrete green-energy projects or profitable waste-to-energy initiatives tied to the speaker, the assertion cannot be substantiated. Given the missing details, I classify it as false under uncertainty.

claim: "The Texas unemployment rate is now the lowest it’s been in 40 years & Texas led the nation last month in new job creation."
rationale: I cannot confirm the two time‑sensitive assertions without current Bureau of Labor Statistics / Texas Workforce Commission data. My cutoff is June 2024 and monthly unemployment and job‑creation rankings change; the claim bundles two specific, date‑dependent facts (lowest in 40 years and led the nation last month) with no source, so it should be treated as unverified and therefore judged false here. To verify would require the latest state unemployment rate and the most recent month’s BLS state job‑change rankings.

claim: "Zach Nunn took money from Adventureland’s CEO, then sponsored legislation to loosen amusement park safety rules. A child died. Zach Nunn put his big donor first, ahead of the safety of Iowa families."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Zach Nunn sponsored federal legislation to loosen amusement-park safety rules or that he prioritized a specific big donor from Adventureland over safety. Amusement ride safety is primarily regulated at the state level, and I am not aware of reporting showing Nunn authored or sponsored a bill to relax those rules or of a documented causal link between any contribution he received and a child’s death. The allegation combines multiple claims (donation, bill sponsorship, and causal responsibility for a death) that are not substantiated by available public records or credible news reporting.

claim: "The yearly cost of religious tax exemptions: $71 billion. If the church paid taxes, everyone would only have to pay 3% taxes."
rationale: The claim conflates an uncertain estimate of tax benefits for religious organizations with an implausible macroeconomic effect. Even if religious tax exemptions amounted to ~$71 billion a year, U.S. federal revenues and spending are in the trillions, so $71 billion could not plausibly reduce everyone's overall tax burden to “only 3%.” The statement also ambiguously refers to “the church” and specific taxes without evidence linking the figure to a universal 3% rate cut.

claim: A photo of Pete Buttigieg in a military uniform without visible patches shows that "he is a fraud."
rationale: The absence of visible patches in a single photograph does not prove someone is a fraud. Pete Buttigieg has publicly documented service in the U.S. Navy Reserve and a deployment to Afghanistan; photographic cropping, angle, lighting, or low resolution can obscure patches and uniforms, and proving fraud requires stronger evidence such as forged records or contradicted service history.

claim: In the recent House special election in Florida, Democrats "got outspent in a Republican district."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which Florida House special election is meant. Spending in Florida special elections has varied by race and cycle — in some recently Republicans outspent Democrats, in others Democrats outspent Republicans — so the blanket claim that Democrats “got outspent in a Republican district” is too vague and cannot be confirmed. Without a specific district and spending totals, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Bikers show up to The Walter Reed Hospital to pray for President Trump."
rationale: There is no reliable, verifiable evidence that an organized group of bikers specifically showed up at Walter Reed Hospital to pray for President Trump as a documented, recurring event. While media reported that supporters gathered outside Walter Reed during Trump's treatment, those accounts describe mixed crowds and vehicles — not a confirmed biker prayer vigil as the claim asserts.

claim: A study found an "82% miscarriage rate" among women between 30 days and 20 weeks pregnant who got an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: No credible, peer‑reviewed study has reported an 82% miscarriage rate after mRNA COVID‑19 vaccination. Large surveillance and cohort analyses (including the NEJM v‑safe/CDC preliminary report and multiple subsequent studies) found miscarriage rates near the expected background (roughly 10–20%), and the 82% figure traces to misinterpretation of very limited or non‑peer‑reviewed data or raw report counts, not an incidence study.

claim: "Every poll you see, the overwhelming majority of people want [E-Verify]."
rationale: The statement is overly absolute. While many polls have found majority support for E-Verify, not every poll does and the size of support varies widely depending on question wording, sample and timing, so claiming an "overwhelming majority" in every poll is inaccurate.

claim: "Joe Biden tells voters he's 'going to beat Joe Biden.'"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified footage showing President Biden telling voters “I’m going to beat Joe Biden.” In his public remarks about elections he consistently says he will beat Donald Trump; clips asserting he said he would beat himself are attributable to edits, misquotes, or misinterpretation.

claim: "Since 2001, higher education in the state has been cut or allowed to erode ... by 35 or 40 percent."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it fails to specify which state or what metric (e.g., appropriations, per-student funding, faculty positions, or total budget) was reduced by 35–40% since 2001. State higher-education funding trends vary widely: some states saw deep cuts after the 2008 recession while others did not, and changes depend on whether you measure nominal dollars, inflation-adjusted dollars, or per-student allocations. Without those specifics the broad numeric assertion cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: "The average age of first marijuana use is 12."
rationale: This claim is inconsistent with national survey data and epidemiological studies, which report typical age of first cannabis use in the mid-to-late teenage years (usually around 16–18), not 12. Age 12 would be far below the population average and more characteristic of a small subset of early initiators rather than the overall mean or median.

claim: "If you became a Medicaid recipient through the Obamacare expansion, you are grandfathered in."
rationale: The statement is false. The ACA Medicaid expansion made more adults eligible in states that chose to expand, but it did not create a blanket "grandfathered" status guaranteeing lifetime coverage. Expansion enrollees remain subject to normal Medicaid eligibility rules, redeterminations, and possible state policy changes that can end or alter coverage.

claim: "The Coast Guard confiscated 200 tons of contraband, heroin, and so forth. At the border they collected 20 tons."
rationale: The statement gives two precise tonnage figures without a timeframe or source and mixes unspecified categories ("contraband, heroin, and so forth"). Public drug-seizure reporting shows heroin is almost always reported in kilograms, not hundreds of tons, and official Coast Guard or border-agency annual reports do not support confiscations of 200 tons of heroin or 20 tons of heroin at the border. Without a clear source or timeframe the numbers are misleading and inconsistent with typical law-enforcement statistics.

claim: "They (Clinton and Obama) have never to my knowledge been involved in legislation nor hearings nor engagement on this issue (climate change)."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: both Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have been actively involved on climate change through legislation, policy and diplomatic engagement. Obama championed climate policy as a senator and especially as president (e.g., Clean Power Plan, U.S. role in the Paris Agreement and regulatory actions via the EPA), and Clinton supported climate legislation as a senator and led U.S. climate diplomacy as Secretary of State and as a presidential candidate. These are direct examples of engagement in legislation, hearings and policy on climate change.

claim: "We have more people working in the state of New Jersey today than we've ever had in our history."
rationale: The claim is an unqualified statement about a historical peak but employment measures vary and have changed over time: New Jersey had record nonfarm payrolls in Feb 2020, then a COVID-era drop, and recovery that may or may not exceed prior peaks depending on the exact measure and date. Because the statement gives no date or definition of 'working' (payroll jobs vs. employed residents), there is insufficient evidence to support a blanket claim that today's level is the highest ever. I therefore judge the broad claim false pending specific data.

claim: Says Obama policies contributed to gas prices rising from $1.89 in January 2009 to $3.51 today.
rationale: The claim implies Obama’s policies were the primary cause of gasoline rising from about $1.89 in Jan 2009 to $3.51 later, which is misleading. National pump prices mainly track global crude oil prices and supply/demand (including OPEC production and global economic recovery after 2009); U.S. domestic oil production actually rose during the Obama years from the shale boom, which would tend to reduce pressure on prices. Presidential policy can have some influence (regulation, leases, SPR releases), but it is not the dominant driver of the large price swing cited.

claim: "Some people are going to die from the vaccine directly. But a large number of people are going to start getting horribly sick and get all kinds of autoimmune diseases."
rationale: Large-scale safety monitoring of authorized vaccines has not shown they cause widespread deaths or a surge of autoimmune diseases. Very rare serious adverse events (and exceedingly rare deaths) have been causally linked in isolated cases, but evidence does not support the claim that "a large number" will become horribly sick or develop all kinds of autoimmune disorders.

claim: "Gov. (Rick) Perry helped balance his budget with about $6 billion worth of federal help, which he happily took, and then started blaming the members of Congress who had offered that help."
rationale: This claim mixes facts and a politicized interpretation. Texas did receive billions in federal stimulus and temporary Medicaid (FMAP) boosts during the recession that eased state budget gaps, and some estimates for particular years approach several billion dollars, but the precise ‘‘about $6 billion’’ figure and the broad assertion that Perry then turned and blamed the specific members of Congress who offered that help is not supported by a clear contemporaneous record. Perry often accepted federal dollars for programs while publicly criticizing federal policies or the Obama administration, but saying he ‘‘happily took $6 billion and then blamed the members of Congress who offered it’’ oversimplifies and conflates separate events and rhetoric.

claim: "Speaker Gingrich for 20 years supported a federal individual mandate" for health insurance.
rationale: Gingrich did endorse an individual mandate-style idea at various points (especially in the late 1980s and early 1990s), but his public positions were inconsistent and often framed around state-level reforms rather than a continuous, 20-year endorsement of a federal individual mandate. He also made statements opposing a federal mandate after Obamacare and shifted emphasis over time, so the claim of uninterrupted 20-year support for a federal mandate is not supported by the record.

claim: Says President Dwight Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out of this country."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While the Eisenhower administration oversaw large-scale immigration enforcement (notably the 1954 'Operation Wetback'), contemporary records and historical research indicate far fewer formal deportations in a single operation (hundreds of thousands in 1954) and administration-era INS removal totals usually cited around 1.1–1.3 million when counting voluntary repatriations and other returns; the 1.5 million figure overstates and conflates different categories and episodes. Moreover, many people removed or repatriated included U.S. citizens or were voluntary returns, so calling them all 'illegal immigrants' is inaccurate.

claim: "Texas law enforcement officer fatally shot upon arriving for work by 3 Muslim refugee."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official records of a Texas law enforcement officer being fatally shot upon arriving for work by three Muslim refugees. High‑profile killings of officers are widely reported by local and national media and by law enforcement agencies; no incident matching these specific details can be found. The claim appears to invent or conflate details (number of attackers, motives, refugee status) without evidence.

claim: Says the U.S. gives Israel "$3 billion annually" in aid and zero to Detroit.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. While U.S. assistance to Israel is commonly cited at about $3 billion a year (more precisely roughly $3.3 billion annually in FMF under the 2016 MOU, plus missile-defense assistance), the federal government does not give Detroit "zero" — the city and its residents receive federal funds via grants, transportation funding, Medicaid, disaster and pandemic relief (e.g., CARES/ARP), and other programs. Thus the juxtaposition that Israel gets $3 billion and Detroit gets nothing is false.

claim: "If Obamacare is fully implemented, 30 million people will still be without health insurance."
rationale: The statement as an absolute is misleading. Official budget- and health-agency projections (e.g., CBO/CMS estimates) commonly projected that the uninsured would fall substantially under full ACA implementation and in many baseline scenarios were in the low- to mid-20 millions rather than exactly 30 million; however, alternate assumptions (state Medicaid non‑expansion, definitions, timing) can produce estimates near 30 million. Because outcomes vary by assumptions, the blanket claim that 30 million will still be uninsured under full implementation is not strictly true.

claim: "Pfizer CEO has not yet had vaccine."
rationale: The claim is false as stated: Pfizer’s CEO (Albert Bourla) has publicly said and been reported to have received a COVID-19 vaccine since vaccines became available. The statement omits any timeframe and may have been true briefly before he was vaccinated, but is not correct now.

claim: Says he got "support all over Raleigh"
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it lacks a named speaker, timeframe, and concrete evidence. Saying someone got 'support all over Raleigh' is a broad, subjective assertion that requires independent data (polls, endorsements, turnout, or reporting) to confirm; without that, it cannot be treated as factual.

claim: By allowing brewpubs to sell beer, Georgia could become like Mexico with only a couple of manufacturers controlling all aspects of market.
rationale: The claim is speculative and not supported by historical or economic evidence. Allowing brewpubs to sell beer typically increases retail channels for small local breweries and tends to boost competition rather than create a market dominated by a few firms. Mexico’s concentration is the result of decades of mergers, national distribution networks, and corporate consolidation—factors a single change in Georgia’s brewpub sales rules would not by itself reproduce.

claim: The United States is "the only developed country in the world that has not cut its corporate tax rate."
rationale: The statement is incorrect. The U.S. enacted a major corporate tax cut in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (federal rate fell from 35% to 21%), and moreover the absolute claim that the U.S. was the only developed country that had not cut corporate taxes is not supported — corporate tax rates have changed in many developed countries over recent decades and the comparison depends on timing and whether one looks at statutory vs effective or combined rates.

claim: Under the new Arizona immigration law, police can't stop someone to check their immigration status unless they think they see something illegal.
rationale: The statement misrepresents Arizona's enforcement standard. Arizona's law (famously SB 1070 and similar later measures) permits officers during a lawful stop, detention, or arrest to inquire about immigration status when they have reasonable suspicion the person is unlawfully present — it does not require that the officer first observe a separate criminal act. Saying police "can't stop someone to check" unless they see something illegal therefore oversimplifies and reverses the law's actual trigger.

claim: "Bernie Sanders wants free health care for all and was asked how he would pay for it. His answer was raise taxes to 52% on anybody making over $29,000 per year."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has advocated Medicare-for-All (universally funded health care) and proposed funding it through employer contributions, specific new taxes and higher taxes on high earners, but he never proposed a blanket 52% tax starting at $29,000. The 52%/"over $29,000" claim misstates his proposals and appears to conflate or misinterpret combined employer/employee charges or hypothetical combined tax incidence rather than an explicit 52% income tax at that low threshold.

claim: Says an appointed board created under Obamacare "will have the ability to come between you and your doctor in determining the best treatment options for you!"
rationale: The claim misstates the role created under the Affordable Care Act (commonly cited as the Independent Payment Advisory Board or similar advisory bodies). That board was authorized to make cost-control recommendations for Medicare, not to directly make clinical decisions or ‘come between’ a patient and their doctor, and the statute included prohibitions on recommendations that would ration care or restrict the doctor–patient relationship.

claim: "The number of killings of citizens by police is at a two-decade high."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not verifiable as stated because it gives no country or time reference; available U.S. data show spikes in some years (notably 2020) but totals have fluctuated and recent years are not uniformly higher than the highest years of the past two decades. Different reputable trackers and the FBI use varying definitions and count methods, so no clear consensus supports a blanket statement that police killings are at a two-decade high right now.

claim: Says he banned texting while driving in Austin.
rationale: The claim is vague about who “he” is and implies a single person unilaterally banned texting while driving in Austin. Traffic regulations are enacted by legislatures or city councils and enforced under state/local law; there is no evidence a single individual imposed such a ban on their own. Austin is governed by municipal ordinance and Texas distracted-driving laws rather than unilateral executive action by one person.

claim: Says Christopher Little has "a history of working against environmental protection by defending the worst types of corporate polluters"
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written: 'Christopher Little' is a common name and no clear, corroborated public record ties a person by that name to a documented pattern of defending 'the worst types of corporate polluters.' Without identifying which Christopher Little (employer, location, or specific cases), the allegation cannot be verified and available biographical/news sources do not support the claim.

claim: Says Barack Obama "robbed Medicare (of) $716 billion to pay for ... Obamacare."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The Affordable Care Act included provisions that federal analysts (CBO and the Medicare actuary) estimated would reduce Medicare spending by about $716 billion over roughly a decade, but those were cuts to projected payments (eg, reduced overpayments to Medicare Advantage and slower provider payment growth), not a literal seizure of beneficiary benefits or trust funds to ‘pay for’ Obamacare. In short, there were projected Medicare savings used to help offset ACA costs, not an outright robbery of Medicare dollars.

claim: "This election marks the largest Senate gains for a president's party in a first midterm election since at least President Kennedy's in 1962."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because the president’s party gained more Senate seats in other first midterms since 1962 — most notably in 2002 when Republicans (under President George W. Bush) netted two Senate seats in his first midterm. Therefore saying the referenced election was the largest Senate gain for a president’s party since 1962 is false.

claim: "Faced with $1 million in campaign debt," Scott Walker "is unloading his campaign security costs onto the backs of Wisconsin taxpayers."
rationale: The claim overstates and simplifies a complicated record. While news reports documented instances where state-paid security accompanied Walker on some campaign appearances and there were questions about reimbursement practices, there is no clear evidence he systematically shifted campaign security costs to taxpayers to pay off $1 million in campaign debt. State law enforcement routinely provides protective details for governors for official duties, and reporting shows a mix of reimbursements and disputed charges rather than an intentional, comprehensive unloading of campaign expenses onto taxpayers.

claim: "Criminals don’t go through (gun) background checks. I think it’s like 3% go through a background check."
rationale: The claim is a misleading oversimplification. Government surveys of people incarcerated for firearms offenses and independent fact-checks find that the sources of crime guns vary and a larger, context-dependent share obtain guns via legal purchases, transfers, straw purchases, or theft—not exclusively outside background-check systems—and the ‘‘3%’’ figure is not supported as a general estimate. Thus the blanket statement that criminals don’t go through background checks and only ~3% do is inaccurate.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and likely incorrect as written. Depending on the exact two‑year window, super PAC fundraising totals and source breakdowns vary: major trackers (e.g., OpenSecrets) show super PACs raised well over $180 million in recent two‑year cycles, and while a small number of wealthy donors provide a large share, the ‘half from fewer than 200 people’ and ‘roughly 20% from corporations’ figures do not match consistently reported aggregates and depend on the exact time period and classification rules. Because the claim gives precise proportions without a clear timeframe or source, it is unreliable.

claim: Georgia has recovered more than $60 million that was lost to Medicaid fraud
rationale: The statement presents a specific dollar figure without a timeframe or source and I cannot confirm from authoritative public records that Georgia has recovered more than $60 million specifically for Medicaid fraud. Official recovery totals for Medicaid fraud vary by year and by reporting agency (Attorney General, Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, Department of Community Health), and available summaries do not unambiguously support this standalone claim. Without a cited period or official report, the claim is not verifiable as stated.

claim: Annual precipitation "has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century."
rationale: Regional and state climate analyses for the Northeastern U.S., including Rhode Island, show increased annual precipitation over the 20th century, but the magnitude is generally a few inches to around 5–10 inches rather than an increase exceeding 12 inches. The claim overstates the documented change for Rhode Island across standard century-long baselines and observational records.

claim: "After years of 5.5 percent average tuition increases, we now have a two-year tuition freeze for the first time in the history of the UW System."
rationale: The claim bundles two specific assertions that are not supported as stated. Average systemwide tuition increases of exactly 5.5% over unspecified years is a precise figure that is not verifiable without a defined timeframe, and the University of Wisconsin System has a long history (established in 1971) with prior periods where tuition was limited or frozen at system or campus levels, so a two‑year freeze is unlikely to be literally the "first time" in its history. Because the statement mixes an unsupported average and an absolute historical first, it is misleading and therefore judged false.
