claim: "In the last decade, the average income of the bottom 90 percent of all working Americans actually declined. The top 1 percent saw their income rise by an average of more than a quarter of a million dollars each."
rationale: The claim is overbroad and depends on unspecified timing and definitions. Public data (CBO, IRS/Saez and other household-income series) show the top 1% did see large gains in many recent years, but whether their average income rose by “more than a quarter of a million dollars” and whether the bottom 90%’s average income “actually declined” varies by the exact decade, whether you count pre- or post-tax income, and whether you use workers vs. households or mean vs. median. For many plausible 10‑year spans (especially after the Great Recession) bottom‑90 incomes rose modestly rather than declined, so the categorical phrasing is inaccurate.

claim: Democrats "want to tax your retirement funds to pay for their new trillion dollar power grab."
rationale: The claim is a misleading generalization: while some Democratic lawmakers have proposed tax changes or limits on tax-advantaged retirement benefits for high-income taxpayers, there is no unified Democratic plan to broadly "tax your retirement funds" to finance a singular "trillion dollar power grab." The phrase "power grab" is partisan rhetoric and not a factual description of specific budget proposals, and proposed revenue changes typically target higher earners or specific rules rather than blanket taxation of ordinary retirement accounts.

claim: The health care law was "a 2,733-page bill! . . . No amendments!"
rationale: This is misleading. The Affordable Care Act’s page count varies by which documents are combined (the main PPACA text is often cited around 2,400 pages and the law plus reconciliation/attachments approaches the mid‑2,700s), but the law was not passed “with no amendments” — it resulted from committee markups, floor amendments, and a separate reconciliation bill and changes during the legislative process. Saying it was a single unamendable 2,733‑page bill is inaccurate.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: The claim combines a luxury fashion label (Saint Laurent) with ‘government issue’, which is inconsistent: governments procure standardized protective gear from industrial/safety suppliers, not couture houses. Saint Laurent is a fashion brand and has not been known to produce government-issued hazardous-materials suits; any resemblance in a photo could be a fashion piece or a look-alike, not official government PPE.

claim: With voting by mail, "you get thousands and thousands of people sitting in somebody's living room, signing ballots all over the place."
rationale: The claim describes a widespread, systemic phenomenon of thousands of people fraudulently signing ballots in living rooms, but empirical investigations and post-election audits have not found evidence of such large-scale, repeated schemes tied to voting by mail. Mail ballots are typically recorded, signature-verified, and processed by election officials with chain-of-custody procedures; while isolated cases of illegal ballot collection or forgery have occurred, they are rare and do not support the broad, generalized assertion in the claim.

claim: "As the election tracker FiveThirtyEight has reported, whoever wins Pennsylvania will be our next President."
rationale: This is false: the U.S. president is decided by the Electoral College, and FiveThirtyEight provides probabilistic forecasts showing many possible paths to 270 electoral votes. While FiveThirtyEight has at times identified Pennsylvania as a pivotal state in a particular election map, it does not assert as a general rule that whoever wins Pennsylvania will necessarily be the next president.

claim: In 2013, under a Democratic Senate, "a majority of the Senate voted in favor of" gun-related legislation sponsored by Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ted Cruz, "but the Democrats filibustered it."
rationale: The 2013 high-profile gun measure expanding background checks was the Manchin-Toomey amendment (sponsored by Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin and Republican Sen. Pat Toomey), not a Grassley/Cruz bill. A cloture motion on that amendment did receive majority support (54–46) but failed to reach the 60 votes needed, and it was Senate Republicans who opposed/blocked cloture — not Democrats. Thus the claim that Democrats filibustered a Grassley/Cruz-sponsored gun bill is incorrect.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Faso "voted for an age tax on seniors."
rationale: The phrase “voted for an age tax on seniors” is misleading and there is no roll-call creating a tax that charges people based on their age. Congressional voting records do not show John Faso voting for any bill that levied taxes specifically by age; while he did vote for broader tax legislation (e.g., the 2017 tax bill) that affected many taxpayers including some seniors, that is not an age-based tax. Thus the claim as stated is false or at least a mischaracterization.

claim: Scott Maddox is a "lobbyist."
rationale: Scott Maddox is primarily known as a former Tallahassee mayor and Florida political operative who was later indicted and convicted in a federal corruption probe; he is not widely described as a professional lobbyist. While he had connections to consultants and lobbyists and may have done consulting work, calling him a lobbyist as a primary label is misleading without evidence of registered lobbying activity.

claim: Ninety-seven percent of Americans do not receive subsidies for health care under the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: The claim is misleading. If one counts only marketplace premium tax credit recipients (roughly 8–11 million people, about 2–3% of the U.S. population) then most Americans do not get those particular credits, but the statement ignores Medicaid/CHIP expansion and other ACA assistance that cover many additional people. Without defining “subsidies” or a time frame the 97% figure is not a reliable general claim.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available labor‑market data. Official statistics (Bureau of Labor Statistics, NCES and other surveys) show unemployment for recent college graduates is generally in the single digits, and even broader measures of underemployment do not show half of graduates unable to find any job nationwide. The statement likely conflates different measures or relies on anecdote rather than representative data.

claim: "20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of (Obamacare)."
rationale: The claim presents a precise, causal number without a cited timeframe or source; available reporting from the ACA rollout shows insurers sent cancellation notices to many plans but state data typically counted canceled policies (not unique people) and do not support a verified figure of exactly 20,000 Kansans who permanently ‘lost their health insurance because of Obamacare.’ Many affected enrollees obtained replacement coverage through employers, the marketplaces, or Medicaid over time, so the blanket causal claim is not supported.

claim: "According to (Barack) Obama’s newest unconstitutionally enacted law, health care professionals are now required to violate HIPAA privacy laws and submit medical data to the government," which is "then used as justification for gun confiscation."
rationale: The claim is false. There is no federal law enacted during Obama’s presidency (or since) that requires health care professionals to violate HIPAA and routinely submit patients’ medical data to the government to be used for automatic gun confiscation. HIPAA still limits disclosures and only permits release of health information in narrow circumstances (court orders, specific public‑health reporting, threats of harm, or other legally required disclosures); any seizure of firearms generally requires separate legal processes (e.g., court orders or state 'red flag' laws), not a blanket healthcare reporting mandate.

claim: Says we could have saved ourselves the cost of building the Powell Butte water reservoir.
rationale: The statement claims the cost of building the Powell Butte reservoir could have been avoided but offers no evidence. Municipal water agencies typically install reservoirs to meet storage, seismic resilience, regulatory and fire-flow requirements, and documented project studies for Powell Butte concluded that alternatives were infeasible or would not meet those needs without comparable cost.

claim: Under President George W. Bush, "we added $4.9 trillion to the debt. Under President Obama … we’ve added $6.5 trillion to the debt."
rationale: The Bush figure (~$4.9 trillion) matches the increase in total federal debt outstanding from Jan 20, 2001 to Jan 20, 2009, but the Obama figure is incorrect. Total federal debt outstanding rose by about $9.3 trillion from Jan 20, 2009 to Jan 20, 2017, not $6.5 trillion. Thus the claim mixes numbers or uses inconsistent measures/dates and is not accurate as stated.

claim: A video shows "massive explosion as Ukraine destroyed 280 Russian tanks to pieces using U.S. Javelin missiles."
rationale: The claim conflates a dramatic viral video with an implausible battlefield tally. Javelin missiles are single-vehicle anti-tank weapons and destroying 280 tanks would require hundreds of missiles, sustained strikes, and corroboration from multiple credible sources — none of which exist for this specific video. Viral footage of large explosions has previously been misattributed to impressive kills when it more plausibly shows depot or munitions detonations or unrelated incidents.

claim: Claims Joe Biden said "coal is more dangerous than terrorists."
rationale: There is no credible transcript or reliable news reporting showing Joe Biden saying the exact line "coal is more dangerous than terrorists." Biden has criticized coal for its environmental and public-health impacts, but the specific quote appears to be a mischaracterization or fabrication rather than a documented statement. Fact-checks and available public remarks attribute criticisms of coal to Biden without that literal comparison to terrorists.

claim: "Thom Tillis cut almost $500 million from education."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and not supported by clear evidence tying Thom Tillis personally to an almost $500 million cut to education. While Tillis was part of Republican leadership in North Carolina when budgets reduced some education spending, budget changes are collective legislative actions and no authoritative summary attributes a nearly $500 million cut solely to him. Without a specific jurisdiction or year the figure appears misleading.

claim: "You didn't see Republicans when we had control of the Senate try to rig the game."
rationale: The claim denies that Senate Republicans ever tried to “rig the game,” but historical actions by Republican Senate majorities contradict that. Examples include refusing in 2016 to hold hearings for President Obama's Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland and later using the so-called 'nuclear option' in 2017 to lower the threshold for Supreme Court confirmation, both widely described as changing rules to secure partisan advantage.

claim: "The platform of the Republican Party says deport everybody and to hell with it."
rationale: This is a rhetorical exaggeration. Republican Party platforms have consistently called for stronger border security and enforcement of immigration laws, including removal of unlawfully present immigrants and criminal aliens, but do not literally state “deport everybody” or use the phrase “to hell with it.” The claim misrepresents and overgeneralizes platform language.

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: Contemporary news investigations (notably AP reporting) have found that more than 2,000 people on federal terrorist watchlists were nonetheless able to purchase firearms because watchlist records were not automatically blocking background checks. The No‑Fly/terror watch system restricts air travel but has not been fully integrated with the FBI’s gun background‑check disqualification process, so being on the list has not consistently prevented gun purchases.

claim: "Measles is one of the most common causes of child blindness worldwide."
rationale: Measles has long been a major cause of childhood blindness globally, especially in low-income settings where measles infection and associated vitamin A deficiency cause corneal ulceration and scarring. While improved measles vaccination has sharply reduced this burden in many countries, measles remains one of the common preventable causes of child blindness worldwide overall.

claim: Says Jon Ossoff is "a socialist."
rationale: Jon Ossoff does not identify as a socialist and campaigned as a mainstream/centrist Democrat; his policy positions and endorsements align with establishment Democratic positions rather than democratic socialism. He is not a member of Democratic Socialists of America and is routinely described in media and public records as a moderate Democrat, so calling him "a socialist" is inaccurate.

claim: Says the Obamas are connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or indictment linking Barack or Michelle Obama to the Varsity Blues college admissions bribery scheme. The DOJ investigation and numerous news reports identified specific parents, college coaches, and racketeering facilitators (e.g., Rick Singer) but did not include the Obamas. Claims of Obama involvement appear to be unfounded conspiracies rather than fact-based reporting.

claim: Says coronavirus is just "the damn flu."
rationale: The claim is false: COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, which is a different virus from influenza and has produced greater rates of hospitalization, death, and unique complications (including long COVID) in many populations. Public health data, clinical outcomes, and distinct vaccines/treatments show it is not simply "the flu."

claim: Says Sen. Chuck Schumer in 2014 "helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall" and now opposes Trump's $5 billion request for a border wall "just because he's a Republican." ​
rationale: There is no record that Sen. Chuck Schumer ‘helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall’ in 2014. Major Senate immigration and border-security actions around 2013–2014 did not create a $25 billion dedicated wall deal that Schumer assembled or signed, and the claim about opposing Trump’s $5 billion request ‘just because he’s a Republican’ attributes motive rather than verifiable fact. The assertion conflates different legislative efforts and misstates both the substance and intent of Schumer’s positions.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown "voted to block American energy production and increase energy taxes."
rationale: The claim is a broad, misleading summary that lacks a specific bill or vote. Sherrod Brown has backed environmental regulations and opposed some fossil-fuel projects (for example opposing Keystone XL and supporting clean-energy policies) and has supported certain tax changes, but there is no single recorded vote where he 'voted to block American energy production and increase energy taxes' as a categorical act. Without a specific legislative reference this characterization overstates and conflates multiple positions and votes.

claim: The United States is "about to have the smallest Army since before WWII, the smallest Navy since WWI and the smallest Air Force ever."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported by available historical comparisons. U.S. Army active-duty endstrength today is higher than the very small pre‑WWII peacetime army levels, and claims about the Navy and Air Force depend on which metric (personnel, ships, or aircraft) and which exact year is used; contemporary data do not clearly show all three services are at their smallest levels in the stated historical comparisons. Because the claim conflates different measures and lacks a timeframe, it overstates and mischaracterizes force-size history.

claim: "Florida is now the No. 1 state in the country for automobile accident fraud."
rationale: The claim is too categorical and lacks a defined time period or metric; there is no definitive, single national ranking that consistently shows Florida as "No. 1" for automobile accident fraud across all measures. Florida is frequently cited by insurers and law-enforcement as a high-incidence state for staged-auto and PIP-related fraud, but other states also lead on different metrics (total dollars, per-capita incidents, referrals), and recent national reports do not uniformly place Florida at the top. Without a specific source or metric, the blanket statement that Florida is "now the No. 1 state" is not supported.

claim: The last private rocket launch "cost $80 million. If the government did it, the same thing would have cost probably 40 or 50 times that amount of money. I mean, literally."
rationale: The claim mixes a plausible commercial price with a wildly generalized multiplier. Commercial small-to-medium private launches are often in the tens of millions (an $80M figure is within known commercial price ranges), but saying a government-run version would cost 40–50× more is unsupported and exaggerated. Government programs can be much costlier for some vehicles (e.g., certain heavy-lift government rockets have per-launch costs in the low billions), but many government launches cost similar orders of magnitude to commercial launches, so a blanket 40–50× factor is inaccurate.

claim: "If it weren’t for me … (illegal immigration) wouldn’t even be a big subject."
rationale: The statement is an untestable counterfactual presented as a factual claim that one person alone is responsible for making illegal immigration a major public issue. Historical and political evidence shows illegal immigration has been a prominent topic in U.S. politics and media for decades, across multiple administrations and parties, so it is implausible that it would not be a ‘big subject’ absent a single individual. Therefore the claim is not supportable as a factual statement.

claim: "The Democrat plan would just obliterate Medicare and terminate Medicare Advantage ... seniors who have been paying for this for years (and) will not be taken care of anymore."
rationale: The claim mischaracterizes mainstream Democratic proposals. Major Democratic platforms and leaders have generally promoted preserving or expanding Medicare (and enacting measures like drug-price negotiation or a public option), not “obliterating” it or wholesale terminating Medicare Advantage; while a subset of progressives back Medicare-for-All (a single‑payer proposal that would replace private plans), that is not a unified Democratic plan to eliminate Medicare and leave seniors uncovered.

claim: The changes to Georgia’s tax and fee structure "is an overall tax cut."
rationale: The statement is too general and unsubstantiated as written: whether a package of changes is an “overall tax cut” depends on the specific provisions, net revenue impact, and timeframe. Many proposals or laws combine tax rate reductions with new or increased fees or narrowed tax bases that can offset or exceed cut amounts, and impacts differ across taxpayers. Without a concrete bill and official revenue estimates showing a net, sustained decline in total tax and fee revenue, the claim cannot be verified.

claim: Says state Senate President Stephen "Sweeney gave us the nation's highest income tax rates, driving out jobs."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. New Jersey never clearly had the nation’s single highest top personal income tax rate during Stephen Sweeney’s tenure (California’s top rate has been higher), and tax-rate changes are enacted by the whole legislature and governor, not a single senator. The assertion that higher rates “drove out jobs” is a strong causal claim that isn’t supported by clear, singular evidence—economic migration and job changes have many causes.

claim: Before 2005, "the percentage of" Texas high school "students meeting the college readiness standards of the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board stood at 28% in English and 42% in math. Those figures stood at 65% and 66% in 2013."
rationale: The specific pair of percentages given (28% English / 42% math before 2005 and 65% / 66% in 2013) do not match published Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board (THECB) data and independent analyses for those years. THECB releases subject-by-subject college readiness rates and while they rose over time, the reported levels and the timing in the claim appear inconsistent with the board's published figures and with common media summaries of those reports. The claim also conflates unclear time frames and measures (e.g., graduates vs. all students, different assessment standards) which makes the exact numbers unlikely to be correct as stated.

claim: The CDC delivers groceries and cleaning products "twice while you’re in quarantine."
rationale: False. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issues public-health guidance and supports response efforts but does not operate a program that delivers groceries or cleaning products to quarantined individuals “twice” (or at all). Delivery assistance during quarantine is typically arranged by local health departments, social services, volunteer groups, or commercial providers, not the CDC itself.

claim: Says Adam Hasner "gives the wealthy tax breaks worth $250,000 a year but hikes middle class taxes $2,000."
rationale: The claim asserts precise dollar amounts but there is no verifiable record that Adam Hasner endorsed a specific tax plan that clearly provided wealthy taxpayers $250,000 per year while raising middle-class taxes by $2,000. Without a named bill, vote, or authoritative fiscal analysis showing those exact figures, the statement appears to be an unverified political attack rather than a documented fact.

claim: "Bryce Reeves chaired a group bankrolled by a New York billionaire who fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China."
rationale: I find no verifiable reporting or public records showing that Sen. Bryce Reeves chaired a group specifically bankrolled by a named New York billionaire who fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China. The claim bundles several specific allegations (chairing a particular group, who funded it, and a mass firing/outsourcing by that funder) that are not corroborated by readily available sources. Given the lack of evidence tying Reeves to such a group and no clear identification of the billionaire or the alleged layoffs/outsourcing, the claim appears unsubstantiated.

claim: Says "$57,000 is the mean [income] in our state" for a family.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it omits which state and which year or data source are meant; U.S. family mean incomes differ substantially by state and over time. Additionally, official statistics more commonly report median rather than mean family income, and 'mean $57,000' may not match recent Census/ACS figures for any given state without specification. Because of these missing details the claim as stated is unreliable.

claim: "The United States is 65th out of 142 nations and other territories on equal pay."
rationale: This specific ranking is not supported by widely used global equality metrics. Major sources such as the World Economic Forum's Global Gender Gap reports and other international comparisons typically place the United States substantially higher on pay-related measures (often in the top 20–40 overall or better on pay equality subindices), not 65th out of 142. The claim lacks a cited year or metric and does not match the commonly reported rankings.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees have long had authority under House rules to take depositions and hold closed sessions (especially for classified or sensitive matters), and the House Intelligence Committee—chaired by Rep. Adam Schiff at the time—conducted closed-door depositions as part of the inquiry. Historical practice shows impeachment inquiries and committee depositions have often been conducted without an initial full House floor vote authorizing each specific closed-door session, so the activity was consistent with committee rules and precedents.

claim: "Hillary Clinton invented ISIS with her stupid policies. She is responsible for ISIS."
rationale: The claim that Hillary Clinton "invented" ISIS is incorrect. ISIS traces its roots to al‑Qaeda in Iraq and figures like Abu Musab al‑Zarqawi after the 2003 U.S. invasion, and its rise was driven by multiple factors including the Iraq war, sectarian policies, regional dynamics and the Syrian civil war, not the actions of a single U.S. official. While U.S. and other countries' policies contributed to conditions that allowed ISIS to grow, attributing sole responsibility to Clinton is factually unsupported.

claim: Says Abraham Lincoln said, "America will never be destroyed from the outside. If we lose our freedoms it will be because we have destroyed ourselves from within."
rationale: There is no evidence in Lincoln’s collected speeches, writings, or contemporary records that he said this. The line appears to be a modern aphorism that surfaced decades after Lincoln’s death and has been widely misattributed to him. Major Lincoln scholars and quotation researchers have not found a primary source linking the sentence to Lincoln.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: The claim that 100% of electric generation in any single U.S. congressional district comes from coal is almost certainly false. Electricity generation in U.S. districts is typically a mix of sources (coal, natural gas, nuclear, hydro, wind, solar) and the grid is interconnected so power flows across boundaries; it is extremely unlikely for generation within a district to be exclusively coal. Even districts with heavy coal plants usually have other generation sources or imports/exports that prevent a true 100% share.

claim: "ISIS is in 32 countries."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by a single authoritative count. Estimates of ISIS presence, affiliate groups, or claimed attacks vary widely by time and definition (control, active cells, affiliates, or claimed attacks), and no consistent, verifiable source confirms exactly "32 countries." Because the number depends on timeframe and definitions, presenting the specific figure as a fact is misleading.

claim: "The average Republican voter thinks there should be some revenue as part of this deal."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be verified: it does not specify which "deal," when, or what phrasing was used. Without a cited, contemporaneous poll showing a clear majority of Republican voters favoring "some revenue" as part of that specific deal, the statement cannot be treated as factual. Republican voter views vary by issue and over time, so asserting the average favors revenue is unsupported.

claim: Says Julie Parrish is "one of Sarah Palin’s mama grizzlies."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Sarah Palin designated Julie Parrish as one of her branded 'mama grizzlies.' Palin's 'mama grizzlies' label referred to a specific set of female conservative candidates she promoted in 2010, and commonly cited endorsement lists do not include Julie Parrish. The claim appears to be unsubstantiated by available public reporting.

claim: Georgia’s unemployment rate has exceeded the national rate for 50 consecutive months.
rationale: The claim asserts a very specific, long uninterrupted run (50 months) that would be verifiable from monthly BLS state and national unemployment series. In practice state unemployment rates fluctuate relative to the national rate, and Georgia has not consistently been above the national rate for a continuous ~4+ year span in recent years; such a precise claim requires current BLS monthly data and is unlikely to be correct without citation. I therefore judge the claim to be false pending a direct check of the BLS series.

claim: Says he did not tell former President Barack Obama "don’t go" after Osama bin Laden
rationale: The claim is vague and there is no verifiable public record of a named individual explicitly saying they told President Obama "don’t go" after the Osama bin Laden operation or later asserting they did not say that. Major reporting on the 2011 raid records discussions among Obama and senior advisers but does not document this quoted exchange; without a specified speaker or reliable source the statement cannot be substantiated and is likely false.

claim: "The only segment in the beer market that is growing is the craft beer segment."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because other beer/alcohol segments have also shown growth; for example, hard seltzers and flavored malt beverages, some premium/import lager lines, and non‑alcoholic beers have expanded in many markets. Craft beer has been a growth driver historically but is not the sole growing segment and has even slowed or declined in some regions and periods.

claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics "supports banning guns."
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. The American Academy of Pediatrics has advocated for gun safety policies—like universal background checks, safe storage, limiting access for those at high risk, and bans on specific weapons (e.g., assault weapons/high-capacity magazines)—but it does not call for a blanket ban on all guns. Statements saying the AAP "supports banning guns" conflate its support for targeted restrictions with an advocacy for a total firearm ban.

claim: Under President Barack Obama’s leadership, "since June 2009, (the auto) industry has added a quarter of a million jobs."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not clearly supported by standard labor data. BLS payroll series for motor-vehicle manufacturing and related dealer/parts categories show different job counts depending on which sectors are included and what end date is used; using conservative, commonly cited categories and mid‑2010s endpoints the gain is generally smaller than 250,000. Because the statement does not define “auto industry” or the precise end date, the assertion that it added a quarter‑million jobs since June 2009 is not reliably true as stated.

claim: The state crime lab under Attorney General Josh Kaul "is testing significantly less items than former AG Brad Schimel and is still taking longer to test many categories of key items in comparison to Schimel, including DNA."
rationale: Available public information (state DOJ crime lab annual reports and statements) does not support a blanket claim that the lab under AG Josh Kaul is testing ‘significantly less’ across the board or uniformly taking longer than under Brad Schimel. Testing volumes and turnaround times have fluctuated year-to-year and by evidence category, with the Kaul administration reporting investments and efforts to reduce backlogs; some categories improved while others varied due to staffing, pandemic impacts, and changes in submissions. The original claim overgeneralizes and appears to cherry‑pick measures rather than reflect consistent, broad declines in testing and speed.

claim: "The  firefighters, the policemen and others who supported (Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker) in his election bid ... don't have to worry about their collective bargaining rights."
rationale: False. Governor Walker’s 2011 “budget repair” reforms (Act 10) substantially curtailed collective bargaining for most public employees; although police and firefighters were treated differently than other public workers, they were not guaranteed full, unchanged bargaining rights and still faced new limits and required contributions. Thus the blanket claim that those who supported him “don’t have to worry” about their collective bargaining rights is misleading and incorrect.

claim: "There's one (study) that came out of Pew in 2008 that showed 14 percent of people who voted were noncitizens."
rationale: No reputable Pew study found that 14% of people who voted in 2008 were noncitizens. The 14% figure is a misinterpretation of a small subset of self‑reported responses in a 2008 Pew survey (participants who identified as noncitizens and some of whom said they voted), which researchers and independent fact‑checks concluded was due to misreporting and sampling error, not evidence that 14% of voters were noncitizens.

claim: "We’re spending tremendous amounts of money to educate our kids. In the world, we're No. 1 per pupil by a factor of four."
rationale: The United States does spend more per student than many countries, but reliable international data (OECD/World Bank) do not show U.S. K–12 per‑pupil spending to be four times that of other countries or the global average. U.S. spending is above the OECD average and among the highest, but the gap is typically tens of percent, not 300%+ as implied by "a factor of four."

claim: "Have the suburbs been inundated with former residents of Atlanta housing projects? Absolutely not."
rationale: The categorical denial is inaccurate: when Atlanta's large public housing developments were demolished under HOPE VI and related programs starting in the 1990s, many displaced residents were given vouchers or relocated and a noticeable share moved to suburbs in the Atlanta metro area. Research and housing-agency records indicate a measurable suburban dispersal of former public-housing residents, though it was not a uniform or majority migration and varied by program and time. Saying suburbs were not inundated at all overstates the absence of any suburban resettlement.

claim: Says Harvard scientists say the coronavirus is "spreading so fast that it will infect 70% of humanity this year."
rationale: No credible Harvard press release or peer‑reviewed study made the exact claim that Harvard scientists said the coronavirus was "spreading so fast that it will infect 70% of humanity this year." Early pandemic models by various groups warned that, without mitigation, a large fraction (some estimates 40–70%) of the population could eventually be infected, but that is different from a specific prediction that 70% would be infected within a single year. The claim appears to conflate general modeling ranges with a direct Harvard quote and an inaccurate timeframe.

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: The statement that both Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio are "missing the vast majority of their votes" is inaccurate. Public Senate roll-call records and contemporaneous reporting show each missed some votes (often while campaigning), but neither senator missed the majority of roll-call votes overall. Saying they miss a "vast majority" overstates their absenteeism without a specified time window or evidence.

claim: "Ninety percent of people born in the 1940s ended up doing better financially than their parents. But those born in the 1980s, the much-maligned Millennials, have only a 50-50 chance of doing better (financially) than their parents, despite being the best-educated generation in our history."
rationale: The precise 90% vs 50% figures are not supported by mainstream, reproducible research and are presented without needed context. Intergenerational mobility estimates depend heavily on the country, whether one measures income or wealth, how parental and child incomes are age-adjusted and inflation-adjusted, and the datasets and cohorts used; major studies (e.g., US work by Chetty and OECD analyses) do not produce a simple, universally applicable 90% for 1940s cohorts and 50% for 1980s cohorts. The claim therefore overstates and oversimplifies complex, context-dependent findings.

claim: When Sara Gideon "knew the truth about" sexual allegations against a state lawmaker, "she could have called for an immediate investigation, but didn’t…Gideon knew for months, using her power to cover up."
rationale: The claim asserts specific knowledge and intent (that Gideon “knew the truth,” delayed investigation for months, and used power to cover up). I am not aware of credible contemporaneous reporting, official findings, or documentation establishing that she had prior knowledge and intentionally suppressed an investigation; public timelines and news coverage do not substantiate such a deliberate cover-up. Absent concrete evidence tying her to a months-long concealment, the strong accusation is not supported.

claim: Says each of the past three years "has been the hottest on record."
rationale: The claim implies three different recent years were each uniquely "the hottest on record." Only one year can hold the single hottest annual global temperature (except in the case of exact ties), and observational datasets from major agencies show some recent years set or tied records but not that each of the last three separate years was the hottest. Because the phrase "past three years" and the choice of dataset are unspecified, the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: Says President Donald Trump's "effort to roll back regulations means that Big Ag now gets to inspect its own pork" and "they decided to stop testing for E. coli."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The Trump-era USDA proposed and implemented a new swine inspection system that shifted some front-line tasks to trained establishment employees at certain plants, but federal inspectors retained oversight and regulatory authority — it was not a blanket policy of “Big Ag inspecting its own pork.” Likewise, the agency did not stop all E. coli testing: FSIS continued testing for pathogenic E. coli (including O157:H7) and maintained enforcement authority, though sampling and testing policies were adjusted in specific programs.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s book "The Art of the Deal" advises: "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated."
rationale: The exact wording quoted does not appear in Donald Trump’s 1987 book The Art of the Deal. The book contains deal-making maxims and boastful anecdotes, but reputable transcriptions and quote lists of the book do not include the line “Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated.” That phrasing appears to be a pithy paraphrase of Trump’s style rather than a verbatim passage from the book.

claim: "Phony" ballots "were printed without my name on it."
rationale: There is no specific context or verifiable evidence provided to support the blanket claim that ‘‘phony’’ ballots were printed without the claimant’s name. Standard election procedures require ballots to be printed under official supervision and include candidate names or identifiers, and widespread instances of ballots omitting a major candidate’s name would be documented and widely corroborated—no such verified documentation is cited here. Without details (which jurisdiction, when, who alleges this), the claim cannot be substantiated and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says a study indicates up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices.
rationale: I am not aware of a reputable, state-specific study that estimates exactly “up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs” for Texas from a bathroom-limiting measure. While independent analyses (e.g., by advocacy groups and academic teams) have projected meaningful economic harms from anti‑LGBT laws in particular states, the magnitudes vary widely by methodology and timeframe and the cited figures appear to be a misattribution or an inflated extrapolation. Without a clear, credible source tying those precise numbers to Texas, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says television host Steve Harvey authored a pro-Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that TV host Steve Harvey authored a pro-Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators; the claim appears to originate from satirical or fabricated posts impersonating public figures. Major news outlets and fact-checkers have not documented any such piece by Harvey, and he has not publicly published or promoted that content.

claim: Says Texas ranks among the nation’s top five states for its high school graduation rate.
rationale: The claim lacks a year, but based on recent federal graduation-rate data (Adjusted Cohort Graduation Rate) Texas typically posts a graduation rate around the low- to mid-90s percent, which generally places it outside the nation’s top five states. Multiple smaller states and several Northeastern and Midwestern states have consistently reported higher ACGRs, so the blanket statement that Texas ranks among the top five is not supported without a specific timeframe or source.

claim: Mitt Romney previously believed "that abortion should be safe and legal in this country." Now he is "prolife."
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly described himself as supporting abortion being "safe and legal" in earlier years (notably in the 1990s) and in later campaigns he has identified as pro‑life, advocating restrictions and running as an anti‑abortion-rights Republican. The statement accurately characterizes a documented change in his public position.

claim: State Rep. Elena Parent "supported Governor Nathan Deal’s plan to slash the HOPE scholarship."
rationale: There is no clear record that Democratic State Rep. Elena Parent endorsed Governor Nathan Deal’s proposal to cut the HOPE scholarship; Democrats in the Georgia Legislature broadly opposed Deal’s 2011/early-2010s proposals to reduce HOPE benefits and Parent campaigned as a defender of education funding. Given her party affiliation and public statements on protecting scholarships and K–12/ higher education funding, it is unlikely she 'supported' Deal’s plan to slash HOPE.

claim: "If they made no changes whatsoever, the [state employees pension] plan still had enough money to go forward for approximately the next 16 years."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as stated because it omits the specific state plan, valuation date, and the actuarial assumptions behind the projection. Projections of how long a pension plan can pay benefits vary widely depending on discount rate, contribution policy, investment returns, and whether scheduled contributions are made; some plans may show ~16 years under certain assumptions while others do not. Without a named plan and official actuarial report, the specific "approximately 16 years" figure is not confirmable.

claim: "Actually, on some procedures, you're more likely to die if you're on Medicaid than if you're uninsured."
rationale: Multiple peer‑reviewed observational studies have reported that for certain operations and acute procedures, patients insured by Medicaid experience equal or higher perioperative or in‑hospital mortality than uninsured patients. These findings have been observed in discrete procedures/conditions and often persist after some statistical adjustment, though results vary by procedure and study design.

claim: "Torture is illegal by our laws. It's illegal by international laws."
rationale: Torture is broadly prohibited under international law (e.g., the UN Convention Against Torture, the ICCPR, and the Geneva Conventions) and is widely regarded as a peremptory norm (jus cogens) forbidding it in all circumstances. Many national legal systems also criminalize torture and provide constitutional protections against cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment (for example, U.S. federal statute 18 U.S.C. §2340A and protections under the U.S. Constitution).

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Michael McCaul is "the sixth-richest person in Congress."
rationale: The statement is a specific ranking but lacks a date and is not supported by consistent public filings or media rankings. Public disclosures and annual “wealthiest members of Congress” lists place Michael McCaul among the wealthier members, but he is not reliably identified as the sixth-richest person in Congress across authoritative, dated lists. Because rankings change year-to-year and depend on valuation methods, the absolute claim as stated is not verifiable.

claim: Says Burisma admitted in a Ukrainian court to paying Joe Biden $900,000.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or Ukrainian court record showing Burisma admitted paying Joe Biden $900,000. Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers reviewed court documents and found no admission or judgment that Burisma paid the former vice president; claims conflate payments to Hunter Biden or misread other legal filings. The available record shows no payment to Joe Biden by Burisma.

claim: Says Donald Trump offered his hotel "to our troops to sleep in after they were put in a car garage."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official statement showing Donald Trump offered his hotel(s) as lodging for troops who were reportedly kept in a parking garage. Coverage of incidents where National Guard or other personnel were housed in substandard locations (for example after Jan. 6) documented logistical responsibility by the Pentagon and local authorities, and did not corroborate a Trump hotel offer. Given the absence of evidence for the specific claim, it is assessed as false.

claim: Says in regard to providing "more tax cuts for the rich," Bill Pascrell said, "Republicans had great ideas. I liked some of their ideas."
rationale: There is no credible record or reporting showing Rep. Bill Pascrell praising Republican proposals for "more tax cuts for the rich" with the quoted line. Pascrell, a Democratic congressman who has generally opposed large tax cuts for high earners, has not been documented saying "Republicans had great ideas. I liked some of their ideas" in that context, so the attribution appears fabricated or out of context.

claim: The shooting in Boulder, Colo., was a "false flag like most of the others."
rationale: The Boulder supermarket shooting was not a staged 'false flag.' Law enforcement identified, arrested, and charged a named suspect and investigators and contemporaneous reporting found evidence consistent with an actual shooting rather than a government-orchestrated operation. Assertions that it was a 'false flag' are conspiracy claims unsupported by credible evidence.

claim: "Covid-19 means ‘certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence.’"
rationale: COVID-19 is the widely accepted name for the disease caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, shorthand for 'coronavirus disease 2019' (CO from corona, VI from virus, D for disease, 19 for the year 2019). It is not an acronym relating to any 'certificate,' 'identification,' 'vaccination,' or 'artificial intelligence.' The claim misrepresents established naming by WHO and public-health authorities.

claim: "We’ve saved over $100 million of (health care) costs" in Milwaukee County. "I did that."
rationale: There is no verifiable, independent evidence that a single official can be directly credited with saving over $100 million in Milwaukee County health-care costs as an accomplished, realized figure. While Milwaukee County has implemented cost-control measures (contract changes, benefit adjustments and administrative reforms) that officials sometimes aggregate as projected or actuarial savings, those totals are typically estimates, shared credit across administrations, or linked to long-term liabilities rather than demonstrated one-time cash savings attributable to one person.

claim: The Democratic Party "is the oldest continuous political party in the world."
rationale: The U.S. Democratic Party traces its origins to the 1828 election of Andrew Jackson and is widely described as the oldest continuously operating political party still active today. No other major national party predates 1828 with an uninterrupted organizational existence; many older political groupings (e.g., Whigs/Tories) either transformed or do not have an unbroken institutional continuity. However, claims can hinge on how one defines a "party" and "continuous" lineage, which fuels occasional dispute among historians.

claim: "If you earn $100 and pay $33 income tax you’re left with $67. You then buy $67 worth of fuel and in doing so pay a 48% fuel tax (fuel tax = $32.16 + $6.70 GST). This means that the government just got $71.86 tax from your hard earned $100."
rationale: The claim miscalculates the GST and misrepresents how fuel excise works. GST is 10% of the pre‑GST price (i.e. 1/11 of the final retail price), so on a $67 final purchase the GST portion would be about $6.09, not $6.70, and the ‘48% fuel tax’ figure is a misleading percentage because excise is a fixed cents‑per‑litre levy (its share of the pump price varies with price). Those errors lead to an overstated total tax take from the $100.

claim: "Hillary replaces Kamala Harris."
rationale: There is no evidence that Hillary Clinton has replaced Kamala Harris in any official role. As of available public records through mid‑2024 and thereafter there have been no reports of Harris resigning or of Clinton being appointed or elected to succeed her. Such a replacement would require a formal process (resignation and appointment or an election) that did not occur.

claim: "Twenty-five percent of our kids in foster care are there because their parents are involved in drugs."
rationale: Stating flatly that 25% of children in foster care are there because their parents are involved in drugs is misleading. U.S. federal data and child-welfare analyses typically show parental substance abuse is a major reason for removals and entries but the share varies by year and state and has often been higher than 25% during the opioid period. The claim oversimplifies and presents a single unsupported percentage as a universal fact.

claim: "Congressman Renacci is under FBI investigation."
rationale: There are no credible news reports, DOJ/FBI statements, or public records indicating that Congressman Jim Renacci is currently under an FBI investigation. Significant federal probes of current or former members of Congress are typically reported by major media and confirmed by official statements; none have surfaced linking Renacci, so the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: The IAEA, or the International Atomic Energy Agency, "last month said the Iranians are not currently living up to their obligations."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it uses the phrase "last month" without specifying a date; I cannot verify a recent IAEA statement after my 2024-06 knowledge cutoff. While the IAEA has repeatedly reported concerns about Iran's compliance with safeguards in prior months and years, I cannot confirm that the agency made the exact quoted statement in the unspecified 'last month.' Therefore the claim as presented is not verifiable and is judged false under uncertainty rules.

claim: "On issue after issue that really were hard to explain or understand, you voted present . . . And anytime anyone raises that, there's always some kind of explanation."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific, verifiable pattern of voting behavior (repeatedly voting 'present' on many hard-to-explain issues and always offering explanations) but gives no subject, timeframe, or concrete votes to check. Without identifying who 'you' refers to and citing the relevant roll calls and public statements, the claim cannot be substantiated, so I judge it false given the lack of evidence.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: The claim is false: prosecutions of former leaders occur in many developed democracies, not only in so-called 'Third World' countries. Notable examples include the conviction of former French president Jacques Chirac, repeated prosecutions of Italy's Silvio Berlusconi, charges against Israel's Ehud Olmert, and the impeachment/criminal prosecution of South Korea's Park Geun-hye. Thus such prosecutions are not exclusive to less-developed countries.

claim: "Mexico’s Next President Calls for An Invasion Of The US"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that any Mexican president‑elect has called for invading the United States; such a statement would have been widely covered and provocatively unprecedented. Mexican leaders and major presidential candidates have consistently adhered to diplomatic norms and would face strong legal, political, and institutional constraints against advocating invasion.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court is "five guys who start determining what contraceptions are legal."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The U.S. Supreme Court has nine justices and decides cases by a majority of those nine; while a five-justice majority can control outcomes, the Court’s membership includes women and the conservative bloc is not accurately summarized as simply 'five guys.' Also, the Court resolves constitutional questions rather than directly passing statutes, so saying it 'starts determining what contraceptions are legal' is an oversimplification of how law and regulation interact with judicial rulings.

claim: "We confer more PhDs each year than any other university in America except Berkeley."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written and likely false: national data on research doctorates show several institutions (e.g., Michigan, Washington, UCLA, Harvard in different years) confer numbers of PhDs comparable to or exceeding most single campuses, and rankings vary by year and field. Without specifying which university and which year, the absolute claim that one campus ranks second only to Berkeley is not supported by consistent, public IPEDS/Survey of Earned Doctorates data.

claim: "449,000 Californians turned down jury duty because they were not citizens… but they were registered voters."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that 449,000 Californians explicitly "turned down jury duty because they were not citizens" while also being registered voters. The 449,000 number has been used in different contexts (data matches, administrative flags, or questionnaires) and appears to be a misinterpretation or conflation of flagged records, duplicates, and mailing lists rather than verified noncitizen registered voters who refused jury service. Official checks and prior fact‑checks show the underlying data are error‑prone and do not support the specific claim as stated.

claim: "AIG insures the pension trust of the United States Congress!"
rationale: Congressional retirement benefits are federal programs (Members typically participate in FERS or CSRS) administered by federal agencies, not a private insurer. Private-sector defined-benefit plans are insured by the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, and there is no credible evidence that AIG "insures the pension trust of the United States Congress."

claim: Says Jon Ossoff "wants total, blanket amnesty and he wants a total lockdown."
rationale: This characterization misstates Ossoff’s positions. He has supported pathways to citizenship and reforms for certain immigrants (e.g., Dreamers) rather than an unconditional, across-the-board amnesty for all undocumented people, and during COVID he endorsed public-health measures and targeted restrictions rather than calling for a perpetual, society-wide “total lockdown.” The claim stretches and conflates advocacy for reform and pandemic mitigation into absolute, blanket demands he did not make.

claim: "The average student will be spending $1,700 to $1,800 more during the life of their loan because of this surcharge."
rationale: The claim lacks necessary context and a verifiable source; the additional lifetime cost from any "surcharge" depends on loan principal, interest rates, repayment plan, and exact policy details. Without those specifics or an accompanying calculation/model, the stated $1,700–$1,800 figure cannot be confirmed and is therefore not supported.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: The Antrim County problem was a local reporting/configuration error that produced initially incorrect totals and was corrected after canvass; multiple state and independent reviews found no evidence that votes were flipped by software or that statewide results were fraudulent. Claims that “47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’” conflate different vendors, versions, or routine tabulation systems and misattribute a localized reporting mistake to a universal software bug. There is no reliable evidence that 47 counties experienced the same defect or that statewide votes are potentially fraudulent for this reason.

claim: "Withheld union dues fund half of Dem (Democratic) campaigns in Florida."
rationale: This claim is false or greatly exaggerated. Public campaign finance records show Democratic campaigns in Florida receive donations from a wide mix of individuals, PACs, corporations and unions, and unions do not provide half of total Democratic campaign funding. Moreover, after the 2018 Janus decision public-sector unions cannot compel dues for political purposes, and political spending by unions is typically from separate voluntary political funds rather than ‘‘withheld dues.’'

claim: "Kasich’s trade deals cost Ohio thousands of jobs - 49,000 jobs to Mexico, 91,000 to China."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported. Trade agreements are negotiated and enacted at the federal level, not by an Ohio governor, and independent fact-checkers and economic analyses do not attribute 49,000 job losses to Mexico and 91,000 to China specifically to actions by John Kasich. While there are studies estimating trade-related manufacturing job displacement in Ohio over time, the numbers and the causal attribution to “Kasich’s trade deals” are unsupported and appear to conflate broader trade trends with one individual’s actions.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I am not aware of a verifiable, reputable Pennsylvania-specific economic impact study that produced the precise claim that every $1 invested in pre-K generates $1.79 in total in-state spending. While there are many state and national analyses showing positive economic multipliers or long-term benefit-cost ratios for early childhood programs, the numbers and definitions (short-term in-state spending vs. long-term societal returns) vary widely and no well-known study matches this exact figure. Because the statement cites a specific dollar multiplier without identifying the study, it appears to be a misstatement or misattribution.

claim: Democrats plan to keep student loan interest rates low  "by raising taxes on small businesses, very small businesses … the kinds of small businesses that give jobs to graduates."
rationale: There is no broad, documented Democratic plan to explicitly keep student loan interest rates low by directly raising taxes on 'small businesses, very small businesses' that hire graduates. Major Democratic proposals to fund higher education or loan relief have generally targeted higher-income households, corporations, or used federal budget allocations rather than explicit new taxes aimed at small employers. The claim overstates and misattributes a specific financing strategy to the Democratic Party as a whole.

claim: "The average age of the minimum wage worker is 35 years old."
rationale: The statement as a general fact is incorrect. Available labor-force data and research (e.g., BLS/CPS analyses and academic studies) show workers earning the minimum or near-minimum wage skew younger, with mean/median ages generally in the mid-to-late 20s rather than 35. While some older workers earn minimum wage, they are not numerous enough in typical U.S. datasets to produce an average age of 35.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi passed a bill awarding a $9 billion contract to her husband’s company.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi ‘passed a bill’ that directly awarded a $9 billion contract to her husband’s company. Congress enacts laws and authorizes spending but federal contracts are awarded through executive branch procurement processes, and public records and news investigations have not documented any $9 billion contract given to Paul Pelosi’s businesses. The claim appears to conflate or misstate how legislation and federal contracting work and lacks supporting documentation.

claim: "There has never been an alderman who has defeated an incumbent mayor in the history of this great city."
rationale: The claim is a blanket universal negative about an unspecified city and therefore implausible: across many municipalities, sitting aldermen or council members have historically challenged and sometimes defeated incumbent mayors. Without a specific city and timeframe the assertion cannot be verified and is unlikely to hold as an absolute historical rule. Thus the claim is judged false given typical patterns of municipal politics and the lack of precise context.

claim: Says Rob Portman was a registered foreign agent whose "client was Haiti, at a time when the Baby Doc, Duvalier, who was a despot, was killing people."
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. politician Rob Portman ever registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act to represent Haiti, and his public career and employment history (Congressional service and senior U.S. administration roles) do not include acting as a registered foreign agent for the Duvalier regime. The Duvalier "Baby Doc" era did involve human-rights abuses, but Portman would have been very young during most of that period and is not known to have worked as a foreign agent for Haiti. The claim appears to conflate or confuse individuals or roles.

claim: "Over-vaccination causes faster mutation of the (COVID-19) virus, which causes a super virus we may not have the ability to fight off."
rationale: Vaccination does not increase the intrinsic mutation rate of SARS-CoV-2; mutations arise when the virus replicates, so reducing infections via vaccination generally reduces opportunities for new variants. While immune pressure can favor emergence of escape mutations, broad vaccination typically lowers overall viral circulation and the likelihood of dangerous variants, and there is no evidence that 'over-vaccination' creates a guaranteed "super virus" we cannot fight. Claims that vaccines cause faster mutation and inevitable unstoppable strains oversimplify viral evolution and are not supported by the scientific record.

claim: "Lindsey Graham threatens to convert to Democrat if Republicans don’t Dump Trump."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Senator Lindsey Graham has publicly threatened to convert to the Democratic Party if Republicans do not "dump" Donald Trump. While Graham has at times criticized Trump and made rhetorical remarks about the GOP, he has remained a Republican and has not announced any conditional switch of party affiliation as described in the claim.

claim: "If Biden wins the election, there are people out there planning on mass murdering poc and lbgtq+ people. Please stay inside during the election and a few days after."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that organized groups have announced plans to carry out mass murder of people of color and LGBTQ+ people specifically contingent on a Biden victory. While election periods can increase the risk of politically motivated violence and isolated plots have occurred in the past, the specific sweeping claim of widespread planned mass murders tied to Biden winning is unsubstantiated. Advisories to stay inside are precautionary but not supported as necessary by confirmed intelligence.

claim: Regarding her State Department email practices, "my predecessors did the same thing."
rationale: This claim is misleading. While some Secretaries of State (notably Colin Powell and Condoleezza Rice) sometimes used personal email accounts for official business, none are documented to have used a private, non-government email server hosted at home or to have handled records in the same way critics said the quoted official did; predecessors generally preserved records and complied with archival practices. Therefore the blanket statement that “my predecessors did the same thing” is false in key respects.

claim: Fox News changed its accreditation to "entertainment."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Fox News was officially reclassified or had its press accreditation changed to “entertainment.” Claims to that effect circulated on social media and were based on misreadings, satire, or isolated website labels, but official credentialing bodies (e.g., White House press office, event organizers) did not reclassify Fox as entertainment. Major reporting and records treat Fox as a news organization, not as having undergone a formal accreditation change to “entertainment.”

claim: Says Vice President Kamala Harris called the unvaccinated "dirty Trump people."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reliable reporting showing Vice President Kamala Harris ever called the unvaccinated “dirty Trump people.” Fact-checks and news coverage of her public remarks on vaccines show she criticized misinformation and some political messaging but did not use that exact insulting phrase. The claim appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote amplified on social media.

claim: "The only people in this town that have voted to cut Medicare spending are the people who voted in favor of Obamacare. That’s a fact."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim attributing all Medicare spending cuts only to those who voted for the Affordable Care Act. Legislative history shows Medicare reductions were included in the ACA but many other lawmakers (including opponents of the ACA) have supported budgets, bills, and amendments that reduce Medicare spending. Because the claim is absolute and context-free it is not supported by the broader voting record.

claim: "There is no reason for these massive, deadly and costly forest fires in California except that forest management is so poor."
rationale: The claim that poor forest management is the sole cause of California's massive, deadly, and costly fires is incorrect. Scientific assessments and fire investigations show multiple contributing causes — climate change (warmer, drier conditions and longer fire seasons), extreme winds, a history of fire suppression and fuel buildup, insect outbreaks and drought, human ignitions and failing utility equipment — so poor forest management may be a factor but not the only reason.

claim: Superdelegates "have never been a determining factor in who our nominee is since they've been in place since 1984."
rationale: Automatic (super)delegates were created in the Democratic Party after 1980 and have existed since 1984. In contested modern primaries where their role was questioned (notably 2008 and 2016), the nominees were decided by pledged delegates or clear pledged majorities rather than superdelegates switching the outcome, and no convention nominee since 1984 was flipped solely by superdelegate votes. The party later limited their first-ballot role in 2018 in response to concerns about their potential influence, but historically they have not been the deciding factor.

claim: The Biden administration "gifted the Taliban with $80 billion-plus" in military-grade weapons but now "wants your 9mm pistols."
rationale: This mixes two different facts into a misleading claim. The commonly cited ~$83 billion number refers to cumulative U.S. security assistance to Afghan forces over roughly two decades, not a single "gift" of $80B in weapons handed to the Taliban; much U.S.-provided equipment was destroyed, disabled, or long deployed and only a portion was captured during the 2021 collapse. Separately, the Biden administration has not proposed a policy to confiscate privately owned 9mm pistols nationwide; reported actions have targeted specific regulations (e.g., ghost guns, braces, or background checks) rather than a mass seizure of common handguns.

claim: Says FEMA is giving essential workers $1,000.
rationale: There is no evidence of a FEMA program that issues a universal $1,000 payment to 'essential workers.' FEMA administers disaster assistance, grants, and reimbursements after declared emergencies, but it has not announced or operated a blanket cash payment to essential workers; fact-checkers and FEMA guidance have debunked social posts making this promise.

claim: A video shows a nurse pretending to vaccinate actor Anthony Hopkins before squirting fluid in the syringe on the floor.
rationale: There is no credible, independently verified evidence that a nurse ‘pretended’ to vaccinate Sir Anthony Hopkins and then squirted vaccine onto the floor. Videos can be misinterpreted by camera angle or editing; standard vaccination practice can include expelling a tiny amount or air from a syringe before injection, which might look like ‘squirting’ in some clips. Without corroborating reporting or provenance for the specific footage, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Workers have begun removing spires of Cinderella Castle at Magic Kingdom ahead of Hurricane Dorian."
rationale: There are no credible contemporaneous reports that Disney dismantled Cinderella Castle's spires ahead of Hurricane Dorian. The castle's spires are permanent architectural features and widely reported fact-checking found the circulating images were misleading or miscaptioned; Disney typically secures loose decorations rather than remove structural elements for storms.

claim: "When you look at the nearly 150 men and women who have served us on the Texas Supreme Court, more than half of them had zero prior judicial experience."
rationale: The claim that a majority (>50%) of the nearly 150 people who have served on the Texas Supreme Court had zero prior judicial experience is unverified and likely incorrect. While many early justices were private attorneys or politicians, especially in the 19th century, a substantial number of later justices had prior judicial service, and I find no authoritative count confirming that over half lacked prior judicial experience.

claim: Says Cory Booker "supports late-term and partial-birth abortion and opposes safety regulations."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Cory Booker has described himself as pro-choice and has said later-term abortions should be permitted in limited circumstances (such as to protect a woman’s health or in cases of severe fetal anomaly), but he has not explicitly advocated for a blanket endorsement of the politically charged term 'partial-birth abortion' and generally opposes laws he views as medically unnecessary restrictions rather than opposing legitimate safety measures. The statement conflates support for reproductive-rights exceptions and opposition to restrictive bans with a blanket endorsement of all procedures and rejection of safety regulation.

claim: Even high estimates for an early draft of the health care plan are "less than the $1.8 trillion cost of the Bush tax cuts."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it compares two ill-defined figures without a common timeframe or specification of which health‑care draft and which cost estimate. Budget scores (e.g., from the CBO and other analysts) vary by window and assumptions; some high-end 10‑year projections for health‑care proposals were comparable to or exceeded multi‑trillion dollar totals, and the commonly cited ‘‘$1.8 trillion’’ for the Bush tax cuts depends on the exact years counted. Without clarifying the period and which estimates are being compared, the blanket claim does not hold.

claim: Says, "Carl proposed a 'windfall' tax on real estate development when he was a Metro Councilor."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and I find no reliable record that a Metro Councilor named Carl formally proposed a specific ‘windfall’ tax on real estate development. Public minutes, news reports, and policy announcements for regional/metro councils typically document such proposals, and none attribute this measure to a councilor named Carl. Without a named individual, jurisdiction, or cited proposal text, the assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Youth unemployment in minority communities is about 40 to 45 percent."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and not supported by national labor statistics. While youth unemployment is higher in many minority communities than the national average, typical U.S. youth unemployment rates for Black or Hispanic youth are generally well below 40–45% in most years, though they can rise during recessions or be much higher in particular cities or neighborhoods. Without a specified group, age range, place, and timeframe the blanket 40–45% figure is inaccurate.

claim: Donald Trump "cancelled Bill Gates project known as ID2020."
rationale: ID2020 is an independent public‑private initiative launched in 2016 with multiple partners; it was not a singular "Bill Gates project" under presidential control. There is no credible evidence that President Trump issued any action that "cancelled" ID2020, and the initiative and related digital ID work have continued through multiple partners beyond his administration. The claim conflates Gates Foundation involvement with ownership and misstates presidential authority over private initiatives.

claim: "John Cornyn has voted to increase the debt, raise taxes, bail out Wall Street banks and fund Obamacare."
rationale: The claim bundles several distinct votes into a single characterization that does not match John Cornyn's record. Cornyn, a conservative Republican senator, voted against the Affordable Care Act and has publicly opposed broad tax increases and major Wall Street bailouts; while he has at times supported procedural or temporary increases in the federal debt limit to avoid default, that is not equivalent to an across-the-board vote to "increase the debt, raise taxes, bail out Wall Street banks and fund Obamacare."

claim: "More people die from hands, fists, feet, than rifles."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated and is misleading without context. In many jurisdictions (notably the U.S.), public-health and criminal statistics show firearms are responsible for the majority of violent deaths while deaths attributed to unarmed assault (hands, fists, feet) are a small share; even though 'rifles' are a subset of firearms, firearms overall kill far more people than unarmed assaults. Without a specific country and time period this blanket comparison is not justified.

claim: "2 million rounds of ammo that ‘went missing’ under Obama turns up in enemy hands"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that exactly “2 million rounds” of ammunition went missing during the Obama administration and later definitively turned up in enemy hands. Reporting does document arms looting and lost weapons (for example after the 2011 Libya conflict) and separate incidents of seized munitions, but authoritative sources do not substantiate the specific 2‑million‑round claim or a direct chain proving they were the same rounds. The statement appears to conflate or exaggerate disparate events without documented proof.

claim: Ebola is "incredibly contagious," "very transmissible" and "easy to catch."
rationale: The claim overstates Ebola's transmissibility. Ebola virus is transmitted primarily through direct contact with blood or other bodily fluids of symptomatic infected people or contaminated materials; it is not an airborne virus and is not as easily caught as highly transmissible respiratory diseases. While it can spread rapidly in settings with close contact and poor infection control, casual proximity does not typically cause transmission.

claim: "Nationwide tuition at public universities is up almost 300 percent ... in the last 20 years."
rationale: U.S. national data from organizations that track college prices (NCES, College Board) show published in‑state tuition and fees at public four‑year institutions roughly doubled over the past ~20 years (on the order of ~100–150% nominal increase), not an almost 300% rise. Adjusting for inflation reduces the real increase further. The claim overstates the increase by conflating different measures (in‑state vs out‑of‑state, sticker price vs net price) or using a different baseline period.

claim: Schools are putting litter boxes in bathrooms to accommodate kids who identify as furries.
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple independent fact-checkers and school districts investigated circulated reports and found no credible evidence that schools are installing litter boxes in bathrooms to accommodate students who identify as furries; most viral examples were hoaxes, misattributions, or involved litter boxes for classroom animals rather than restroom accommodations. There is no documented policy or widespread practice of schools providing restroom litter boxes for students based on ‘‘furry’’ identity.

claim: "94 percent of winning candidates in 2010 had more money than their opponents."
rationale: The claim gives a precise percentage without specifying office or whether it refers to fundraising or spending; available historical analyses of U.S. federal races show winners commonly outspend opponents but not as uniformly as 94% across all contests in 2010. Because the statistic is ambiguous and unusually high compared with typical reported rates for that year and across race types, the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: More than one-quarter of America’s young adults are too fat to serve in the U.S. military
rationale: Department of Defense and public-health analyses have repeatedly found that roughly 25–30% of 17–24-year-olds exceed military weight/body-fat standards, so more than one-quarter of U.S. young adults are commonly reported as ineligible to serve for weight/obesity reasons. The exact share varies by year, age bracket, and measurement definitions, but commonly-cited estimates around 27% support this claim.

claim: "There have been more than 300 mass shootings in the United States this year – more than any other country in the world."
rationale: Major U.S. trackers that use the common definition of a mass shooting (four or more people shot) report well over 300 such incidents in recent years, and those counts are substantially higher than numbers reported for any other single country. While totals depend on the definition and data source, the United States consistently records more mass-shooting incidents than other countries.

claim: "Washington State Legislature votes to change its name because George Washington owned Slaves."
rationale: There is no record that the Washington State Legislature voted to change the state's name; while activists and a few lawmakers have proposed or discussed renaming because George Washington owned enslaved people, no bill to officially rename the state has been passed.
