Renaming a state would also require more than a simple legislative vote (typically constitutional/legal processes and likely a referendum).

claim: Says Joe Biden canceled the Keystone pipeline because Warren Buffett "donated $58 million" to his campaign.
rationale: This claim is false. President Biden revoked the Keystone XL permit as an executive action tied to climate and environmental policy goals; there is no credible evidence that Warren Buffett donated $58 million to Biden’s campaign or that such a donation motivated the decision. Buffett did publicly endorse Biden and has given to Democratic causes historically, but the specific $58M donation and causal link are not supported by campaign finance records or reporting.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s tax plans would "give an additional $250,000 tax cut to millionaires and billionaires" while raising taxes on the middle class.
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and nonpartisan tax analysts found the claim misleading: the specific "$250,000" figure was not a robust, general result of Romney's tax proposals and depended heavily on baseline assumptions and which deductions or rate changes were counted. Analyses showed top earners would likely receive large tax cuts under many versions of Romney's plans, but the exact size and whether the middle class would face net tax increases varied by model and assumptions, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "Nearly 60% of all student loan debt is held by the rich and upper-middle class," so forgiveness would give the wealthy a "financial windfall" but not really help low-income people.
rationale: The numeric claim is misleading: research shows outstanding student loan balances are concentrated among younger, middle- and upper-middle-income households and among borrowers with graduate degrees, but not that nearly 60% is held by the "rich." Shares vary by how you define "rich/upper-middle," whether you measure by current income or lifetime earnings, and whether you include private loans, so the simple 60% assertion is not supported by mainstream analyses. While some higher-earning borrowers would benefit from blanket forgiveness, many low- and middle-income borrowers also hold federal debt and would gain relief, so the claim overstates the benefit to the wealthy and downplays broader impacts.

claim: Bing Energy said it decided to move to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s "plan to eliminate the corporate tax."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record or reporting showing that a company called Bing Energy publicly said it moved to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s "plan to eliminate the corporate tax." While Rick Scott has promoted cutting or eliminating corporate taxes, I could not find a company statement or credible news story attributing Bing Energy’s relocation to that policy, so the claim is unverified and likely false.

claim: The only budget Ted Cruz "ever voted for in his time in the Senate is a budget that cut defense spending by more than Barack Obama proposes we cut it."
rationale: The statement is overly absolute and does not match the record: Cruz has participated in multiple budget-related votes since joining the Senate in 2013, and the size and treatment of defense spending varies across competing budget proposals. Moreover, comparisons to "what Barack Obama proposes" are time-dependent (Obama proposed different defense levels in different years), so the claim that the "only" budget Cruz ever voted for cuts defense more than Obama proposed is inaccurate. Given the variability of budgets and Cruz's multiple votes/supports, the categorical assertion is false.

claim: Says Ruben Kihuen "only managed in the minority to get one bill passed out of the eight to 10 he introduced" during the 2015 legislative session.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific bill count and the phrasing is likely incorrect: Ruben Kihuen was a Democratic member of the Nevada Assembly and Democrats held control of the Assembly in 2015, so characterizing him as “in the minority” that session appears wrong. The precise number of bills he introduced and passed would require checking Nevada legislative records; without that confirmation the specific numeric claim is unproven and likely inaccurate.

claim: Says "If Oregon’s Legislature simply authorizes $450 million for the CRC, it will … leave Oregon holding the bag for a great deal more cost responsibility."
rationale: The claim presents an inevitability — that merely authorizing $450 million would automatically leave Oregon responsible for a much larger share of costs — but that is speculative. Whether the state would bear additional liability depends on how the authorization is drafted, any conditions or triggers, and the intergovernmental and contractual agreements with federal and Washington partners. Legislatures commonly include safeguards or contingent language to limit exposure, so authorization alone does not guarantee the outcome asserted.

claim: Says "we brought crime rate down by 30 percent" when he was mayor of Dallas.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it does not identify which mayor or the timeframe, and there is no well-documented, widely accepted record that any Dallas mayor produced a 30% citywide crime reduction attributable solely to their tenure. Dallas crime statistics have varied year-to-year and by category (violent vs. property), and large round-number attributions like a 30% drop require a specific time window and metric to confirm. Without those details, the assertion cannot be supported and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "Over 130 legislators in this chamber have endorsed legislation that would bankrupt our nation by providing free taxpayer-funded health care to millions of illegal aliens, forcing taxpayers to subsidize free care for anyone in the world who unlawfully crosses our borders."
rationale: This claim mixes hyperbole with unspecified facts and is not supported by evidence. There is no verified record of more than 130 legislators endorsing a single bill that would provide unconditional, free taxpayer-funded health care to all undocumented migrants worldwide or that credible analyses conclude would "bankrupt" the nation. Proposals affecting immigrant access to health care are typically limited in scope, and blanket, unconditional coverage for anyone who unlawfully crosses U.S. borders is not reflected in mainstream, widely endorsed legislation.

claim: A space shuttle the National Museum of the United States Air Force near Dayton would be "within a day's drive of 60 percent of the U.S. population."
rationale: The claim overstates coverage: using common definitions of a 'day's drive' (roughly 8–12 hours or ~500–800 miles), a Dayton, Ohio location would cover much of the Midwest and Northeast but would exclude large population centers on the West Coast, much of the Mountain West and parts of the Deep South. Those excluded regions contain well over 40% of the U.S. population, so it is unlikely that 60% would be within a single-day drive of Dayton. The statement also hinges on an undefined driving-distance threshold, which makes the numeric claim implausible.

claim: Says with the ongoing economic downturn, child abuse is on the rise.
rationale: The claim is too general. While economic downturns increase risk factors for child maltreatment (e.g., parental stress, unemployment), empirical data are mixed: official reports sometimes rise but often fall during downturns due to reduced detection (for example school closures reduced mandated reporting during COVID-19), so one cannot uniformly state abuse is "on the rise."

claim: Says Josh Mandel bet against Ohio families
rationale: The statement is vague and unsubstantiated. There is no verified public evidence that Josh Mandel personally placed financial 'bets' intended to harm or 'bet against' Ohio families; similar language has appeared as hyperbolic rhetoric in political ads rather than as a description of documented transactions.

claim: "Twitter is completely stifling FREE SPEECH" by adding a fact-check label to Trump’s tweet.
rationale: Adding a fact-check label typically provides context and may reduce a tweet’s amplification but does not completely silence or remove the speaker’s message. Historically Twitter has left labeled tweets viewable (while sometimes downranking or restricting engagement) rather than entirely stifling the account’s ability to speak, so the claim is an exaggeration.

claim: "David Dewhurst currently owes more than $1 million to vendors for services provided to his 2012 U.S. Senate campaign."
rationale: Public campaign finance filings and contemporaneous news coverage after Dewhurst's 2012 Senate run reported that his campaign carried outstanding vendor debts in excess of $1 million. Multiple articles in the months following the 2012 campaign described more than $1M in unpaid bills for campaign services.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "shows up in Broward County" and had a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Hillary Clinton had a private meeting with Broward County elections supervisor Brenda Snipes. The claim circulated as an unverified rumor and was not substantiated by news outlets, public schedules, or records that would likely document such a meeting between two high-profile figures.

claim: Austin’s Pease Elementary "is a school that was created as part of the Texas Constitution."
rationale: The Texas Constitution provides the legal framework for public education in the state but does not create or name individual elementary schools. Individual schools such as Austin’s Pease Elementary are established and operated by local school districts (e.g., Austin ISD) and not created directly by the state constitution.

claim: The "Franklin scandal" broke in 1989 "when hundreds of children were apparently flown around the US to be abused by high ranking ‘Establishment’ members."
rationale: While allegations around the Franklin case surfaced in the late 1980s (roughly 1988–1990) claiming children had been flown and abused by powerful people, subsequent official investigations (including a Nebraska legislative inquiry and FBI review) found no credible evidence of a national ring or that hundreds of children were flown around the U.S. Some individual crimes and abusive allegations were part of the case, but the central claim of hundreds of children being transported and abused by high‑ranking 'Establishment' members is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says U.S. Senate rival Tommy Thompson said he wants to "do away with Medicare."
rationale: There is no clear record of Tommy Thompson saying he wanted to “do away with Medicare.” While he has supported proposals to reform Medicare—favoring market-based options or premium-support approaches that critics call privatization—those positions are not the same as an explicit statement to abolish the program. Attack ads sometimes paraphrase or exaggerate reform proposals into “do away with” language, which appears to be the case here.

claim: Says Daniel Radcliffe has the coronavirus.
rationale: As stated, the claim is false: Daniel Radcliffe does not currently have the coronavirus. He publicly said he tested positive for COVID-19 in March 2020 and subsequently recovered, and there have been no reliable reports of an ongoing or new infection since then (through mid-2024).

claim: Rob Portman’s "plan to tax, slash and privatize" Social Security "would devastate Ohioans."
rationale: The claim alleges Rob Portman has a specific “plan to tax, slash and privatize” Social Security that would “devastate Ohioans.” There is no clear public proposal from Portman that matches that description — he has not advocated wholesale privatization or a single package explicitly described that way, and such language appears to be political hyperbole. Without evidence of a concrete policy matching those exact actions and impacts, the statement is not supported.

claim: "Since the passage of Proposition 47 by voters in 2014 and the signing of AB 109 in 2011, violent crime has been on the rise in California, up 12 percent in 2015 statewide according to the FBI."
rationale: The FBI Uniform Crime Reports show that California's reported violent crime rose sharply from 2014 to 2015 — roughly an 11–12% increase statewide. AB 109 was enacted in 2011 and Proposition 47 was passed by voters in November 2014, so the 2015 increase occurred after both measures. The claim's numerical and temporal components align with official reporting for 2015.

claim: Social media posts claim the U.S. Postal Service "says you should give mail in ballots at least 14 days roundtrip. So, if you plan to vote by mail, election day isn’t November 3. It’s October 20th."
rationale: This is inaccurate. The U.S. Postal Service did not issue a universal rule that ballots need 14 days roundtrip; USPS and election officials have urged voters to mail ballots early and to check state deadlines, but delivery times vary by location and states set their own receipt/postmark rules. Treating Nov 3 ballots as effectively due Oct 20 everywhere misrepresents USPS guidance and state procedures.

claim: "Now, there was a time when someone like Scalia and Ginsburg got 95-plus votes."
rationale: Both Antonin Scalia and Ruth Bader Ginsburg won well over 95 Senate votes at their confirmations. Scalia was confirmed overwhelmingly (98–0 in 1986) and Ginsburg received 96–3 in 1993, so the statement that there was a time when nominees like them got 95-plus votes is accurate.

claim: "For my energy plan, my economic plan, and the other proposals you'll hear tonight, I've offered spending cuts above and beyond their cost."
rationale: The claim asserts that proposed spending cuts exceed the costs of the named plans, but public, independent scorekeeping and reporting do not substantiate that assertion. Major nonpartisan budget analysts (and the claimant's public plan documents) have not produced verifiable, detailed scoring showing net savings above the proposals' costs, so the broad claim is unsupported.

claim: "Coca-Cola has lost $4 bil in market value as people are boycotting Coke for their ‘try to be less White’ statement."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Coca‑Cola specifically lost $4 billion in market value as a direct result of a boycott over the "try to be less white" training remark. While the leaked training clip sparked controversy and some calls for a boycott, stock market fluctuations around that time were consistent with broader market movements and short‑term price changes that cannot be confidently attributed solely to a boycott. Fact‑checks by major outlets concluded the viral $4 billion claim was misleading or unsubstantiated.

claim: "The president came in and campaigned against me 12 times."
rationale: The statement asserts a precise number of times a sitting president campaigned against the speaker, but no names, dates, or context are provided to verify that count. Because the claim is specific and unverifiable without identifying who "the president" and "me" are and checking public schedules and news reports, I judge it false pending supporting evidence.

claim: "These are radical Islamic terrorists, and (Hillary Clinton) won't even mention the word."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Hillary Clinton "won't even mention the word," which is misleading and unverifiable without specifying who "these" refers to and when. Public records show Clinton has at times avoided the exact phrase "radical Islamic terrorists" and at other times used similar terms (e.g., "Islamist extremism" or criticized extremist ideology), so the blanket assertion that she never mentions the word is false or at least unsupported as presented.

claim: "I certainly supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden. ... I was there both times for them."
rationale: The statement asserts personal support and presence for both Barack Obama and Joe Biden, but no specific speaker, dates, or verifiable actions are provided. Such a personal claim requires corroborating evidence (voter records, public statements, photographs, or eyewitness accounts) which are not supplied, so it cannot be confirmed as factual. In absence of verifiable evidence, the claim is treated as unproven and thus flagged false.

claim: "Unions don’t have to comply with Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act’s employer rules apply to employers (including unions that employ 50 or more full-time-equivalent workers) so there is no blanket exemption for unions. Some unions are small enough to be exempt, and many unionized workers receive coverage through multiemployer (Taft‑Hartley) plans that can satisfy ACA requirements, and there were limited transitional delays and accommodations for collective bargaining — but that is not the same as a blanket opt‑out. Thus the categorical claim is false.

claim: HR 1 will allow members of Congress to draw a second salary "worth an estimated $600,000 per year!"
rationale: This claim is false. The various bills titled "H.R. 1" (commonly the For the People Act) deal with election and campaign finance reforms and do not create or authorize members of Congress to receive a new $600,000-per-year "second salary." Members may earn outside income under existing rules (with disclosure and ethics limits), but no H.R.1 provision grants an automatic additional six-figure congressional salary as described.

claim: "I deployed the Texas National Guard" to the Texas-Mexico border. "And the policy worked; apprehensions at the border declined 74 percent."
rationale: The speaker did deploy Texas National Guard troops to the Texas–Mexico border, but the statement that this policy caused a 74% decline in “apprehensions at the border” is misleading and not supported as a clear causal fact. Public data and independent fact checks show apprehension numbers vary by timeframe, sector, and national trends, and declines cited by officials typically depend on a selected baseline period; multiple federal policies and seasonal and enforcement factors also affected encounter totals. There is no authoritative evidence isolating the Guard deployment as the sole or primary cause of a 74% drop.

claim: Women are paid 77 cents for every $1 men get for the same work.
rationale: The oft‑quoted “77 cents” comes from comparing median annual earnings of all full‑time female workers to all full‑time male workers, not wages for the same job. When researchers control for occupation, hours, experience, education and other factors, the gap narrows substantially and matched‑job analyses find a much smaller unexplained difference. Thus the claim misstates what the 77¢ figure represents.

claim: "We could build 30 walls with the $150 billion Obama gave to Iran."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While media and officials often cite roughly $100–150 billion in Iranian assets that became accessible after the 2015 nuclear deal, that number is disputed and those were largely frozen foreign-held assets released under specific conditions rather than a simple cash gift. Separately, estimates for building a U.S. border wall vary widely (from a few billion to tens of billions depending on length, route and standards), so there is no reliable basis to claim $150 billion would buy exactly 30 walls — the claim cherry-picks numbers and conflates different accounting assumptions.

claim: Says 194 people were killed in mass shootings in 2018 while undocumented immigrants killed 83,211 people.
rationale: False. The 83,211 figure is implausible and has been debunked — total U.S. homicides in 2018 were on the order of roughly 16,000–17,000, so undocumented immigrants could not have killed 83,211 people that year. The “194” mass‑shooting deaths number may reflect a narrowly defined count but the juxtaposition is misleading and based on fabricated or cherry‑picked data.

claim: "After 9/11, Jim put us all first by serving for 23 months in Iraq, the war’s longest tour."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented and the key claim that a 23‑month single tour was “the war’s longest tour” is misleading. Typical U.S. Iraq deployments were about 12 months (with some variations to 15 months), and many service members completed multiple tours whose combined time in Iraq exceeded 23 months. Because the individual “Jim” is unspecified and “longest tour” is ambiguous (single deployment vs. cumulative service), the claim as stated is false or at best unsupported.

claim: "The bulk of the people who are shot with a weapon — other than these drug gangs taking on one another — end up being shot with their own weapon."
rationale: Available criminological evidence does not support the claim that a majority of shooting victims (outside drug‑gang-on‑gang violence) are shot with their own weapon. Most homicides and assaults involving firearms are committed with a weapon possessed by the assailant (or a third party), while accidental self‑shootings and cases where victims are struck by their own firearm are a minority. Therefore the statement that the "bulk" are shot with their own weapon is unsupported.

claim: Congressman Jeff Denham "has agreed all illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute policy position — that Rep. Jeff Denham "has agreed all illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported." Public record shows Denham advocated stronger immigration enforcement and deportation of criminal aliens, but he has not been documented endorsing a blanket policy to detain, arrest, and deport every undocumented person. The claim overstates and misrepresents his positions, which were more nuanced and focused on criminal enforcement and border security.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because no specific election, jurisdiction, or metric of “close” is specified; determining whether an election was unusually close requires comparing its margin to historical norms for that race. Without that context the statement cannot be confirmed, so I mark it FALSE per the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: "We haven't had any legislation which took away one gun in the past 20 years from anybody in this country--not one."
rationale: This is false. Over the past 20 years numerous state laws—most notably extreme risk protection order (“red flag”) statutes and laws requiring surrender of firearms when someone is subject to a domestic violence protective order or convicted of disqualifying crimes—authorize courts or police to seize and have resulted in removal of firearms from individuals. Therefore legislation has in fact led to guns being taken away from people during that period.

claim: David Perdue did not support the 2014 farm bill that U.S. Sens. Isakson and Chambliss did.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Senators Johnny Isakson and Saxby Chambliss voted for and supported the Agricultural Act of 2014, while David Perdue was not a U.S. senator until January 2015 and therefore did not cast a Senate vote on the 2014 farm bill. Saying Perdue “did not support” it as a comparable congressional actor is inaccurate absent clear public statements opposing the bill.

claim: Says U.S. Senate opponent Tommy Thompson "personally made over $3 million" from a federal contract granted to his healthcare company, but left  9/11 first responders "without the care they were promised."
rationale: I found no credible evidence that former HHS Secretary and Wisconsin Governor Tommy Thompson personally pocketed over $3 million from a federal contract awarded to a healthcare company he owned, nor that his company was shown to have left 9/11 first responders without promised care. Thompson has held government office and later private-sector roles, but major investigative reporting and public records do not substantiate the specific $3 million payment or the asserted failure to provide care to 9/11 responders as described in the claim.

claim: Says that "the way to reach ‘herd immunity’ is for >70% of the population to get vaccinated."
rationale: This statement is an oversimplification. The herd‑immunity threshold depends on the pathogen's basic reproductive number (R0) and vaccine effectiveness; for many pathogens and for SARS‑CoV‑2 variants the required immune proportion can be below or well above 70%, and immunity can come from vaccination or prior infection. Saying >70% vaccinated is the way to reach herd immunity is therefore not universally correct.

claim: ICE está en Uvalde, Texas, "entonces los padres indocumentados tienen que temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos están vivos".
rationale: No hay evidencia creíble de que ICE realizara redadas de deportación en hospitales o en la escena de Uvalde; verificaciones periodísticas distinguen entre ICE y agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza/CBP que pudieron estar presentes para apoyo o control, pero no para deportar. Además, existen políticas que desalientan operaciones de inmigración en lugares sensibles como hospitales. Aunque es comprensible que padres indocumentados tuvieran miedo, la afirmación literal es inexacta.

claim: Says "11 straight years of no major hurricanes striking land" in the United States "bores a hole right through the whole climate change argument."
rationale: While it is true that the United States experienced a stretch of about 11 years (roughly 2006–2016) without a Category 3+ hurricane making U.S. landfall, using that short regional interval to dismiss the entirety of climate change is misleading. Climate change conclusions rest on long-term global trends and physical mechanisms (warming increases storm intensity, rainfall and sea-level rise), and a decade-plus of regional variability does not invalidate that evidence.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people living in abject poverty are women."
rationale: The assertion that 70% of people in abject (extreme) poverty are women is a widely repeated claim but is not supported by global data. Major sources (including UN Women clarifications and World Bank poverty statistics) find no robust evidence for a 70% share; estimates depend heavily on definitions and often show near parity or much smaller gender gaps. Therefore the flat 70% statement is inaccurate as a global fact.

claim: "Every engine manufacturer in the United States is now in the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is false. Major engine manufacturers and dozens of smaller firms are headquartered or operate facilities across many U.S. states (for example, Ford and General Motors in Michigan, Cummins in Indiana, Caterpillar in Illinois, Pratt & Whitney in Connecticut), so they are not all located in Texas. There is no evidence that every U.S. engine manufacturer has relocated to Texas.

claim: "In a very real sense, (Oklahoma has) flattened the curve. ... The number of cases in Oklahoma — it's declined precipitously."
rationale: The statement is time-dependent but gives no date or metric, so it cannot be reliably verified as written. Oklahoma did have periods when cases declined and other periods of resurgence during the COVID-19 pandemic, so the blanket claim that the state ‘flattened the curve’ and cases ‘declined precipitously’ is misleading without a specific timeframe and supporting time-series data.

claim: "George Floyd’s ‘murder’ filmed before COVID-19."
rationale: George Floyd was killed and the widely seen video was recorded on May 25, 2020. The COVID-19 outbreak and pandemic were already underway by that time (initial cases in late 2019 and the WHO pandemic declaration on March 11, 2020), so the filming did not occur before COVID-19. Therefore the claim is false.

claim: "101 utilities cut rates, credit GOP tax cuts."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and utility press releases following the 2017 GOP Tax Cuts and Jobs Act documented roughly 101 utilities announcing reduced customer bills or one‑time credits and explicitly citing the tax law as the reason. However, many of the announcements were temporary bill credits or small adjustments rather than permanent, across‑the‑board rate cuts, and counts depend on inclusion criteria.

claim: "In eighth grade math, we’ve fallen to ninth place."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported as stated: it does not specify which country, which assessment (e.g., TIMSS or PISA), or which year. International math rankings differ by test and year, and there is no clear, consistent evidence that 'we' (presumably the U.S.) specifically fell to ninth place in eighth‑grade math. Without a defined context, the statement cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: "South Korea sprays rioters with dye so they can be identified & arrested later."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that South Korean police routinely spray rioters with dye to mark them for later arrest. South Korea's documented crowd-control measures are water cannons (typically without dye), tear gas, pepper spray, and arrests; dye-marking has been reported in other jurisdictions (notably Hong Kong) but not as a standard South Korean practice. Given the absence of reliable reporting of such a tactic in South Korea, the claim is unsupported.

claim: The White House "created a fake set for (President Joe) Biden to get his booster shot. The entire Biden presidency is one giant charade."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the White House staged a fake set for Biden's booster; the event was documented with official photos, video, and staff accounts showing the vaccination took place in the White House medical clinic. Multiple independent fact-checkers and reporters investigated and found the claim unsupported. The additional assertion that the entire presidency is a "giant charade" is a subjective political opinion, not an established factual claim.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: The specific numbers in the claim are not supported by publicly available summaries from the federal Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) rebate program. CMS MLR reports give annual totals and per-consumer amounts that have varied year-to-year, but they do not corroborate a clear sequence of 13 million rebates last year plus another 8.5 million this summer averaging about $100 each across all 50 states. Without a clear source or matching CMS/state insurer data, the claim appears inaccurate or at least misleading.

claim: Says George LeMieux was one of two Republicans who voted for President Barack Obama's jobs bill.
rationale: George LeMieux served in the U.S. Senate from January 2009 to January 2011 and was not in office when President Obama’s major 'American Jobs Act' votes took place in 2011; there is no record of him being one of two Republicans to back an Obama jobs bill. Contemporary roll-call records and coverage do not list LeMieux as one of two GOP senators who voted for such a bill, and he generally voted with his party during his brief Senate tenure.

claim: "90 percent of fires in Arizona are human-caused."
rationale: This statement is an overgeneralization. While a majority of wildfires in Arizona are indeed human-caused, the exact share varies by year and by whether one counts all ignitions or only large wildfires, and official data do not uniformly support a blanket, timeless "90 percent" figure without a cited source or time period.

claim: The United States spent "2 trillion dollars to train and equip the Afghan military over the past 20 years. They fell in a week."
rationale: The US did not spend $2 trillion specifically to train and equip the Afghan military. Government oversight reports (SIGAR, DoD) place cumulative spending on training, equipping, and sustaining Afghan security forces at roughly $80–90 billion over two decades, while the commonly cited ~$2 trillion refers to the broader, overall cost of the Afghanistan war (operations, reconstruction, and veterans' care). The Afghan forces did collapse rapidly in August 2021 (over about a week to two weeks), but the spending figure in the claim conflates distinct categories of costs.

claim: Quotes Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things."
rationale: This sentence is a verbatim quote attributed to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from a recorded interview in which she said, “I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things.” The remark was widely reported and circulated in news coverage and social media as an authentic quote from the interview.

claim: "Gene Green is the NRA’s favorite Democrat in Congress. ... "It’s no wonder the congressman has a lifetime A rating from the NRA."
rationale: The statement bundles a subjective label and a verifiable rating. While Gene Green historically received high NRA scores (including a lifetime 'A' grade from NRA publications), calling him “the NRA’s favorite Democrat in Congress” is an opinion unsupported by objective evidence (no clear metric showing he was uniquely favored). Framing the opinion as a fact is therefore misleading.

claim: Originally "almost all models predicted" Dorian would hit Alabama.
rationale: Contemporary forecasts and model ensembles for Hurricane Dorian did not show that "almost all" models predicted a landfall in Alabama. Most operational models and the NHC forecast cone showed a track near Florida's east coast and then up toward Georgia/Carolinas, with only a minority of individual model runs suggesting a farther westward track into Alabama. Thus the blanket claim that almost all models originally predicted Alabama is inaccurate.

claim: "Across the country, $174 billion of the Recovery Act have been committed in its first 130 days."
rationale: This matches contemporaneous reporting from the Obama administration and independent fact-checkers: the administration reported about $174 billion in Recovery Act funds had been "committed" in the program's first 130 days. That figure was a tally of obligations, awards, and funding commitments reported on Recovery.gov rather than cash actually spent to recipients. The claim accurately reflects the administration's reported committed total for that period.

claim: "We are spending more on affordable housing than we're spending on Dix Park right now."
rationale: The statement is unverified because it omits critical context (which government or entity 'we' refers to and the specific time period and budget categories). Public records show Dix Park (Dorothea Dix Park in Raleigh) has attracted tens of millions in capital spending, while affordable housing spending is fragmented across city, state, federal, and nonprofit programs and can be higher or lower depending on scope. Without specified jurisdiction and timeframe, the claim cannot be confirmed and is therefore judged false.

claim: "We actually have this critical race theory moved into all our schools in Virginia."
rationale: The claim that critical race theory has been "moved into all our schools in Virginia" is false. There is no statewide K–12 curriculum mandating CRT in every Virginia public school; while some local districts or trainings may address systemic racism or include materials critics label as CRT, that does not establish a universal, mandated rollout across all Virginia schools.

claim: Says his proposed payroll tax cut "will mean an extra $1,500 in your pocket compared to if we do nothing."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as a blanket fact because whether a payroll-tax cut yields an extra $1,500 "in your pocket" depends on the size and duration of the cut, which payroll tax is changed, individual wages (and Social Security wage caps), and whether the employer share is affected or wages adjust. Without those specific parameters the dollar figure cannot be universally true and would only apply to limited income profiles under particular proposal details.

claim: I am the only U.S. Senate candidate who spoke out against bombing Syria, and who challenged Georgia’s governor and insurance commissioner over obstruction to the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: The assertion of being the sole U.S. Senate candidate to both oppose bombing Syria and challenge Georgia officials over ACA obstruction is demonstrably unlikely. Multiple Senate candidates have publicly opposed military action in Syria, and various Georgia politicians, activists, and candidates have criticized or legally challenged the governor and insurance commissioner over ACA implementation, so the claimed uniqueness is contradicted by public record.

claim: There were "$2 billion in earmarks in fiscal year 2012."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The House instituted an earmark ban in 2011 and reported zero House earmarks for FY2012, while the Senate used different rules and reported its own congressionally directed spending; totals and definitions vary, so a plain statement that there were “$2 billion in earmarks in FY2012” does not match how Congress reported earmarks that year. Because of differing definitions and reporting by chamber, the single $2 billion figure is not an accurate, verifiable summary.

claim: "No Republicans voted for" recent hikes in the income tax, payroll tax, capital gains tax, dividend tax and estate tax. "These taxes were all passed under … Obamacare."
rationale: The claim mixes correct and incorrect assertions. The Affordable Care Act did create new taxes affecting high earners (a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax on investment income and a 0.9% Additional Medicare payroll tax), and the major ACA measures were passed with essentially no Republican support—but the law did not raise ordinary marginal income tax rates for most taxpayers nor broadly increase the estate tax as stated. Saying “income tax, payroll tax, capital gains, dividend and estate tax hikes” were all passed under Obamacare and that no Republicans voted for those specific hikes is therefore misleading and partly false.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: The statement is misleading and likely incorrect because the totals and party split depend entirely on how one counts and attributes job changes to parties. BLS private‑sector employment series and multiple independent fact‑checks show different totals and splits when you vary the start/end dates or attribute jobs to presidential terms vs. congressional control; the claim presents one cherry‑picked tally as definitive. Because the methodology is unstated and sensitive, the numeric claim should not be treated as a verified fact.

claim: "Bill Gates is behind the monkeypox outbreaks."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill Gates or his foundations caused or engineered monkeypox outbreaks. Public health investigations attribute monkeypox spread to zoonotic transmission and human-to-human contact, and major health organizations have not identified any individual as responsible. Claims tying Gates to outbreaks rely on conspiracy thinking and misinterpretation of his public health funding.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The claim is too general and lacks a time frame or specific metric; COVID trends vary over time and by metric (cases, test positivity, hospitalizations) and across Wisconsin counties. Without current, state-level surveillance data showing a sustained multi-week decline across those indicators it is not supportable to say Wisconsin is "clearly" seeing a decline. Some areas or indicators may be down while others are flat or rising, so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "All the money the Department of Citrus has is paid for by the citrus growers. You don't save dollars by eliminating the Department of Citrus."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because funding for state departments of citrus (for example Florida's) is primarily from grower assessments but is not exclusively paid by growers. Such agencies can also receive federal grants, fees, and occasionally state appropriations or other revenue, so eliminating the agency could still affect public funds or federal programs. Moreover, even if growers pay most assessments, abolishing the department would change who bears costs rather than necessarily 'saving dollars' for government or overall economy.

claim: "Since 2010, Republicans have won unaffiliated voters in every general election."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. National exit polls and survey data show independents/unaffiliated voters backed Democratic candidates in multiple general elections since 2010 (for example, Obama won independents in 2012; Democrats carried independents in the 2018 midterms; Biden won independents in 2020), so Republicans have not won unaffiliated voters in every general election over that period. Independent/unaffiliated support has varied by year and contest rather than consistently favoring Republicans.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school in the United States "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law."
rationale: There is no U.S. Supreme Court ruling that uses the quoted phrasing that public schools “will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law.” The Court has long held under the Establishment Clause that public schools may not endorse or inculcate religious doctrine (e.g., school-sponsored prayer or devotional Bible reading) but they may teach about religions in a neutral, academic context. The claim misstates and overgeneralizes existing case law.

claim: As a Member of Congress, Chris Murphy "was raking in $1 million in salary."
rationale: This is false. U.S. Members of Congress receive a statutory salary (around $174,000 per year for rank‑and‑file members in recent years), and no senator or representative receives a $1 million annual congressional salary. While members may report other income (investments, book advances, spouse income), the congressional pay itself is far below $1 million.

claim: Sarah Palin "already has more executive experience" than Barack Obama and Joe Biden "combined."
rationale: The claim lacks a time frame and is misleading: currently and in the historical record both Barack Obama and Joe Biden have substantially more executive experience (each having served as U.S. President; Biden also as Vice President) than Sarah Palin, who served a single partial term as Alaska governor. The assertion would only have been true in 2008 before Obama or Biden had held executive office, so without that context the statement is false.

claim: "President Obama himself attempted to filibuster Justice Alito, who now sits on the Supreme Court."
rationale: A filibuster is a Senate procedure carried out by senators; a sitting U.S. President cannot filibuster. Barack Obama was not President during Samuel Alito's 2005–2006 confirmation (he became President in 2009) and, while he opposed Alito as a senator, he did not personally attempt a filibuster. Thus the specific claim that 'President Obama himself attempted to filibuster Justice Alito' is false.

claim: "Barack Obama will somehow manage to add more than $8 trillion to the national debt, which is more debt than the 43 presidents who held office before him compiled together."

Says for otherwise healthy people "experiencing mild to moderate respiratory symptoms with or without a COVID-19 diagnosis … only high temperatures kill a virus, so let your fever run high," but not over 103 or 104 degrees.
rationale: The statement is misleading and factually incorrect. While fever is part of the immune response and can inhibit some pathogens, viruses are not universally “killed” simply by high body temperature, and deliberately allowing a fever to run up to 103–104°F is not a recommended universal treatment strategy — high fevers can cause harm (dehydration, organ stress, febrile seizures) and vulnerable people require earlier intervention. Clinical guidance advises treating based on patient comfort, age, underlying conditions, and specific clinical signs rather than aiming to let fevers reach a high set point to 'kill' viruses.

claim: "We’ve got an average of 5,600 soldiers committing suicide. That’s about 20 a day."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and misleading. Numerically, 5,600 deaths per year equals about 15 per day, not 20; and the term “soldiers” is ambiguous—official U.S. data show far fewer active-duty service-member suicides (a few hundred per year) while recent VA reports put veteran suicides roughly in the 5,000–6,000 per year range (about 15–17 per day), not 20.

claim: "98 percent of small businesses make less than $250,000" and would not see a tax increase under Barack Obama's plan.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Whether 98% of ‘small businesses’ earn under $250,000 depends on how ‘small business’ and ‘make’ are defined (gross receipts vs. taxable income), and fact‑checks show the 98% figure is an imprecise summary of IRS data. Likewise, Obama’s proposal targeted individual high incomes (above $250,000) and did not categorically exempt all entities defined as small businesses — some pass‑through owners with incomes near the threshold or affected by other tax provisions could see changes. Because the statement conflates different definitions and asserts a categorical effect, it is false as stated.

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: I found no reliable record or transcript showing Mika Brzezinski uttered that exact line. While Brzezinski has criticized tech figures and discussed media influence on air, the quoted sentence appears to be a misquote or altered clip rather than a documented statement from her show. Given common circulation of edited excerpts, the claim as written is not supported by verifiable sources.

claim: Says only about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.
rationale: The figure is a substantial understatement. Since 9/11 U.S. military killed in action totals across Iraq, Afghanistan and related operations number in the thousands (roughly 6–8k), and Texas — with a large military population and proportional share of service members — accounts for well more than 250 KIA; state and memorial casualty lists record several hundred to over a thousand Texans killed in post‑9/11 combat. Therefore the claim that only about 250 Texans have been killed in action is false.

claim: "Less than 500 people a year killed by all rifles combined" and "4,000 a year killed by illegals."
rationale: Official U.S. data sources (FBI UCR and CDC mortality statistics) show homicides involving rifles/long guns are a small fraction of firearm homicides and have typically been under 500 per year in recent years, so the first part is broadly consistent with available data. The second part—that 4,000 people a year are killed by "illegals"—is not supported by crime-data analyses or federal reports; researchers and government data do not attribute anywhere near 4,000 homicides per year to undocumented immigrants, and immigrants generally have lower homicide rates than natives. Because the claim bundles a roughly accurate rifle figure with a false and unsupported immigration number, the overall claim is false.

claim: The Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. "cannot account for creating one single job."
rationale: Audits and reporting showed WEDC had issues documenting and verifying the number of jobs tied to some incentives, but they did report and claim creation/retention of thousands of jobs — auditors found record-keeping and performance-measurement weaknesses rather than proof that the agency created zero jobs. Therefore the absolute claim that WEDC "cannot account for creating one single job" is misleading and false.

claim: Quotes Albert Einstein as saying "I fear the day technology will surpass human interaction. The world will have a generation of idiots."
rationale: This quotation is widely misattributed to Albert Einstein but there is no evidence he ever said or wrote it. The phrasing appears in late 20th/21st-century internet sources and is not found in Einstein's published works, letters, or reputable biographies; established fact-checkers have debunked the attribution.

claim: "Republicans are attempting to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s Presidential Ballot in 2012."
rationale: There is no evidence that the Georgia Republican Party or leading Republican officials mounted a successful or official effort to remove Barack Obama from the 2012 Georgia presidential ballot. At most, isolated private challengers (often linked to the 'birther' movement) filed lawsuits in various states that were routinely dismissed; courts and election officials in Georgia kept Obama on the ballot.

claim: Says Scott Walker "has taken money away from internet expansion in our state."
rationale: The claim is too vague and not supported by clear, specific public records tying Scott Walker to a deliberate, documented action of "taking money away from internet expansion" in a particular state. State budget and policy changes affecting broadband are specific and publicly reported; without a named program, year, or veto/amendment, there is no clear evidence to verify the broad accusation. Because the assertion lacks context and corroborating details, it cannot be upheld as fact.

claim: "Nancy Pelosi Removed From Benefit for ‘Being So Drunk She Couldn’t Stand Up’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable news reporting that Nancy Pelosi was removed from a benefit for being 'so drunk she couldn't stand up.' Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers have not corroborated this claim, which appears to originate from unverified social-media and tabloid sources. Given Pelosi's continued public appearances and the absence of official confirmation, the allegation is unsupported and likely false.

claim: "An attack on a healthy 22-year-old homosexual man would be more protected under the law than an attack on an eight-year-old child."
rationale: The claim is false as an absolute statement. Most jurisdictions have specific criminal statutes and enhanced penalties for offenses against children (child abuse, sexual offenses involving minors) that often carry equal or greater punishment than general hate‑crime enhancements for attacks on adults; while some places add hate‑crime enhancements for sexual orientation, that does not make an assault on a healthy 22‑year‑old categorically "more protected" than an assault on an eight‑year‑old.

claim: There are "many unanswered and obvious questions" about the 2001 death of a staff member of Joe Scarborough.
rationale: The assertion that there are "many unanswered and obvious questions" implies unresolved official uncertainty about the 2001 death of a staffer for Joe Scarborough. Public records and contemporary news reporting indicate the death was investigated at the time, with no evidence that led to charges or an official finding of foul play; subsequent reporting has repeatedly debunked claims of a suspicious unresolved homicide. While some commentators continue to pose speculative questions, those do not reflect an official or evidentiary consensus of many unanswered, obvious facts.

claim: Wall Street megabanks that received bailouts in 2009 now get taxpayer-funded advantages not available to community banks in Ohio.
rationale: Large banks that received government support in 2008–09 continue to benefit from taxpayer-backed privileges (an implicit "too-big-to-fail" backstop and easier access to Federal Reserve emergency liquidity and other government-sponsored facilities) that reduce their funding costs and risks compared with small community banks. Those specific advantages (implicit guarantees, routine access to certain Fed programs and market confidence) are not generally available to community banks in Ohio.

claim: The census "for years and years and years, decades, has asked, ‘Are you a citizen of the United States of America?’"
rationale: If the claim is taken to mean the decennial short-form census has routinely asked “Are you a citizen?” for decades, that is false: the decennial census last included a direct citizenship question in 1950. However, long-form surveys and the ongoing American Community Survey (ACS) have asked about citizenship or naturalization status for many decades, which likely causes confusion.

claim: Says photo of beaten woman is Aracely Henriquez, a pregnant woman who George Floyd assaulted during an armed robbery.
rationale: Independent fact-checkers examined the viral image and found no evidence it depicts Aracely (or Aracely Hernández/Henriquez) as a victim of George Floyd; the photo has been misattributed online. While Floyd had prior criminal convictions, reliable reporting and court records do not support the specific claim that the shared photo shows the alleged robbery victim.

claim: Says Michelle Obama said Florida shooting "is clearly our president’s fault."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Michelle Obama saying the Florida shooting “is clearly our president’s fault.” Major news coverage and transcripts of her public remarks about shootings (including the 2018 Parkland incident) show she condemned gun violence and urged civic engagement, but she did not attribute blame in that quoted phrasing to the president. The claim appears to be a misattribution circulating on social media.

claim: "I can send every qualified person to a four-year college in their state for $150 billion."
rationale: The claim is implausible as stated because simple arithmetic with publicly known figures exceeds $150 billion. The U.S. high‑school graduating cohort is roughly 3.5–4 million students per year and average in‑state public four‑year tuition is on the order of ~$8–10k per year; multiplied over four years that is roughly $32–40k per student, which implies about $112–160 billion just for one incoming cohort’s tuition and does not cover room, board, support services, or existing college students. The claim also gives no timeframe or definition of “qualified person,” and ignores capacity and state funding variation, so $150 billion is an underestimate or at best a very incomplete figure.

claim: A person’s immune system "tanks" after their second COVID-19 vaccine dose.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a person’s immune system ‘tanks’ after the second COVID‑19 vaccine dose. Clinical trials and real‑world studies show vaccines stimulate immune responses and increase protection; at most some people have short, mild side effects and rare immune‑mediated adverse events. Small, transient changes in blood lymphocyte counts have been observed briefly after mRNA vaccination, but these are temporary and do not represent overall immune collapse.

claim: "Most young Americans right now, they’re not covered" by health insurance.
rationale: National data since the Affordable Care Act show that most young Americans do have health insurance — through employers, parents' dependent coverage, Medicaid or marketplace plans — and uninsured rates for typical 'young adult' age groups are well below 50%. Therefore the statement that 'most young Americans...they’re not covered' is inconsistent with broadly reported survey and Census trends. The claim is misleading or incorrect as phrased.

claim: Obama "says he'll raise taxes on electricity."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of Barack Obama saying the explicit promise “I’ll raise taxes on electricity.” He supported policies like cap-and-trade and emissions regulations that critics said could increase electricity costs, but that is not the same as a direct pledge to impose an electricity tax. Ads and opponents often conflated potential price effects from regulation with a stated promise to raise an electricity tax.

claim: Says Mike DeWine "flip-flopped on the gun issue and has earned an F from the NRA."
rationale: The claim mixes a subjective charge of 'flip-flopped' with an objective rating that is incorrect. Public records and NRA scorecards historically do not show Mike DeWine receiving an 'F' from the NRA; as a long-time Republican officeholder he has generally received favorable or mixed ratings, though he has supported some gun-safety measures as governor which critics call a reversal. Thus the specific factual assertion that he 'has earned an F from the NRA' is not supported.

claim: "Since that famous day in February where the governor campaigned with Barack Obama on behalf of the stimulus program, 211,000 Floridians have lost their jobs."
rationale: The claim ties a precise job-loss figure (211,000) to an unspecified “famous day in February” and to a governor campaigning with Obama, but no reliable labor data or authoritative reporting supports that exact number being the net job loss in Florida since a clearly defined February date. Labor statistics are published monthly by the BLS and Florida state agencies and do not corroborate this precise, date-linked figure; the statement is ambiguous about which February and timeframe and appears to conflate political events with a specific employment change. Because the claim lacks verifiable sourcing and a clear temporal anchor, it cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: Says Marco Rubio took "three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives" during the 2016 Senate election.
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that Marco Rubio personally received exactly $750,000 from ‘‘fossil fuel executives’’ during the 2016 Senate race. Campaign-finance totals for the energy sector are reported in different categories (individual executives, corporate PACs, trade associations) and public FEC summaries do not clearly support that precise figure tied solely to executives. Without a clear breakdown or citation to FEC filings showing that specific amount from named executives, the claim is not substantiated.

claim: "In six years, (U.S. Rep. Gary) Peters introduced zero bills that became law."
rationale: False. Gary Peters served in the U.S. House from 2009–2015 and congressional records and independent fact-checkers show he had at least one sponsored measure that was enacted or had provisions he sponsored included in laws during that span, so the blanket statement that he introduced zero bills that became law over six years is incorrect.

claim: Rare is the president "who's passed more legislation, who's done more things than what we've done, between the executive orders and the job-killing regulations that have been terminated."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad comparative claim that cannot be substantiated. Presidents do not 'pass' legislation — Congress does — and many presidents (e.g., FDR, Lyndon Johnson, others) presided over far greater legislative output and transformative statutes. Executive orders and regulatory rollbacks are different tools than enacted legislation, and describing terminated regulations as uniformly 'job-killing' is subjective and disputed.

claim: "CNN-NPR photojournalist Jade Sacker was embedded with antifa leader" during the U.S. Capitol attack.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a CNN or NPR photojournalist named Jade Sacker was 'embedded with' an antifa leader during the U.S. Capitol attack. Major news reporting and law enforcement investigations found no organized antifa leadership directing the riot, and similar social-media allegations tying journalists to antifa have been debunked.

claim: Says detained immigrant parents separated from their children at the border are being charged "as much as $8 a minute to call their children."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and investigations of phone charges in U.S. immigrant detention show high variability but do not substantiate a routine rate as high as $8 per minute. Typical per‑minute rates cited by news outlets, NGOs, and congressional investigations were generally well below $8 (often cents to a few dollars per minute), with additional one‑time fees and PIN charges sometimes increasing overall cost but not creating a standard $8/minute charge.

claim: Says Leah Vukmir "wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault."
rationale: I found no credible reporting or primary-source evidence that Leah Vukmir wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault. Major local and national coverage of Wisconsin legislative scandals and related statements by colleagues do not attribute such a leniency plea to Vukmir. The claim appears uncorroborated and may conflate events or actors.

claim: Forty percent of union members voted Republican in 2008.
rationale: 2008 national exit-poll data show that the Republican nominee received roughly 39–40% of the vote among union households/members, so stating that 40% of union members voted Republican is a reasonable, rounded summary. The exact figure depends on whether sources report 'union members' or 'union households,' but the Republican share was about 39–40%.

claim: "The minimum number of infrastructure (needs) in Atlanta is $900 million."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: it gives a single dollar figure ($900 million) without defining timeframe, scope, or source. Publicly available estimates of urban infrastructure needs vary widely by category (transportation, water, schools, etc.) and are often in the billions for a major city like Atlanta, so asserting a minimum of $900 million as a definitive figure is misleading and not verifiable as stated.

claim: "The current (agriculture) commissioner allowed tainted beef to be sent to school cafeterias."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written because it names no specific agriculture commissioner, jurisdiction, timeframe, or evidence. There are no widely reported credible investigations showing a current agriculture commissioner knowingly allowed tainted beef into school cafeterias. Food safety and meat inspections are typically handled by USDA/FSIS and state inspection agencies, and a deliberate allowance of tainted meat would be a major documented scandal.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi said, "Employers cutting hours is a good thing. It then gives that person time to pursue their dreams and passions."
rationale: Multiple fact-checkers investigated this quotation and found no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi ever made that statement; it appears to be a misattributed or fabricated social-media meme. The quote is inconsistent with verified Pelosi remarks during debates over employer hours and the Affordable Care Act and was rated false by established fact-checking organizations.

claim: Says Tom Barrett plans "to spend $100 million on a trolley that goes barely two miles on the east side of Milwaukee."
rationale: As Milwaukee mayor Tom Barrett supported construction of the city streetcar (known as The Hop), whose initial starter line was roughly two miles long and whose publicly reported cost was on the order of $100–125 million. Saying he planned to spend about $100 million on a trolley that goes barely two miles accurately reflects the core facts, though the commonly cited cost is slightly higher than $100 million.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: The claim is not supported by reliable reporting and lacks necessary context (no date or mechanism for the alleged raise). Wisconsin gubernatorial pay is set by statute/commission and there is no clear evidence that Scott Walker personally received a one-time $7,300 pay increase; fact-checks and public salary records do not corroborate the specific figure. Without a precise timeframe or source the assertion appears inaccurate.

claim: "After one year, Tennessee’s students made their biggest single-year jump in achievement ever recorded in the state."
rationale: The claim is presented as an unqualified statewide record but lacks specifics about which year, grade levels, or assessment. Tennessee did report notable post-pandemic gains on some standardized tests, and officials sometimes described certain subject- or grade-specific increases as unusually large, but those statements were qualified and not a clear, unambiguous ‘biggest ever’ across all statewide achievement measures. Without a specific assessment and timeframe this broad statement is not supported.

claim: "Over 40 percent of small and mid-size banks that loan money to small businesses have been wiped out since Dodd-Frank has passed."
rationale: The claim is not supported. While the number of small and mid‑size (community) banks has fallen since the financial crisis and since Dodd‑Frank (2010), the statement that “over 40% … have been wiped out” is a misleading oversimplification: many institutions exited via mergers/acquisitions or failed during the 2008–2010 crisis, and the decline percentage and causal attribution to Dodd‑Frank are inaccurate. Regulatory compliance likely contributed to consolidation for some banks, but it is not the sole or clearly quantified cause.

claim: "The Railroad Commission of Texas has nothing to do with railroads."
rationale: The Texas Railroad Commission does not regulate railroads today; its core duties are regulation of oil and gas production, pipelines, natural gas utilities, and surface mining. The agency's name is historical — railroad oversight was removed long ago and rail regulation is handled by other state and federal bodies.

claim: "Oregon school districts are directing 24 percent of their food budgets to purchase local foods. That’s the highest percentage in the country."
rationale: I cannot verify that Oregon school districts direct 24% of their food budgets to local foods or that this is the highest share nationally. National Farm to School data and state surveys report varying figures depending on year and how “local” is defined, and no consistent, authoritative source confirms Oregon uniquely at 24% as the top state. Without a specific year or data source the claim is unsupported.

claim: Canadian-born Ted Cruz "has had a double passport."
rationale: While Ted Cruz was born in Canada and therefore had Canadian citizenship by birth in addition to U.S. citizenship through his father, there is no reliable evidence he ever concurrently held both a U.S. and a Canadian passport. He also formally renounced his Canadian citizenship in 2014, so the claim that he "has had a double passport" is misleading or unsupported.

claim: Says Bubba Watson wrote a viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter.
rationale: There is no well-documented instance of professional golfer Bubba Watson authoring a widely shared, viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter. Public discourse and media coverage about BLM statements from public figures more commonly reference NASCAR driver Bubba Wallace, so this claim likely conflates the two 'Bubba' figures. Without verifiable reports tying Watson to a viral BLM post, the claim is not supported.

claim: Rhode Island voters are moving away from the Democratic party to non-affiliation
rationale: The claim overstates available evidence. While unaffiliated registration has grown modestly in many states (including Rhode Island) over the past decade, Rhode Island Democrats have generally remained the largest registered group and there is no clear sign of a large, rapid exodus from the Democratic Party into non‑affiliation; changes reported in official registration data are gradual and involve new registrants and shifts from multiple parties. Therefore the blanket statement that voters are "moving away" is not supported without more specific, recent registration data showing a sustained net outflow from Democrats to unaffiliated status.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative DOJ position that consent decrees “don’t work” and routinely cause immediate crime increases. The Department of Justice has frequently used consent decrees and pattern-or-practice litigation to reform police agencies and has cited improvements in training, accountability and reductions in misconduct; academic and agency studies show mixed results on crime trends after reforms rather than a consistent immediate rise. While some critics and individual officials have argued consent decrees can be ineffective or have unintended consequences in specific cases, that is not a settled DOJ-wide finding that matches the quoted blanket claim.

claim: "A family of four can make up to $88,000 a year and still get a subsidy for health insurance" under the new federal health care law.
rationale: Under the Affordable Care Act, premium tax credits (subsidies) are generally available to households with incomes between 100% and 400% of the Federal Poverty Level. For a family of four, 400% of the poverty level in recent years has been roughly in the mid‑$90,000s, so an $88,000 household income is below that cap and would typically qualify for a subsidy. There are exceptions (e.g., Medicaid expansion rules, offer of affordable employer coverage, immigration status) that can affect eligibility.

claim: "I did very well with young people in Ohio, Massachusetts, California."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no speaker, timeframe, election, or metric for what “did very well” means. Youth support varies widely by state and by election cycle; without specific exit polls, survey results, or vote shares for young voters in Ohio, Massachusetts, and California the assertion cannot be confirmed. Given the lack of supporting data and specificity, the statement cannot be treated as factual.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "doesn’t even have any oil for America."
rationale: The Keystone XL pipeline was designed to carry crude oil from Alberta through the United States to Gulf Coast refineries, so it would supply oil to U.S. refinery capacity and therefore the U.S. market. While some refined products from that crude might be exported, it is incorrect to say the pipeline would deliver "no oil for America."

claim: "The richest 1 percent of America will get a bigger tax cut through this bill than the family income of the average family here in Central Texas."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it fails to specify which legislative bill and which precise measures are meant, and it mixes a national aggregate (the richest 1%) with a local income comparison without defining terms. Typical fact‑checks require the bill text, an estimate of the average tax cut for the top 1%, and a clear local income figure (median or mean household income in Central Texas) to compare; those details are missing. Without that data, the claim cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "Toomey crossed party lines… to stop gun sales to suspects on the terror watch list."
rationale: This claim overstates Toomey’s record. While Senator Pat Toomey has worked across the aisle on some gun-policy measures (notably the 2013 Manchin–Toomey background-check effort), he did not famously ‘cross party lines’ to back a blanket ban on gun sales to people solely because they appear on the terror watch list; he has repeatedly voiced due-process concerns about using watchlists to deny gun purchases. Public roll calls and his statements show he opposed 'no‑fly, no‑buy' style proposals without stronger procedural safeguards.

claim: Hillary Clinton "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her."
rationale: The statement presents a precise, timeless baseline (47% of the country against her) but public-opinion figures for Hillary Clinton varied by time, poll, and question wording. While some polls at points in 2015–2016 showed roughly mid-40s unfavorable ratings, there is no single authoritative measure that she “starts off” with exactly 47% opposed nationwide. The claim therefore overstates and mischaracterizes the variable polling evidence.

claim: The snow is government-generated or fake.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that ordinary snow is manufactured or faked by governments. Snow forms through well-understood meteorological processes (condensation and freezing of atmospheric moisture) and observed weather patterns match those processes; while cloud seeding and artificial snowmaking exist, they are limited, localized interventions and do not amount to government-produced widespread 'fake' snow. The claim conflates rare local activities with a global, systematic program, which is implausible and unsupported.

claim: More private-sector jobs were created in the second year of the Obama administration than in the eight years of the Bush administration.
rationale: BLS payroll data show that the cumulative private‑sector job gains over the full eight years of the George W. Bush presidency exceed the private‑sector job gains recorded in President Obama’s second year. One year of job gains under Obama did not surpass the total private‑sector job creation across Bush’s two terms. The claim therefore is not supported by official employment statistics.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: The claim blends two different trends in a way that is misleading. While overall violent crime rates fell from their 1990s peaks and were lower through much of the 2010s, homicides and some violent-crime measures spiked in 2020–2021 and remain elevated in some places, so it’s inaccurate to say we are uniformly in a time of “historically low” violent crime. It is true that the number of civilian-owned firearms is at historically high levels (and some surveys show rising household ownership recently), but the phrasing overstates uniformity across crime categories and ownership measures.

claim: The U.S. has "over $62 trillion in unfunded liabilities."
rationale: The claim is misleading. There is no single official U.S. accounting that lists “over $62 trillion” in unfunded liabilities; that figure arises from particular long‑horizon, present‑value calculations that aggregate different measures (Social Security, Medicare, federal debt, federal employee pensions, etc.). Official sources (CBO, Treasury, Social Security and Medicare Trustees) report different metrics and time horizons, and estimates vary widely depending on assumptions.

claim: Says Mitt Romney opposes requiring employers to cover contraception and would eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood.
rationale: This accurately reflects Mitt Romney’s publicly stated 2012 positions: he criticized the federal contraception mandate on employers and said he opposed requiring employers to provide contraception coverage, and he said he would seek to end federal funding for Planned Parenthood. Both positions were repeatedly stated during his presidential campaign.

claim: "A portion of everything you pay A.A.R.P goes directly to the Democratic Party."
rationale: AARP does not funnel a portion of every membership payment directly to the Democratic Party. AARP is organized as nonprofits (including a 501(c)(4) and a charitable 501(c)(3)) and uses dues for services, advocacy, and operations; its political activity is conducted through a separate PAC that makes limited, itemized contributions and historically gives to both parties. There is no mechanism by which 'everything you pay' is automatically sent to the Democratic Party.

claim: Says she is a registered nurse.
rationale: The claim contains no named subject or supporting evidence, so I cannot verify that any particular person is a registered nurse. Without a specific person and jurisdiction, the statement is unverified and must be treated as false under the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: "Florida ranks first in the nation for access to free prekindergarten."
rationale: The claim is misleading because rankings vary by year and by how “access” is measured. Florida’s Voluntary Prekindergarten (VPK) program is large and the state is often among the leaders in state-funded pre-K enrollment, but other states (e.g., Oklahoma, Georgia) have routinely ranked at or above Florida on measures of universal access/enrollment; Florida is not unambiguously first across standard metrics. Without a specific year or definition of “access,” the blanket statement that Florida ranks first is not supported.

claim: Says "Claire McCaskill receives the second-most contributions from insurance companies in the entire Senate."
rationale: This claim is not supported by public campaign finance data. OpenSecrets/FEC contribution records do not show Claire McCaskill as the second-largest recipient of insurance-industry money across the Senate in commonly cited datasets, and rankings change by cycle and definition of 'insurance contributions.' Without a specified time period or data source the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Thanks to President Trump and Republican leadership, the number of people collecting food stamps has declined by more than two million."
rationale: The statement asserts a causal link that is not supported: while SNAP caseloads did decline by several million in the 2017–2019 period as the economy improved and some administrative/policy changes occurred, enrollment later rose with the COVID-19 recession in 2020. There is no clear evidence that the decline was primarily or solely 'thanks to President Trump and Republican leadership,' so the claim is misleading.

claim: Says an investigative report concluded Ken Cuccinelli "should have been prosecuted" for disclosure violations, but Virginia's law was too weak.
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence that an investigative report explicitly concluded Ken Cuccinelli “should have been prosecuted.” Contemporary coverage documents probes and identified disclosure problems or technical violations, but reporting generally said prosecutors or ethics officials declined to bring criminal charges because of legal limits or insufficient grounds rather than a report formally calling for prosecution. Because I cannot identify the cited report or a direct quote recommending prosecution, the precise claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "The government will be infiltrating" personal text messages.
rationale: The claim states a definitive future action without specifying which government, legal authority, or timeframe and lacks supporting evidence. While some governments have programs or legal processes to access communications in specific cases (e.g., with warrants or via targeted hacking), there is no verified, general plan that all governments will broadly "infiltrate" personal text messages. Encryption and legal protections in many countries also limit blanket interception.

claim: Says Kanye West got 40,000 votes in the presidential election in Kentucky.
rationale: This is false. Kanye West was not a major vote-getter in Kentucky in the 2020 presidential race and received far fewer votes than 40,000 there; his nationwide total in 2020 was only on the order of tens of thousands and he was on the ballot in only some states, with Kentucky showing only a small number of write-ins for him in official results. The claim overstates his support in Kentucky by a large margin.
